# Sūrah al-Nisāʾ (Chapter 4) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:1

> O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women. And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties. Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Single Origin That Undercuts All Claims of Rank**

This opening places the entire sūrah on a single foundation before any law is given. Mankind is addressed together — *yā ayyuhā al-nās* — not as tribes, clans, or ranks, but as the offspring of one soul and its mate. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may know one another”* (49:13), and again *“He created you from a single soul”* (39:6). By beginning legislation about orphans, women, inheritance, and marriage with creation, the verse teaches that law does not invent equality; it remembers it. Every claim that one lineage is higher than another collapses at the first sentence. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the purpose of reminding the audience of a common parentage at this exact point is to soften hearts for the duties that follow, because a person who feels his link to others is more likely to guard their rights. That psychological link matters here: the sūrah will command protection for the weakest — the orphan girl, the widow, the heir with a small share — and it grounds those commands not in pity but in kinship. If all spread from one soul, then wronging another is wronging one’s own extended family.

**From One Soul and Its Mate to Countless Men and Women**

The phrase *min nafs wāḥidah* — from a single soul — is understood by the vast majority of exegetes to mean Adam, with the mate understood as Ḥawwāʾ. The Arabic word *nafs* is grammatically feminine while *zawj* is masculine, yet commentators do not see a problem in the pairing, because the terms describe roles in creation rather than grammatical genders. What the verse stresses is sequence: singularity, then duality, then multiplicity. One became two, and two became countless. That pattern mirrors how the Qur’an elsewhere describes the spreading of humanity as a sign of divine power. Some modern readers have asked whether *minhā* — from it — means from the same substance or from the same kind. The majority read it as indicating that the mate was created from the same nature as the first soul, consonant with the usage of *min anfusikum* in other passages to mean of your own kind (3:164; 9:128; 16:72). Al-Rāzī observes that the Qur’an does not narrate the mechanism of Ḥawwāʾ’s creation in detail; the ḥadīth literature mentions creation from a rib, but the Book itself keeps the language brief, keeping attention on the moral point rather than the biology. That brevity is deliberate: the verse wants the reader to see a shared root before seeing any difference.

**Why Taqwā Comes Twice**

The command *ittaqū* — be mindful, guard yourselves — appears twice in one verse, and both times it points to God. *Ittaqū rabbakum* opens the verse, and *wattaqū Allāh* returns near its middle. In Arabic, *taqwā* carries the sense of placing a shield between oneself and what one fears; the Qur’an uses the same root for protecting oneself from the Fire and for keeping duty to kin. Here the shield is awareness of the Lord who created and who watches. Repetition in such a short space is not decoration. It frames the social duties that sit between the two commands — the appeal to one another in God’s Name and the honouring of womb-ties — as acts of God-consciousness, not merely good manners. The verse also shifts from *rabb* — Lord, Sustainer — to *Allāh*, the divine Name that gathers all attributes. The first is the Lord who creates and spreads; the second is the Name by which people adjure one another. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that the second *ittaqū* prepares the reader for the specific rights that follow through the sūrah; without that inner guard, the coming laws about property and marriage would be treated as technicalities to be evaded.

**In Whose Name You Appeal to One Another**

The clause *alladhī tasāʾalūna bihi* — in Whose Name you appeal to one another — captures a living practice of the Arabs. People would say, I ask you by God, or I adjure you by God, to settle a debt or to grant a need. The Qur’an does not abolish that speech but sanctifies it, reminding the speaker who the Name belongs to. If you already use God’s Name to ask others for your rights, then be mindful of Him when you are the one being asked. The placement matters: the verse first ties humanity to one origin, then ties daily transactions to God’s Name, making every request and every agreement a place where piety is tested. Another reading vocalises *tasāʾalūna* with a light *sīn* and reads *al-arḥām* in the genitive, yielding and the wombs — do not cut family ties — which many reciters transmitted. The two readings converge in meaning: guard God and guard kinship, because both are invoked in oaths and both are easily violated when advantage beckons. The verse presents God and kinship side by side to show that betrayal of kin is not a private fault; it breaks a tie that was sworn by God’s Name.

**The Womb-Tie and the Name of Mercy**

*Al-arḥām* — family ties, literally wombs — comes from the same root as *raḥmah*, mercy, and the divine Name *al-Raḥmān*, the Compassionate. That shared root was not lost on the first audience. A womb is the first home a human knows, and mercy is the first treatment he receives. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs devotion to God with goodness to kin, as in *“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents and relatives”* (4:36). This verse elevates the tie further by placing it immediately after the divine Name people use in their oaths. A well-known ḥadīth, transmitted widely and cited by commentators on this verse, says that *al-raḥim* — the womb-tie — is derived from *al-Raḥmān*, and that God says, whoever maintains it, I will maintain him, and whoever cuts it, I will cut him off. The sūrah will return to relatives repeatedly, assigning them shares, presence at distribution, and kind speech. Here the principle is given before the detail: honour the tie because it shares a name with mercy, and because your own existence passed through it. To be mindful of Allah and then to sever what He linked is a contradiction the verse refuses to allow.

**Watchful Over You Even When No One Else Is**

The verse closes with *inn Allāha kāna ʿalaykum raqībā* — surely Allah is ever Watchful over you. The Name *al-Raqīb* gathers seeing, guarding, and reckoning. It is not only that God knows what people do behind closed doors; it is that He keeps watch like a guardian keeps watch over a ward. That closing fits the sūrah’s character as a book of law for the vulnerable. Guardians of orphans, holders of dowries, distributors of estates — all handle property that the owner cannot yet claim or cannot defend. No court can see every handover. The verse answers that gap with a single assurance and warning: the Watcher is already present. Elsewhere the Qur’an says *“Allah is Witness over all things”* (4:33; 58:6), and the same idea returns at the end of the orphan test in verse 6 with *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6). That thread links creation to accountability. The God who spread countless men and women from one soul is not distant from the countless transactions among them; He observes each one, and what is entrusted to people in this world will be measured with precision in the next.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:2

> Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺, and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables, nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own. For this would indeed be a great sin.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Restoring What Was Never Yours**

The command is direct: give orphans their wealth. The Arabic *ātū al-yatāmā amwālahum* does not say hold it longer or invest it indefinitely; it says hand it over when the owner is ready. An orphan in Qur’anic usage is a child who has lost the father who would have guarded his property, and the community steps in as trustee, not as new owner. The verse treats that trust as real ownership by the child. The guardian is a keeper, and the wealth remains titled to the one who cannot yet defend it. That is why the same sūrah will later say *“Test the orphans until they reach a marriageable age”* (4:6) and only then return what is theirs. Between command and return lies a period of management, and this verse governs its ethics. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs justice to orphans with justice in measure and worship itself, as in *“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans”* (4:36), showing that how the strong handle the property of the weak is a measure of faith, not a footnote to it.

**Exchanging the Bad for the Good**

The prohibition *wa lā tatabaddalū al-khabīth bi al-ṭayyib* — do not exchange the worthless for the valuable — was explained by early exegetes in very concrete terms. A guardian might take a healthy animal from the orphan’s herd and replace it with a sick one from his own, or take sound coin and give back debased coin, keeping the difference. Others read it more broadly as swapping a bad practice for a good one: replacing the good trust of preservation with the bad act of consumption. Both readings point to the same habit of dressing up taking as trading. The Qur’an names that trick by calling one side *khabīth* — foul, worthless — and the other *ṭayyib* — good, wholesome. The labels stick to the act, not only the object. A transaction that looks equal on the surface is exposed by what each party actually receives. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse forbids even a supposedly balanced swap if the guardian’s portion remains mixed and self-preferential, because the power imbalance makes fair valuation impossible. The orphan cannot negotiate, so the law closes the door to negotiation entirely and commands simple restoration.

**Do Not Mix Their Wealth With Yours to Consume It**

The second prohibition *wa lā taʾkulū amwālahum ilā amwālikum* — nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own — addresses a subtler form of taking. Instead of an open exchange, the guardian merges accounts, spends freely from the combined sum, and tells himself the orphan’s share is still in there somewhere. The Qur’an calls that eating — *akl* — a word it uses elsewhere for illicit gain, as in *“Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29). Eating suggests both pleasure and disappearance; what is eaten does not return. The verse warns that mixing makes eating easy because boundaries blur. After this verse was revealed, some guardians became so scrupulous that they separated food, pots, and even cooking fires, fearing any mixing would count as sin. The hardship that followed was eased by a later clarification: *“If you intermingle with them, they are your brothers”* (2:220), which permits shared living with fairness, while this verse forbids shared living as a cover for consumption. The distinction is intention and accounting. Living together remains allowed; living off the orphan does not.

**Why the Warning Ends With a Great Sin**

The clause *innahu kāna ḥūban kabīrā* — for this would indeed be a great sin — uses a rare word, *ḥūb*, which the linguists connect with a grave crime that weighs heavily. By calling the act a great sin rather than merely a mistake, the verse places misappropriation of orphan wealth among major wrongs, alongside the other major sins the sūrah will later say to avoid to earn forgiveness for lesser ones (4:31). The occasion of revelation recalled by commentators sharpens the point: a boy whose parents had died was under his uncle’s care; when he grew and asked for his property, the uncle refused, and the matter was brought to the Prophet ﷺ. The verse came down to order return and to name refusal as more than stinginess. It is easy to treat a child’s property as a family buffer, especially when the child has no advocate. The verse answers that ease with a weighty noun. What feels like a small domestic adjustment is, in the ledger that matters, a heavy crime. That naming matters because guardians often reassure themselves that no one will notice; the Qur’an says the act is already noticed and already classified.

**Guardianship as a Test of Character**

The verse does more than regulate a transaction; it defines what guardianship means in this faith. A guardian is not rewarded with the orphan’s wealth for his trouble, except for the modest provision the next verses will allow to a poor guardian who is doing real work (4:6). The standard case is service without compensation, witnessed at return (4:6), and watched by God (4:1). That structure turns guardianship into a visible proof of *taqwā*, which is exactly how the sūrah opened. If humanity shares one origin and God is watchful over all, then the treatment of a child who cannot hire a lawyer becomes the clearest mirror of whether that awareness is real. The Qur’an elsewhere promises double reward for justice to the weak and severe penalty for exploiting them, as in *“Those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth consume fire into their bellies”* (4:10). This verse sets the rule; that later verse sets the consequence. Together they frame the guardianship period as a moral testing ground where the adult is the one being tested, not the child.

**A Principle Beyond Orphans**

Although the verse addresses orphans, its three prohibitions outline a broader ethic of entrusted wealth. Do not substitute the inferior for the superior, do not blur ownership to make use easier, and do not rename taking as keeping. Those moves appear in many other relationships where one party holds for another — partnerships, endowments, public treasuries, and care for those who lack legal capacity. The Qur’an’s choice to name the sin *kabīr* — great — signals that the issue is not the amount but the structure. Taking advantage of entrusted power corrupts the social fabric in a way that ordinary overspending does not. The verse therefore trains the reader to ask, whenever he holds what is not his, whose name remains on it while it is in his hand. If the answer is someone weaker, the command still stands: give it, keep it separate, and keep it whole. The next verse will extend that concern from property to marriage, showing that the same vulnerability can be exploited in a different contract, and that the same vigilance is required there.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:3

> If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their ˹due˺ rights ˹if you were to marry them˺, then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four. But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice, then ˹content yourselves with˺ one or those ˹bondwomen˺ in your possession. This way you are less likely to commit injustice.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Justice to Orphans Before Permission for Marriage**

This verse links two matters that seem separate — care for orphans and the number of wives a man may take — by the single concern of justice. The opening *wa in khiftum allā tuqsiṭū fī al-yatāmā* — if you fear you might fail to give orphan women their due rights — recalls the previous verse’s warning about mixing and consuming their wealth, now in the specific case where the orphan is a girl under a guardian’s authority. A guardian who also acts as marriage guardian could exploit that double role: marry the girl to himself with a reduced dowry, marry her off without her consent to secure her wealth, or block her marriage entirely to keep control of her property. The Qur’an interrupts that line of temptation with a clear exit: if you fear you cannot be just there, marry other women. The permission that follows is therefore not an encouragement to add wives but a redirection away from a particular injustice. Al-Ṭabarī records this as the core occasion, transmitted from ʿĀʾishah, who explained that men holding orphan girls would covet their beauty and wealth and then short-change them in dowry and upkeep. The verse tells such a man to leave that girl alone and choose elsewhere, where consent and valuation can be more honestly assessed.

**Two, Three, or Four — A Limit, Not a Target**

The phrase *mathnā wa thulātha wa rubāʿ* — two, three, or four — sets an upper bound, not a recommended number. Before this sūrah, there was no Qur’anic ceiling stated in this form; pre-Islamic custom allowed a man to take many wives without fixed limit. By capping the number at four, the Qur’an limited what was previously open-ended, just as it elsewhere limited retaliation, divorce pronouncements, and waiting periods. The choice of two, three, then four with the conjunction *wa* was understood by grammarians to mean any number up to four, singly or in combination, not eight or nine. The same sūrah later adds the inner condition that makes the outer number meaningful: *“You will never be able to be perfectly just between wives, even if you try”* (4:129). That later verse does not cancel this one, but it deepens its warning. A man who can manage justice outwardly — in support, housing, time — may still fall short in affection, and he is told to remain aware of that limit. The sūrah’s aim across both verses is to keep marriage inside the capacity for fairness, whether fairness to the orphan girl not yet married or to the wives already taken.

**When One Is the Just Choice**

The condition *fa in khiftum allā taʿdilū fa wāḥidah* — but if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice, then one — makes monogamy the safeguard for those who doubt their ability to be equitable. Justice here was explained by the early authorities to cover material provision, division of nights, and decent companionship, not only coin. The Qur’an does not treat the number of wives as a display of status; it treats it as a bearing of responsibility, and it advises the lighter burden when the heavier one risks wrongdoing. The clause *aw mā malakat aymānukum* — or those bondwomen in your possession — addressed a seventh-century institution that the Qur’an elsewhere encourages to dissolve through manumission and marriage, specifying that such women, though entitled to kind treatment, did not carry the same financial and conjugal claims as a free wife (4:25). The verse’s logic is practical: a man who cannot afford the obligations of a free marriage should not incur them and then fund them from an orphan’s property, which the previous verse had already forbidden. That economic thread connects verses 2 and 3 directly: overextension of dependents tempts a man to reach for wealth that is not his.

**The Meaning of Not Committing Injustice**

The verse closes with *adhālik adnā allā taʿūlū* — this way you are less likely to commit injustice. The verb *taʿūlū* was read by most early lexicographers as to act unjustly or to deviate, related to *ʿawl* as oppression, while a minority read it as to be overburdened with dependents. Both senses converge: limiting wives keeps a person nearer to justice and farther from being overwhelmed. That dual sense matches the sūrah’s broader pattern of keeping law inside human weakness. Two verses later it will say *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak”* (4:28), and here it already lightens the load by telling the anxious man to take one. The Qur’an does not treat the desire for more as shameful in itself; it treats the risk of wronging others through that desire as the decisive factor. A man is asked to judge his own case honestly before acquiring new duties. That self-assessment — am I able to be just? — is itself an act of piety, because it puts the rights of yet-unmet wives ahead of present preference.

**A Reading That Protects Consent and Dowry**

The widespread report from ʿĀʾishah ties this verse to verse 127, where the Qur’an returns to the same group: *“They ask you about women. Say, Allah answers your query concerning them, and what is recited in the Book about orphan girls whom you do not give what is ordained for them though you desire to marry them”* (4:127). That later verse was presented as clarification: men were withholding the prescribed bridal gift from orphan girls under their care while wanting to keep them. Read together, verse 3 and verse 127 draw a consistent boundary: the guardian’s authority over property does not extend to discounting the woman’s due at marriage. The dowry belongs to her, as verse 4 will immediately confirm: *“Give women their due dowries graciously”* (4:4). The connection also shows how the Qur’an reforms a power asymmetry step by step. First it orders return of wealth, then it redirects marriage away from exploitation, then it secures the woman’s personal gift, ensuring that at no point does the guardian’s stewardship become ownership of the person. The sequence is intentional and cumulative.

**Justice as the Sūrah’s Steady Measure**

This verse makes justice — *qisṭ* and *ʿadl* — the measuring stick for family formation. The same standard will recur for inheritance shares where male and female each receive a fixed portion (4:7, 4:11–12), for treatment of wives where kindness is commanded even when affection wanes (4:19), and for arbitration where mediators are sent from both families (4:35). By opening the marriage discussion with a warning about orphans, the verse teaches that entry into marriage is not only about attraction or alliance but about aptitude for fairness. That aptitude is not assumed; it is to be examined. The Qur’an pairs permission with caution in a way that keeps the law humane: what is allowed is immediately bounded by whether it can be done justly, and what is just is measured by whether the weakest party’s right remains intact. A man who hears *“two, three, or four”* and hears only an allowance has misheard; the sentence began with fear of injustice to a girl who could not argue her own dowry, and it ends with the choice that stays nearest to avoiding that wrong.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:4

> Give women ˹you wed˺ their due dowries graciously. But if they waive some of it willingly, then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Gift That Belongs to the Woman Herself**

The command *ātū al-nisāʾ ṣaduqātihinna niḥlah* — give women their dowries graciously — establishes a property right that cuts against the customs around it. The word *ṣaduqah* is not a price for the woman; its root *ṣ-d-q* signals truthfulness and sincerity, as though the payment proves the seriousness of the commitment. *Niḥlah* deepens that sense: a free gift, given warmly and without grudging, not a bargain extracted under pressure. Earlier practice allowed a guardian or family to intercept the bridal gift, or to trade women in ways that diverted wealth away from the bride. This verse closes those paths by making the woman herself the owner. The Qur’an elsewhere confirms that wealth a woman receives through dowry, inheritance, or earnings remains hers to manage, as reflected in the very next laws where women are named as heirs alongside men (4:7) and where their property is not to be handed to those unable to manage (4:5) without proper terms. Al-Ṭabarī reads *niḥlah* as a gift with no return expected, which distinguishes it from a loan or a conditional transfer. Once given, it belongs to her in the full legal sense.

**Why the Language of Joy Matters**

The second half of the verse permits a husband to benefit from part of the dowry only if the wife offers it — *fa in ṭibna lakum ʿan shayʾ minhu nafsan* — if they waive some of it willingly, with a contented soul. The condition *ṭibna ... nafsan* is deliberate. It is not enough that she says yes while under pressure; her soul must be at ease. Classical commentators stressed that the gift must be without coercion, shame, or manipulation, because a yes extracted by persistence is not a good will. The Qur’an then adds *fa kulūhu hanīʾan marīʾan* — then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience. The pair *hanīʾ* and *marīʾ* was understood as food that is pleasant going down and wholesome afterward, with no aftertaste of guilt. That food image was chosen for a reason. Wealth taken wrongly is elsewhere described as fire in the belly (4:10); wealth given gladly is described as wholesome enjoyment. The same act — a husband receiving from his wife’s property — changes its moral nature entirely depending on whether her heart consented. The wording trains the reader to ask not only did she give, but how did she feel while giving.

**From Guardian Control to Personal Ownership**

Read after verse 3, this verse completes a movement from stewardship to ownership. Verse 2 ordered guardians to return orphan property; verse 3 told them not to marry orphan girls to discount their dowries; this verse names the dowry as the woman’s personal entitlement and makes its transfer to the husband dependent on her uncoerced will. That sequence dismantles a system where a guardian could control both wealth and marriage. The Qur’an also addresses practices where widows were inherited like property or where a father kept his daughter’s dowry. By naming women directly — *al-nisāʾ* — as recipients, the verse bypasses intermediaries. It does not say give it to their families or to those who arrange their marriages; it says give it to the women. The sūrah will later reinforce that a husband who has given a great amount and then wishes to replace one wife with another may not take back any of it, *“even if you have given the former a stack of gold”* (4:20), and it asks *“how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment?”* (4:21). Those later verses show that the dowry is not a deposit to be reclaimed when the relationship ends; it is a settled gift that the woman retains.

**What Coercion Looks Like in Practice**

The condition of willingness invites careful attention to real life. Consent is not only a signature; it is a state of heart at the moment of giving. Pressure can be open — threats, anger, withdrawal — or quiet — repeated hints, appeals to loyalty, or making the wife feel that refusal equals disloyalty. The verse’s wording excludes all such pressure, because *ṭīb al-nafs* cannot coexist with fear or embarrassment. Jurists drew from this a practical rule: if it becomes clear that the wife gave while feeling straitened, the husband should return it, even if she voiced consent. The principle extends beyond dowry to any gift between spouses. The Qur’an elsewhere describes marital wealth in terms of mutual consent generally, as in *“not in fornication”* but through lawful marriage sought *“with your wealth”* (4:24), and the same consent standard governs trade in *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but trade by mutual consent”* (4:29). The dowry rule is thus one instance of a larger ethic where lawful enjoyment depends on the other party’s genuine willingness, not merely on a formal yes.

**A Free Gift, Not a Fee**

The root of *ṣaduqah* deserves attention because it corrects a common misunderstanding. The dowry is not a purchase price, and the size of the gift does not measure the worth of the woman. The Qur’an elsewhere calls the marital bond *“a firm commitment”* (4:21), *mīthāq ghalīẓ*, language used for covenants of gravity. A gift that seals such a covenant is naturally significant, but its meaning comes from sincerity, not from amount. The Prophet ﷺ accepted dowries that were substantial and ones that were modest, including teaching verses of the Qur’an where wealth was lacking, which shows that what matters is the genuine transfer of something valued. Verse 4 does not fix an amount; it fixes an owner. That shift from amount to owner explains why the verse immediately allows the wife to give back a portion if she wishes. Once ownership is secure, generosity can flow either way without confusion about entitlement. What the law prevents is confusion in the other direction — treating her entitlement as his asset to collect.

**The Wholesome Enjoyment That Follows**

The permission to enjoy what is freely given teaches that property in marriage is not a zone of constant suspicion. The sūrah will later set careful limits for those unable to manage wealth (4:5) and testing for orphans (4:6), but here it speaks about the ordinary case where a wife, content and unpressured, chooses to share. In that case the Qur’an does not require witnesses or paperwork; it says *eat it as pleasant and wholesome*, language that signals moral ease. Two ideas meet in that ease: her autonomy is preserved, and his use is then blessed. The pairing matters for the sūrah’s overall vision of family wealth, where men and women each have shares (4:7, 4:11–12), each has obligations, and kindness is commanded alongside calculation. A household where the dowry was honored freely becomes a place where later sharing is also more likely to be free. The verse therefore does more than settle a single transfer; it shapes a habit. It trains the husband to receive only what is given with an untroubled heart on the other side, and it trains the community to see a woman’s wealth as hers to keep, to keep whole, or to give — as she herself decides.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:5

> Do not entrust the incapable ˹among your dependants˺ with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you—but feed and clothe them from it, and speak to them kindly.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wealth Made to Support, Not to Scatter**

The verse opens with a prohibition that sounds like withholding, but its aim is preservation. *Wa lā tuʾtū al-sufahāʾ amwālakum allatī jaʿala Allāhu lakum qiyāman* — do not entrust the incapable among your dependants with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you. The noun *qiyām* — support, standing, establishment — describes wealth by its purpose. It is what keeps a household upright, what keeps obligations met and needs covered across time. The Qur’an elsewhere calls wealth *“a means of support”* precisely to teach that spending is not only about desire but about keeping a life standing. Al-Rāzī notes that the phrase *allatī jaʿala Allāhu lakum qiyāman* reminds the owner that wealth is not purely his creation; it is entrusted by God to keep people standing, and stewardship includes not placing it where it will be quickly wasted. The verse therefore does not deny the eventual rights of dependants; it orders a better way of delivering those rights, as the second half immediately shows with feeding, clothing, and kind speech.

**Who Are the Incapable**

The term *al-sufahāʾ* — the incapable, often translated the feeble-minded — was explained by the early authorities as those unable to manage property soundly, whether due to youth, inexperience, weak judgment, or a condition that impairs prudence. The word is masculine plural, and commentators who considered that grammar concluded it does not single out women as such. That matters, because verses 2 and 4 have just secured women’s ownership of property, and verse 6 will return that property to orphans when they show sound judgment, regardless of gender. To read *sufahāʾ* as women in general would contradict that immediate context, and the sūrah’s later inheritance laws that name women as obligatory heirs (4:7, 4:11–12). The sounder reading, held by the majority including al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, is that the term covers any dependant whose judgment is not yet reliable for guarding wealth — minors, those with cognitive impairment, or those whose habits show they would scatter funds quickly. Some added that the term also warns against handing financial control to those outside the faith who would not observe the limits the sūrah is laying down, such as the prohibition of consuming wealth illegally (4:29), though the primary reference remains within the household.

**Your Wealth and Their Wealth**

The phrasing *amwālakum* — your wealth — has been discussed carefully. Does it mean the guardian’s own wealth, or the wealth of the incapable that is legally theirs but presently in the guardian’s hands? Both readings have support, and both lead to the same care. If it is your wealth, the verse warns a provider not to hand the household’s capital to a member who will dissipate it, because the whole household will then need help. If it is their wealth held in trust, the verse warns not to hand it over prematurely, which would simply undo the protection the sūrah has been building since verse 2. The sūrah will clarify that orphans’ wealth must be returned only after testing and when sound judgment appears (4:6), with witnesses and with *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) as the closing audit. This verse sits between those two points and supplies the principle that timing matters as much as ownership. To recognize that someone owns a thing is not the same as deciding he is ready to manage it today. The law can affirm the first while delaying the second for his own protection.

**Feed, Clothe, and Sustain From It**

The alternative the verse commands is not to withhold care but to provide it directly: *wa arzuqūhum fīhā wa aksūhum* — feed and clothe them from it. The preposition *fīhā* — from it, literally in it — was noted by grammarians to suggest spending from the wealth itself while keeping its capital intact as a standing support, investing and drawing yield rather than liquidating all at once. The sūrah elsewhere describes wealth as a trust to be grown and guarded, not merely stored or spent. The practical image is a guardian who, instead of handing a lump sum to a young heir who would spend it in weeks, maintains the property, uses its produce to feed and clothe the heir, and hands over the principal when maturity and judgment align. That pattern also appears in the rule for witnesses at handover (4:6) and the warning against hasty consumption before the orphan grows up (4:6). The food and clothing here are therefore not a reduction of the dependant’s right; they are its faithful delivery in installments, matched to capacity, until full delivery becomes safe.

**Speak to Them Kindly**

The third element, *wa qūlū lahum qawlan maʿrūfā* — and speak to them kindly — adds a dimension that law alone cannot enforce. *Qawl maʿrūf* is speech that is decent, familiar, and recognized as good — words that acknowledge the person while managing the delay. A dependant told you cannot yet control this wealth hears that as a verdict on his maturity; the verse requires that the message be given with dignity, explanation, and reassurance. The Qur’an pairs this speech elsewhere with kindness at distribution time to non-heirs present (4:8), and with equitable speech when imagining one’s own children left behind (4:9), showing that how the community speaks in financial transactions is part of justice itself. Ibn ʿĀshūr observes that the command to speak kindly prevents two harms at once: the guardian becoming harsh or contemptuous toward the incapable, and the dependant feeling humiliated and then acting recklessly to prove independence. Words that keep the relationship intact make the waiting period humane. Without them, the law may be observed while the bond is damaged; with them, the law protects both wealth and kinship.

**Keeping Law Inside Human Weakness**

This verse keeps the sūrah’s legislation humane by acknowledging weakness without exploiting it. The same chapter that will say *“humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens”* (4:28) already acts on that truth here. Weak judgment is not mocked, it is managed with provision and kindness until strength appears. The approach differs from two equal errors: handing everything over immediately out of sentimentality, which harms the weak by giving him what will ruin him, and withholding everything indefinitely out of mistrust, which harms him by denying him his right. The middle path — preserve the standing support, provide ongoing care from its yield, and accompany the delay with decent words — honours both ownership and welfare. It also prepares the reader for the testing that follows. The next verse will set the time and the test for return — reaching a marriageable age and showing *rushd*, sound judgment — and it will require that return to be documented and witnessed. Together, verses 5 and 6 build a complete guardianship ethic: keep wealth standing, meet daily needs from it, speak well while you wait, and restore fully when the person is ready.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:6

> Test ˹the competence of˺ the orphans until they reach a marriageable age. Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment, return their wealth to them. And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up ˹to demand it˺. If the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation; but if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision. When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses. And sufficient is Allah as a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Testing Before Returning**

The command *wa abtalū al-yatāmā* — test the orphans — makes return conditional on evidence, not on age alone. A child reaches a marriageable age — *ḥattā idhā balaghū al-nikāḥ* — which the jurists linked to physical maturity and the capacity to assume family duties, but that alone does not prove financial competence. The Qur’an therefore adds a second threshold: *fa in ānastum minhum rushdan* — if you feel they are capable of sound judgment. *Rushd* in this context was explained as the ability to preserve wealth, to distinguish profitable from wasteful, and to avoid being easily deceived. Some authorities required that *rushd* be shown in both financial handling and general uprightness, while others focused on financial prudence as the immediate concern. The verse does not leave the test abstract. Guardians were expected to observe how the young person handled small amounts, fulfilled commitments, and responded to temptation. That practical testing turns guardianship from passive custody into active preparation. The orphan is not simply waited for; he is trained, supervised, and then trusted with his own property when his conduct shows he can keep it.

**Do Not Eat It Before They Can Ask**

The warning *wa lā taʾkulūhā isrāfan wa bidāran an yakbarū* — do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up to demand it — exposes a temptation that grows as the test nears its end. A guardian who senses the handover approaching may spend quickly, telling himself that small withdrawals will not be noticed or that the orphan will not know what was there. The words *isrāf* — wastefulness — and *bidār* — haste — name two distinct motives: spending beyond need, and spending ahead of time to pre-empt the claim. The Qur’an links both to eating — *akl* — as it did in *“do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables”* (4:2) and *“consume nothing but fire into their bellies”* (4:10), keeping the image of illicit gain as consumption that will later be consumed as fire. The clause *an yakbarū* — before they grow up to demand it — is psychologically precise. The sin depends on the victim’s inability to speak; once he can speak, the opportunity closes. By naming that window, the verse teaches guardians to treat the approaching adulthood not as a deadline to exploit but as a trust to complete. The best guardian is one who, as the account grows, feels more cautious, not more entitled.

**When the Guardian May Take and When He Must Refrain**

The rule *wa man kāna ghaniyyan fa al-yastaʿfif, wa man kāna faqīran fa al-yaʾkul bi al-maʿrūf* — if the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation; but if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision — balances two risks. On one side is the well-off guardian who might justify a fee for his effort; the verse asks him to abstain — *yastaʿfif* — to be chaste, to hold back, preserving the trust with no deduction. On the other side is the poor guardian who does real work maintaining property, farming, trading, or managing a share, and who may need support while doing so; he is permitted *bi al-maʿrūf* — according to what is recognized as fair. Early jurists differed on measuring that fair amount — some tied it to the wage for similar work, others to what suffices for need — but all agreed it must be known, moderate, and not a hidden share. The sūrah elsewhere commands *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29) and permits only what is by mutual consent; here, where consent cannot be fully given by a child, the law substitutes a standard of fairness judged by the community and watched by God. The guardian’s own wealth therefore sets the starting point for his attitude: the richer he is, the more he should give freely; the poorer he is, the more he must keep his taking measured and open.

**Call In Witnesses at Handover**

The instruction *fa idhā dafaʿtum ilayhim amwālahum fa ashhidū ʿalayhim* — when you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses — secures the moment of return. A handover without witnesses leaves both sides exposed: the orphan may later claim he received less, or the guardian may be accused of shortfall. Witnesses close that ambiguity and give both parties a record. The practice also appoints the community as guarantor of transparency. The Qur’an elsewhere requires witnessing for debts and bequests, as part of a larger system where property moves with documentation, and this verse brings orphans inside that system. The command does not suggest distrust of every guardian; it normalizes a procedure that protects the honest as much as it restrains the dishonest. In a society where much property was livestock, coin, and household goods without formal registries, two witnesses at the moment of transfer were the registry. Modern documentation fulfills the same purpose when it achieves the same clarity: the orphan knows what was returned, the guardian can show what he returned, and others can confirm it.

**Sufficient Is Allah as Reckoner**

The verse closes with *wa kafā bi Allāhi ḥasībā* — and sufficient is Allah as vigilant Reckoner. *Ḥasīb* gathers counting, reckoning, and sufficing; He counts precisely and He suffices as judge when human accounting is imperfect. That closing follows every stage that came before: testing, sensing sound judgment, refraining from hasty eating, taking only what is fair, and calling witnesses. After all visible steps are taken, the final audit belongs to God, who saw the small transfers no witness recorded and the intentions behind the timing. The same divine Name returns throughout the sūrah as a refrain for entrusted wealth, matching *“Allah is ever Watchful over you”* (4:1) at the opening and *“Allah is a Witness over all things”* (4:33) later. The repetition creates a frame: what was entrusted by creation is measured by reckoning at return, and the one who kept watch at the beginning is the one who reckons at the end. For the honest guardian, the phrase is reassurance; his care, done for God’s sake without fee, has a witness who misses nothing. For the careless, it is warning that the ledger is already complete.

**From Guardianship to Ownership Without Harm**

Taken together, verses 2 through 6 trace a full arc of trust. Return the wealth (4:2), do not exploit marriage to discount it (4:3–4), do not place it prematurely in weak hands while still meeting daily needs with kindness (4:5), and then, after testing, return it fully, without haste, with witnesses, and with God as the final auditor (4:6). The step *“test until they reach a marriageable age”* ensures that age is not a mechanical trigger and that judgment is not assumed; the phrase *“if you feel they are capable of sound judgment”* makes the guardian answerable for his perception, not only for a date. That balance protects both sides: the orphan from being handed what would ruin him, and from being held indefinitely under tutelage when he is ready. The sūrah therefore teaches a guardianship that ends well. The last image is not a child forever dependent, but a young adult, tested and found capable, receiving his property back in the presence of witnesses, with a clear record and a sufficient Reckoner over all.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:7

> For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave—whether it is little or much. ˹These are˺ obligatory shares.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Fixed Share for Both Sexes**

This verse establishes a principle that prior custom had denied: both men and women have a fixed portion in what parents and close relatives leave. The Qur’an states it twice in one sentence, once for men and once for women, with the same wording *naṣīb mafrūḍ* — an obligatory share — closing the verse. Repetition here is legislation. In the pre-Islamic order only adult men who could bear arms and produce revenue were counted as heirs; women and young children were excluded on the ground that they did not fight and did not earn. The Qur’an set that reasoning aside and assigned entitlement by kinship, not by military utility. Commentators link the revelation to the case of a widow with daughters who were left without support because male relatives took the estate. By saying *whether it is little or much*, the verse prevents the dismissal of small estates as not worth sharing; even a modest amount carries the same obligation. The Qur’an elsewhere confirms the same ethic with precise fractions for daughters and parents (4:11) and for spouses and siblings (4:12), but this verse is the foundation: no heir of either sex is erased from the ledger.

**Why the Verse Repeats the Same Formula**

The parallel phrasing — *lil-rijāl naṣīb ... wa lil-nisāʾ naṣīb* — does more than grant; it equalises the language of entitlement. Both have a *naṣīb*, a share that is known and assigned, not a gift left to generosity. The closing *naṣīban mafrūḍan* was read by grammarians as emphasizing obligation from above; *farḍ* in the Qur’an denotes what God fixes as duty, as in the limits that will be called *ḥudūd Allāh* two verses later (4:13–14). By naming women’s portion with the same noun and the same adjective as men’s, the verse teaches that the share does not depend on the goodwill of male relatives after death; it arrives as law. That point mattered because the initial reception of these laws met resistance. Reports recall companions who were stunned that women and children who did not ride out for booty should inherit a significant fraction from fathers and husbands. The verse answers that surprise by rooting the share not in contribution to war but in closeness of womb and in divine decree. What God has made obligatory is not open to being bargained away by custom.

**Little or Much — No Estate Too Small to Divide Justly**

The clause *mimmā qalla minhu aw kathur* — whether it is little or much — closes a loophole that frugality might have opened. In a large estate, sharing is expected; in a small one, heirs might argue that division would scatter what needs to stay together, or that the widow and daughters can be provided for informally while the core property stays with the men. The Qur’an rejects that economy of excuse. If the amount is small, the share remains, and the division must still be just. That rigor protects the most vulnerable heirs precisely when the temptation to consolidate is strongest. The sūrah will reinforce this by ordering that even bystanders at distribution be offered something and spoken to kindly (4:8), and by warning guardians to imagine their own helpless children left behind (4:9). The principle across those verses is consistent: presence creates a claim, kinship creates a share, and the size of the pot does not nullify either. A community that honours small shares trains itself to honour large ones without fraud.

**An Obligatory Share, Not a Favour**

The words *naṣīban mafrūḍan* carry legal weight that the sūrah will specify in fractions two verses later. Jurisprudence built on this verse a whole science of inheritance — *ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ* — where fixed heirs receive fixed portions after debts and bequests are settled. That science later contributed to the development of algebra, because its calculations require precise proportional reasoning, a historical detail that shows how a verse about family rights generated tools for mathematics. The deeper point is theological. Upon death, property returns to God, *“and to Allah belongs the heritage of the heavens and the earth”* (3:180), and He redistributes it by His own ordinance. The heirs do not inherit because the deceased gifted it to them; they inherit because God assigned it. That is why the verse says the shares are obligatory — imposed, not suggested — and why verses 13 and 14 will frame obedience to these limits as the difference between Gardens and Fire. What seems like a domestic settlement is, in the Qur’an’s account, an act of worship.

**The Case That Brought the Principle Down**

Early reports connect this verse to a specific family: a man died leaving a wife and daughters, and his brothers took the estate, saying women and children who did not fight should get nothing. The wife complained to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came down, followed by the detailed shares of 4:11–12. Whether that exact story covers every instance or one of several similar cases, the pattern is clear: a new rule arrived to correct a living wrong, not to pose a theoretical ideal. That setting explains the verse’s brevity and force. No argument is offered about women’s capacities; the verse simply assigns a share and calls it obligatory, leaving debate aside. The brevity also explains why the verse does not yet give fractions; it first breaks the old rule that exclusion is permissible, then the next passage quantifies. That two-step pedagogy — first the principle, then the portions — helps listeners absorb a social revolution without treating it as optional advice. Once the principle was accepted that women as such have a share, the fractions could be heard as detail rather than shock.

**From Principle to Practice Across the Sūrah**

This verse opens a corridor that runs through the rest of the opening third of al-Nisāʾ. Verse 8 will ask those dividing to remember the non-heirs present; verse 9 will ask them to judge as they would want others to judge their own children; verse 10 will warn that consuming orphans’ wealth is eating fire; verses 11–12 will set the arithmetic for children, parents, spouses, and siblings; verses 13–14 will promise reward and warn of disgrace for crossing the limits; and verses 19–21 will close the circle by forbidding inheritance of women themselves and forbidding seizure of dowries. The common thread is that property and persons are not to be taken by the strong from the weak under cover of custom. By naming men and women side by side in the same sentence with the same noun, verse 7 makes that thread visible from the start. It does not argue for equity in the abstract; it assigns shares and calls them obligatory, and it leaves the community to learn the rest — how to calculate, how to speak kindly while calculating, and how to live with a Watchful Reckoner over every division (4:6).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:8

> If ˹non-inheriting˺ relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution, offer them a ˹small˺ provision from it and speak to them kindly.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When Those Without a Fixed Share Are Present**

This verse imagines a scene that still repeats at every estate division: relatives who do not inherit a fixed portion, along with orphans and the needy, are present when property is being apportioned. The law has already assigned obligatory shares to primary heirs in the verse before (4:7) and will quantify those shares in detail after (4:11–12), but this verse pauses at the moment of presence itself. *Wa idhā ḥaḍara al-qismata ulū al-qurbā wa al-yatāmā wa al-masākīn* — if they are present at the distribution — does not say if they have a legal claim under inheritance law; it says if they are there. Presence alone generates a duty of generosity. The Qur’an elsewhere makes presence a moral trigger for giving, as in the command to feed the poor who appear, and the sūrah will repeat the same ethic of kind speech in that context. The point is that a legal settlement is also a human gathering, and how the gathering is handled forms part of the law’s spirit. To distribute with cold precision while those who hoped are sent away empty would keep the fractions correct while injuring the community the fractions were meant to serve.

**Offer Them a Provision From It**

The command *fa arzuqūhum minhu* — offer them a provision from it — was understood in two complementary ways. Some exegetes read it as a recommendation to give a small amount from the estate itself before the fixed shares harden into entitlements, a voluntary gift from the heirs after the estate is known. Others read it as a charge upon the heirs to provide food or a modest gift from what they have received, especially when the estate includes items that can be shared without breaking the prescribed portions. Both readings agree that the gift is not a fixed inheritance share that rivals the ordained portions; it is a discretionary provision that honours presence without overturning the law. The sūrah’s phrase *“whether it is little or much”* (4:7) already guarded small estates from being swallowed; this verse guards small hopes from being ignored. The amount is not specified, leaving room for circumstance — the size of the estate, the number present, the closeness of kin, and the degree of need. That lack of a fixed fraction is not vagueness; it is flexibility that lets generosity fit the moment while law fits the structure.

**The Status of the Command**

Commentators differed on whether this verse remains legally binding, was abrogated by the fixed shares of 4:11–12, or refers to bequests made before death up to one-third of the estate. Many authorities, including al-Ṭabarī, held that it remains recommended and praiseworthy, even if widely neglected, and that the choice to give and how much rests with the legal heirs. Others treated it as abrogated in the strict legal sense but preserved as an ethical ideal. The sūrah itself seems to anticipate that neglect by adding the second half — speak to them kindly — which would be unnecessary if the gift were always given. That addition suggests the verse aims to shape behaviour even where the gift is small or where the estate cannot bear much. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs giving with gracious speech and warns against following charity with hurtful reminders (2:263). Here the same pairing appears in reverse: if you give, give with kindness; if you cannot give much, at least speak well. The moral weight therefore does not rest on the amount; it rests on not making those present feel erased while others receive.

**Speak to Them Kindly**

The clause *wa qūlū lahum qawlan maʿrūfā* — and speak to them kindly — uses the same phrase the sūrah used for the incapable dependant who must be provided for without being handed premature control (4:5). *Qawl maʿrūf* is speech that is decent, familiar, and recognized as good — words that acknowledge dignity while explaining limits. In this scene, that speech does practical work. A relative who expected a share, an orphan who hoped for help, a needy neighbour who came because he heard there was property — each will watch the division and interpret silence as rejection. A clear, gentle word that explains what is being given and why, that promises future help, or that invokes God’s blessing on what they do receive, softens the moment and preserves ties. The sūrah will commend such speech again when it asks guardians to imagine their own children left behind (4:9) and to speak equitably. Across those verses, speech is treated as part of wealth management, not as an afterthought. How people are addressed while property moves is part of justice.

**A Distribution That Remembers the Community**

The verse sits deliberately between the principle that men and women have obligatory shares (4:7) and the detailed arithmetic for those shares (4:11–12). By placing generosity to bystanders between principle and calculation, the sūrah teaches that law and largesse belong together. The fixed shares protect heirs from being denied; this provision protects the wider circle from being forgotten. That balance reflects the Medinan context in which al-Nisāʾ was revealed, where a new community of migrants and hosts was learning to handle wealth without clan seizure. The Qur’an elsewhere praises those who give relatives, orphans, and the needy from what they love (2:177), and it lists providing for orphans and the needy among the signs of true piety. Here that same triad — relatives, orphans, needy — reappears at the very table where estates are divided, as though to say: let your first act with new wealth be to notice who is present. A distribution that begins with that notice is less likely to end with resentment.

**Learning the Habit Before the Fractions**

For modern readers the verse trains a habit that remains before any estate exists: to think of property as a trust that is divided by rule and softened by kindness. The heirs who have just received a share are immediately asked to become givers, even if only with a small provision and a kind word. That move prevents the new owner from hardening into a claimant who sees only his portion. The next verses will return to precise fractions and severe warnings about consuming orphans’ wealth (4:10) and about knowing who is more beneficial to you (4:11). This interim verse ensures those powerful passages are not heard in a mercenary spirit. A person who has learned to offer something to the relative who has no fixed share, to feed the orphan who came to watch, and to speak decently while doing so, is more ready to handle the arithmetic that follows with a heart that counts people as well as portions. The verse therefore does not interrupt the sūrah’s legal sequence; it humanises it.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:9

> Let the guardians be as concerned ˹for the orphans˺ as they would if they were to ˹die and˺ leave ˹their own˺ helpless children behind. So let them be mindful of Allah and speak equitably.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Imagine Your Own Children Left Behind**

This verse asks the guardian to reverse perspectives. *Wa al-yakhsha alladhīna law tarakū min khalfihim dhurriyyatan ḍiʿāfan khāfū ʿalayhim* — let the guardians be as concerned for the orphans as they would if they were to die and leave their own helpless children behind. The image is specific: not children in general, but *dhurriyyatan ḍiʿāfan* — weak offspring, small children who cannot yet stand on their own, whose future depends on how others will treat them. Every guardian knows the fear that image brings. The Qur’an takes that natural fear and turns it into a rule for conduct. Deal with the orphan in your care the way you would want strangers to deal with your children tomorrow. That single substitution — put your child in the orphan’s place — does more work than a list of penalties, because it recruits love and worry on behalf of justice. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not kill your children out of fear of poverty”* (17:31) and praises those who prefer others over themselves, but here the appeal is quieter: remember your own vulnerability, and let that memory govern your hand when it holds another’s wealth.

**Be Mindful of Allah**

The command *fa al-yattaqū Allāh* — so let them be mindful of Allah — returns the sūrah to its opening word. Verse 1 began with *ittaqū rabbakum* — be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul — and verse 1 closed with *Allah is ever Watchful over you* (4:1). This verse’s call to *taqwā* therefore completes a short arch: creation to kinship to accountability. For the guardian, *taqwā* is not an abstract piety; it is caution in accounting, restraint in spending, promptness in testing and returning, and care in wording at distribution. The sūrah has already detailed those steps: return wealth without substitution (4:2), do not use marriage to discount dowries (4:3–4), do not hand wealth prematurely while still providing generously and speaking kindly (4:5), test and return with witnesses under God as Reckoner (4:6), honour fixed shares for both sexes (4:7), and offer provision to those present with decent words (4:8). This verse gathers those particulars into a posture. To be mindful of God here is to handle the orphan’s affair as one who knows he is watched while others cannot watch him.

**Speak Equitably**

The phrase *wa al-yaqūlū qawlan sadīdan* — and speak equitably — was read by early commentators as speech that is straight, sound, and hits the mark, like an arrow that flies true. *Sadīd* in Arabic conveys both correctness and directness, a word that lands where it should. In this context it covers several kinds of speech at once. To the orphan, it is the decent word that explains why property is being managed and when it will be returned, already commanded as *qawlan maʿrūfā* (4:5) and *qawlan maʿrūfā* at distribution (4:8). To oneself, it is the inner speech of intention — to mean to act justly and to commit to fairness when tempted to delay or to take. To others, it is the counsel a person would give about an orphan’s affairs if consulted by a dying friend about his children. The verse was also read as guidance for bequests: when a person with children advises another who is writing his bequest, or when he gives a deathbed instruction that would impoverish his own heirs, he should speak *sadīd* — straight — and advise equity, as in not bequeathing beyond one-third to the detriment of children. Al-Ṭabarī cites examples where a man on his deathbed wanted to give away so much that his children would be left needy, and the counsel was to say what is sound and balanced instead.

**Counsel About Bequests**

That bequest reading deserves attention because it ties verse 9 to the detailed inheritance fractions that follow. Some commentators understood the verse to address those who are present when a person is drafting a bequest and who might encourage him to dispose excessively. The fear-for-your-own-children test applies directly: would you want someone to encourage your father to leave you little? If not, then speak what is straight. The Qur’an elsewhere limits bequests to what does not harm heirs (4:12) and restricts the harms that can be done through wills. This verse therefore does double duty. For the guardian of existing orphans, it says handle their property as you would want yours handled. For the adviser of a future estate, it says counsel the testator toward equity as you would want others to counsel your own kin. In both cases the measure is the same: imagine your children weak behind you, and let that image straighten your words. The phrase *qawlan sadīdan* thus becomes more than politeness; it becomes the verbal form of justice, the counterpart to the just division of portions that the sūrah is about to quantify.

**A Verse That Completes Guardianship**

Read with verses 2 through 8, this verse finishes the sūrah’s opening ethic of trust. Verse 2 commanded return; verse 3 redirected marriage away from exploitation; verse 4 secured dowries; verse 5 taught sustaining provision without premature handover and with kind speech; verse 6 set testing, restraint, fair compensation, witnesses, and divine reckoning; verse 7 established obligatory shares for both sexes; verse 8 added voluntary provision for bystanders with kind speech. Verse 9 supplies the inner motive that makes those steps sincere: fear on behalf of your own weak offspring, *taqwā* of God, and straight speech. Without that motive, the procedures could be performed technically while the heart remains hard. With it, the procedures become acts of mercy. The sequence also shows how the Qur’an legislates through empathy as well as rule. It does not only say do this; it says feel this, remember this, imagine this, and then do this. That method keeps law from becoming a set of evasions. A guardian who can picture his own child asking for bread tomorrow will not easily tell himself that the orphan in his house will not need his property until later.

**A Standard the Community Can Apply**

The verse’s test is portable beyond individual guardians. A judge settling an estate, a committee dividing a legacy, a family meeting to agree on shares — each can ask the same question: if these were my children left weak, what would I want the table to decide? That question does not replace the fixed shares of 4:11–12, but it governs the discretionary spaces around them — timing, valuation, generosity to those present, tone of words, and speed of return. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Allah is a Witness over all things”* (4:33) and *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6), and this verse places that watchfulness inside human imagination. Before the next verse warns that consuming orphans’ wealth is eating fire (4:10) and before the long arithmetic of inheritance begins, the sūrah secures the disposition that will make the arithmetic honest. It asks for fear that leads to *taqwā*, and for *taqwā* that leads to straight speech, and for speech that leads to action where the weak child, whether yours or another’s, is left neither unprotected nor unheard.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:10

> Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies. And they will be burned in a blazing Hell!

**Expanded Commentary**

**Eating What Will Become Fire**

The image is stark and physical. *Inna alladhīna yaʾkulūna amwāl al-yatāmā ẓulman innamā yaʾkulūna fī buṭūnihim nāran* — those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth consume nothing but fire into their bellies. The Qur’an uses the verb *akala* — to eat — for illicit wealth elsewhere, as in *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29), but here the metaphor completes itself: what is eaten as wealth in this world will be present as fire in the stomach in the next. The restriction *ẓulman* — unjustly, wrongfully — is essential, because guardians do handle orphans’ property legitimately when they preserve it, invest it, and spend from it for the child’s need (4:5–6). What the verse condemns is consumption that is *ẓulm*, the putting of a thing where it does not belong, the use of a trust for the trustee’s own appetite. The sūrah has spent eight verses defining that trust — return without substitution (4:2), marriage without exploitation (4:3–4), provision without premature handover (4:5), testing and witnessing under divine reckoning (4:6–9) — and now it states the inner reality of violating that trust in a single picture. What felt like food will be felt as fire.

**Why Fire in the Belly**

The choice of belly as the place where fire settles was noted by commentators as precise justice. The sin passed through the belly as enjoyment; the punishment revisits the same place as burning. A ḥadīth vision cited in exegesis describes those who consumed orphans’ wealth with flames coming from their bodies, a narration that matches the Qur’anic image without adding to it. The sūrah’s wording does more than threaten; it re-describes the act while it is happening. A guardian who tells himself he has merely borrowed, or taken a small fee, or mixed accounts as a matter of convenience, is told that in the unseen record his stomach is already being filled with fire. That present tense — *innamā yaʾkulūna* — they are only eating fire — collapses the gap between now and then. The fire is not only a future sentence to be served; it is the true name of what is being eaten now. The verse that follows confirms the outer consequence — *wa sa yaṣlawna saʿīrā* — they will be burned in a blazing Hell — but the first clause already moves the punishment into the body, making the sin self-consuming before the Judgment even begins.

**A Great Sin Among Great Sins**

The sūrah classifies this consumption among major wrongs. The earlier phrase *ḥūban kabīrā* — a great sin — for mixing and substituting orphan wealth (4:2) anticipated this, and the later principle *“If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your lesser misdeeds”* (4:31) shows that the Qur’an grades sins and links forgiveness of smaller faults to avoidance of larger ones. Consuming the property of a child who has lost his protector sits in that larger category, and Prophetic tradition counts *akl māl al-yatīm* — eating the orphan’s wealth — among the seven destructive sins, alongside associating partners with God, sorcery, and killing a soul. That pairing is instructive. A person might rank financial wrongs as less serious than doctrinal or violent wrongs, but the sūrah places this financial wrong beside them because it strikes at the community’s most defenceless member. The warning is also proportionate to the trust involved. The guardian was chosen precisely because no one else could check him easily; violating that invisibility is a betrayal of *amānah*, a trust that the Qur’an elsewhere says the heavens and mountains refused to bear.

**What Counts as Unjust Consumption**

The qualifier *ẓulman* excludes legitimate management. Feeding and clothing the child from his property while keeping the principal as a standing support (4:5), investing with care, paying a fair provision to a poor guardian who works on the estate (4:6), and spending within what is recognized as fair — all of that is not eating unjustly. What remains forbidden is waste, haste before the child grows to claim his right (4:6), substitution of bad for good (4:2), and any use that serves the guardian’s household at the orphan’s expense. Jurists detailed many forms: taking a loan from the orphan’s funds without intent to return, selling his property cheaply to oneself, or charging an inflated fee for custody. The common element is benefit to the strong that corresponds to loss for the weak without the weak’s considered consent. The sūrah’s remedy has been procedural throughout — test, witness, account, speak kindly — precisely to make that consent meaningful when it comes. Where those procedures are bypassed and the orphan’s wealth is simply lived on, the consumption is *ẓulm* even if the guardian tells himself he meant to repay later.

**The Second Half — Burning in a Blazing Hell**

The closing *wa sa yaṣlawna saʿīrā* adds the external fire to the internal one. *Saʿīr* — blazing, fierce — describes a fire that is already kindled and intense. The sūrah pairs this with *sa yaṣlawna* — they will be burned, they will roast — a verb that suggests direct contact, not distant punishment. The two fires — in the belly and in the blaze — mirror the two stages of the sin. First, the guardian made the orphan’s wealth his own food; then, that food becomes his own punishment. The Qur’an elsewhere warns *“do not kill yourselves”* and *“whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire, and that is easy for Allah”* (4:29–30), and this verse specifies one path to that Fire. The sūrah’s next movement will turn to the constructive counterpart — precise shares for children, parents, spouses, and siblings (4:11–12) — but it earns that turn by first clearing the ground of exploitation. No fair division can thrive where one party has already been eaten. By naming the meal as fire, the verse makes return and restraint feel not only lawful but self-preserving.

**How the Sequence Trains the Heart**

Read with what came before, verse 10 closes the opening guardianship cycle that began with *“be mindful of your Lord”* (4:1) and *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1). Verses 2–9 built the practices — give, do not mix, do not exploit marriage, sustain with kindness, test and witness, share, remember bystanders, imagine your own children — and verse 10 states the inner truth of failing them. That order matters for how law shapes character. The sūrah does not begin with fire; it begins with a common origin and a call to awareness, then details, then motive, and only then the stark image. By the time the reader hears *“they consume fire into their bellies,”* he has already been given every tool to avoid it. The verse therefore functions both as warning and as clarification: what feels like quiet use of another’s property is, in the language the sūrah has been teaching, already a consumption that ends in burning. The following verses will show the opposite use of wealth — measured, witnessed, and distributed by decree — as the path that keeps both the orphan’s right and the guardian’s soul from being consumed.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:11

> Allah commands you regarding your children: the share of the male will be twice that of the female. If you leave only two ˹or more˺ females, their share is two-thirds of the estate. But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half. Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring. But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third. But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. ˹Be fair to˺ your parents and children, as you do not ˹fully˺ know who is more beneficial to you. ˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Divine Command, Not a Family Suggestion**

The verse opens with *yūṣīkum Allāhu fī awlādikum* — Allah commands you regarding your children. The verb *yūṣī* carries the sense of a binding directive, a bequest that the speaker expects to be carried out. By framing shares as something God enjoins, the Qur’an removes them from the realm of preference, negotiation, or clan custom. The sūrah has already moved from creation to guardianship to kinship, and now it turns that moral preparation into arithmetic. The community had just heard that men and women have obligatory shares whether little or much (4:7), and that the division should be witnessed and watched by God (4:6) and softened by provision for bystanders (4:8). Here the fractions arrive: a son’s share equal to two daughters when they inherit together, two-thirds for two or more daughters alone, one-half for a single daughter, one-sixth for each parent when there are offspring, one-third for the mother when there are no offspring and no siblings, and one-sixth for the mother when siblings exist. The verse closes with *farīḍatan min Allāh* — an obligation from Allah — matching its opening and making clear that these portions are not advice about fairness; they are the fair measure set by the One who knows.

**The Share of the Male Twice the Female Among Children**

The first rule — *li al-dhakari mithlu ḥaẓẓ al-unthayayn* — the male receives the equivalent of two females among children — has drawn the most discussion, and the sūrah itself supplies part of its context. The next verse will set the spouse shares where the husband receives half or a quarter and the wife receives a quarter or an eighth (4:12), showing a consistent pattern where the party bearing the duty of maintenance receives the larger portion. The Qur’an elsewhere explains that men are tasked with supporting women financially (4:34), and the law of inheritance follows that assignment of duty rather than a judgment of worth. When children inherit together, the son who will later be expected to maintain his own wife, children, and often his sisters and parents receives twice the daughter’s share, while the daughter’s share remains hers to keep, not to spend on others, including her husband’s family. Early commentators noted that when parents are the only heirs alongside a daughter, the equal sixth for each parent shows that the two-to-one ratio is not a universal male-female rule but a specific rule for siblings sharing as children. Shiite jurisprudence offers a further variation where remaining portions after fixed shares differ, but all schools agree that the daughter’s half, two-thirds, and the parents’ sixths are fixed by text.

**Daughters, Parents, and the Role of Siblings**

The verse details cases that had remained unsettled in custom. If there are only daughters — two or more — they receive two-thirds; if one, one-half. That single-daughter half leaves room for other fixed heirs and for the residue that goes to the nearest male relative, often the father, who in practice receives his sixth plus the remainder when he is that nearest kinsman. When offspring exist, each parent receives one-sixth, equally, which abrogated the earlier practice where parents received only through a discretionary bequest. When there is no offspring and parents are the sole heirs, the mother receives one-third, with the father taking the rest as residue, effectively two-thirds, which preserves the two-to-one pattern at the parental tier as well. When siblings exist alongside parents, the mother’s share drops from one-third to one-sixth. Commentators debated whether that reduction requires two siblings or one, and whether siblings inherit at all when the father is alive, with the majority holding that siblings are excluded by a living father and that the mother’s sixth in that case leaves five-sixths for the father. All shares are *min baʿdi waṣiyyatin yūṣī bihā aw dayn* — after bequest and debt — and Prophetic practice clarified that debts are paid first, then bequests up to one-third, then the fixed shares, a sequence that protects creditors and prevents a testator from disinheriting heirs by will.

**After Bequests and Debts — The Standing Order**

The repeated clause *after the fulfilment of bequests and debts* appears three times across verses 11 and 12, anchoring the whole inheritance system in a clear order. A person’s debts travel with his estate before any heir is considered; the Qur’an elsewhere warns against harming heirs through a will, and the addition *ghayra muḍār* — without harm — in the next verse (4:12) makes that explicit. A bequest that favours one heir over others, or that exceeds one-third when it reduces fixed shares, is counted as harm and therefore invalid. That limit surprised those who assumed a dying person’s word could reshape divine portions, but the sūrah treats the estate at death as already belonging to God, who then redistributes. The phrase *“you know not which of them are nearer to you in benefit”* (4:11) explains why God fixed the shares rather than leaving them to affection. A parent may love one child more, or expect more help from a son than a daughter, yet none knows who will be nearer in benefit in this life or the next, or who will serve the parent in old age or pray for him after. By assigning the math, the verse frees the testator from guessing and frees heirs from the bias of being favoured or forgotten.

**You Do Not Know Who Is More Beneficial**

The clause *ābāʾukum wa abnāʾukum lā tadrūna ayyuhum aqrabu lakum nafʿan* — your parents or your children, you do not know which are nearer to you in benefit — was read as both theological and practical. Theologically, benefit includes intercession, supplication, and the good deeds that continue after death; a child’s prayer or a parent’s loyalty may outweigh present utility.
