Practically, fortunes change, and the child who seemed least able may become the most supportive, or the parent thought independent may later need care. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse therefore asks the testator to surrender the illusion of foresight and to trust the division of the One described as *ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — All-Knowing, All-Wise. Those two Names close the verse for a reason. Knowledge covers every family configuration the law anticipates, and wisdom covers why the portions differ across tiers. The sūrah will repeat the same pair of Names after the spouse shares (4:12, 4:17, 4:26), creating a refrain that what seems intricate to people is known and wise with God. That refrain is not decoration; it is reassurance that the law is not arbitrary even where it is not immediately intuitive.

**An Obligation That Generates Knowledge**

The specificity of these verses produced a discipline. Because the fractions must be applied without error — halves, thirds, sixths, eighths, two-thirds — Muslim jurists developed the science of the shares, *ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ*, whose calculations require finding common denominators and handling residuary portions, a practice that contributed to the growth of algebra. The historical point matters because it shows how a verse read for family settlement generated tools for mathematics itself. More immediately, the verse taught the community that piety includes precision. Worship is not only prayer but also measuring correctly when emotion tempts to round up or round down. The sūrah will follow these shares with a promise — Gardens for those who keep God’s limits — and a warning — a humiliating punishment for those who transgress them (4:13–14) — showing that the arithmetic is also an act of obedience. A household that divides by these portions after debts and bequests, with witnesses and with *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) still echoing, has turned a potential quarrel into an act of submission, and has honoured both the parents and the children without claiming to know better than the One who assigned each a share.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:12

> You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless. But if they have children, then ˹your share is˺ one-fourth of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless. But if you have children, then your wives will receive one-eighth of your estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister ˹from their mother’s side˺, they will each inherit one-sixth, but if they are more than one, they ˹all˺ will share one-third of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm ˹to the heirs˺. ˹This is˺ a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Shares for Spouses After the Children’s Shares**

This verse completes the fixed portions begun in the previous one by turning from children and parents to spouses and siblings. The husband inherits one-half of his wife’s estate when she leaves no child, and one-fourth when she leaves a child; the wife inherits one-fourth of her husband’s estate when he leaves no child, and one-eighth when he leaves a child. The pattern is consistent: the presence of offspring reduces the spouse’s share because the offspring themselves have the larger fixed claims detailed in *“Allah commands you regarding your children”* (4:11). The Qur’an counts grandchildren through a son among children for this purpose, and it directs that where there is more than one wife — the sūrah having limited wives to four (4:3) — the one-fourth or one-eighth is divided equally among them. That last point matters because it shows how the sūrah’s earlier permission is immediately bounded by arithmetic. A man who takes an additional wife does not create an additional estate share; the existing share is partitioned. The fractions are therefore not only about entitlement but about keeping the household’s expectations inside a known economy.

**The Meaning of Child and of Heirlessness**

The phrase *wa lakum niṣfu mā taraka azwājukum in lam yakun lahunna walad* was understood to include sons, daughters, and grandchildren from a son, because all of them are *walad* in inheritance law. The same inclusion applies on the wife’s side. The reduction from half to quarter and from quarter to eighth therefore applies whenever there is a descendant who will inherit as a child. When no such descendant exists, the spouse’s share rises, but it never consumes the whole estate where other fixed heirs exist. The verse’s third case turns to *kalālah* — a person who leaves neither parent nor child — and assigns shares to brothers and sisters from the mother’s side: one-sixth for one, one-third shared equally when there are more. The qualification *from their mother’s side* is supplied by the recitation and consensus of the early authorities and by the contrast with verse 176, where full or paternal siblings receive a different, gender-differentiated share. Here, maternal siblings share equally regardless of gender, one-third divided evenly, which again shows that the Qur’an does not apply a single ratio everywhere.

**After Bequests and Debts — Without Harm**

The refrain *min baʿdi waṣiyyatin yūṣā bihā aw dayn* — after bequests and debts — appears for a third and fourth time, with the addition *ghayra muḍār* — without harm to the heirs — attached to this verse. The repetition teaches sequence and limits. Debts are paid first, then bequests within one-third, then the fixed shares. To attempt to harm heirs by a bequest that favours one, that disguises a gift as a debt, or that exceeds the known limits is forbidden, and Prophetic tradition invalidated any bequest to a fixed heir that was meant to enlarge his portion beyond what God assigned. The clause without harm therefore guards the fixed shares from being undone by testamentary manoeuvring. The sūrah’s earlier command to be mindful of God when handling orphans’ wealth (4:9) and its warning that consuming it is eating fire (4:10) find a legal counterpart here: the estate is not a private hoard to dispose of at whim; it is a measured trust whose portions are already set. Even the bequest that the Qur’an permits is not a tool to rewrite the fractions but a space to remember those without a fixed share, the very group verse 8 asked distributors to notice with provision and kind speech.

**Why the Shares Differ Between Husband and Wife**

The difference between half and quarter, and between quarter and eighth, at times raises the same question as the two-to-one share among children: why not equal? The sūrah’s answer is structural, not evaluative. The husband is charged with maintenance — *“Men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially”* (4:34) — and his larger share corresponds to the larger ongoing obligation he bears after the estate is divided. The wife’s share, while smaller, is hers alone, to keep and to dispose of as she wishes, and the sūrah has already secured that autonomy with *“Give women their due dowries graciously”* (4:4) and with the protection of her property in guardianship rules. Moreover, the total economy of the family often balances across generations: a daughter receives a smaller share from her parents but may later receive a dowry, maintenance, and a share from her husband, while a son receives more but spends it on others. Commentators who traced these flows over a single family’s cycle concluded that the system aims at overall sufficiency rather than identical fractions at each node. The closing Names — *“Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing”* (4:12) — frame that structure with knowledge of every household’s needs and forbearance toward those who find the division difficult to accept.

**Maternal Siblings Share Equally**

The kalālah clause for maternal siblings deserves separate attention because it breaks the gendered pattern. *Wa in kāna rajulun yūrathu kalālatan aw imraʾatun wa lahu akhun aw ukhtun fa li-kulli wāḥidin minhumā al-sudus* — if a man or woman leaves neither parent nor child but has a brother or sister, each receives one-sixth — treats brother and sister identically when they are linked only through the mother. When there are more than two, they share one-third equally. That equal sharing was read as reinforcing the principle that where the link is maternal and the deceased leaves no parent or offspring, the siblings represent the mother’s line and are therefore given like portions. The contrast with verse 176, where a full sister may receive one-half and full siblings divide with the male receiving twice the female, is not a contradiction but a distinction between types of siblinghood. Jurists detailed many further cases — grandparents, grandchildren, paternal siblings — building outward from these texts, but the two poles remained: fixed Qur’anic shares where the text speaks, and residuary distribution to the nearest male agnate where it does not. Even there, the sūrah’s earlier refrain — *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) — keeps the calculator humble.

**A Commandment That Closes With Forbearance**

The verse ends with *waṣiyyatan min Allāh wa Allāhu ʿAlīmun Ḥalīm* — a commandment from Allah, and Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing. To call the fractions a *waṣiyyah* from God places them beside the human bequests just mentioned but above them. A person’s bequest is his wish; God’s *waṣiyyah* is law. Yet the Name that follows is not only All-Knowing but also Forbearing — *Ḥalīm* — the One who does not hasten to punish. That forbearance is directed at recipients who may struggle with the division, especially the intense moment when a spouse or sibling is present and the reduced share feels personal. The sūrah will immediately follow with *“These are the limits set by Allah”* (4:13) and the promise of Gardens for keeping them and Fire for crossing them (4:13–14), showing that forbearance does not remove accountability. It simply marks that the lawgiver knows the difficulty and still asks for compliance. In that light, the precise arithmetic of half, quarter, eighth, sixth, and third becomes more than calculation; it becomes the measured way a community that began from a single soul (4:1) learns to part with wealth at death without parting from one another.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:13

> These ˹entitlements˺ are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. That is the ultimate triumph!

**Expanded Commentary**

**Limits That Protect Rather Than Confine**

The pronoun *tilka* — these — gathers the entire inheritance code that runs across verses 7 through 12 and names it *ḥudūd Allāh* — the limits set by Allah. In Qur’anic usage *ḥadd* marks a boundary that may not be crossed, like the edge of a field or the wall of a sanctuary. To call fractions *limits* teaches that arithmetic has a moral edge. The same term appears elsewhere for fasting, divorce procedure, and penal law, showing that where people are most likely to follow appetite — with food, with family ties, with profit — the law draws a clear line. Here the line runs through property that families have long treated as theirs to divide by custom or by favour. By naming those divisions limits set by God, the verse lifts the shares from negotiation to reverence. A heir who asks for more than his portion is not merely asking family for generosity; he is stepping beyond a boundary God drew. Commentators noted that the sūrah pairs *ḥudūd* with obedience to God and His Messenger precisely because the shares were revealed in a setting where resistance was open.

**Obedience to Allah and His Messenger Together**

The promise *wa man yuṭiʿi Allāha wa rasūlahu yudkhilhu jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār* — whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow — joins two obediences in one reward. The shares were recited by the Messenger ﷺ and clarified by his practice — which debts come first, which bequests stand, how the residue goes, how multiple wives share a single portion — so obeying God here includes following the Messenger’s explanation. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah”* (4:80), and this verse makes that union concrete at the moment of estate division, when a person might obey God in prayer yet follow custom in property. The sūrah therefore makes the counting table a place of obedience. Measuring a half, a quarter, an eighth, a sixth, or two-thirds correctly is no longer mere accounting; it is the form obedience takes when wealth changes hands at death. The promise that follows is proportionate: the one who respects limits with wealth is welcomed into a space described as abundant water flowing below — a image of plenty without dispute.

**Gardens Under Which Rivers Flow as the Appropriate Reward**

The description *jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā* — Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever — appears across the Qur’an as the counter to the quarrel over portions. The inheritance code divided fixed pools; the Garden is described as water that does not need to be divided because it flows continuously and suffices all. The sūrah elsewhere promises that avoiding major sins leads to being absolved of lesser ones and admitted to a place of honour (4:31), and this verse shows one concrete major limit whose keeping leads to that honour. The language of permanence — *khālidīna fīhā* — staying forever — answers the impermanence of estates. What a person surrendered in this world — a fraction he thought was his, a bequest he was tempted to write to harm others — returns as a dwelling that does not shrink or expire. The Qur’an elsewhere contrasts the brief enjoyment of this world with the lasting home of the next (4:77), and the same contrast operates here. The limits on wealth today secure wealth that never needs dividing tomorrow.

**That Is the Ultimate Triumph**

The closing *wa dhālika al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm* — that is the ultimate triumph — names the outcome as success on the largest scale. *Fawz* in the Qur’an is not merely entering a pleasant place; it is being delivered from the Fire and admitted to the Garden, as the next verse will make explicit by describing the opposite. The phrase appears elsewhere for those who obey and keep trusts, and it gathers both the inner and outer dimensions of triumph: right relation with God and lasting well-being for the self. By placing that phrase immediately after the fractions, the verse teaches that the triumph is not in securing a larger share through pressure, but in receiving the share God assigned and trusting His promise about what follows. Al-Rāzī observes that the sūrah deliberately links the technical laws of inheritance to the highest theological promise, so that no one treats them as secondary or worldly. What looks like civil law is placed on the same ledger as faith and worship. A person who divides an estate while mindful that *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1) and that *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) is already living the triumph the verse names.

**Why the Promise Comes Here Before the Threat**

The sūrah gives the Garden before the Fire, the reward before the warning. That order reflects a consistent Qur’anic method of inviting obedience through hope before reinforcing it with fear. The list of shares was demanding in a context where Male relatives had taken full estates; to hear first that keeping the limits leads to perpetual Gardens makes the demand feel like guidance rather than burden. The sūrah will shortly add *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak”* (4:28), and this promise already lightens the specific burden of parting with wealth by showing what parting correctly secures. The verse also frames the limits as entitlements — *tilka ḥudūd Allāh* can be read as these shares are limits — so that the promise belongs to the rightful recipient as much as to the executor. The widow who receives her quarter or eighth, the daughter who receives her half or two-thirds, the mother who receives her third or sixth — each is not only receiving property but standing inside a limit that, if honoured by all, will be counted as obedience.

**The Limits That Hold the Community Together**

Read with verses 7 through 12, this verse seals the sūrah’s first legal suite with theology. Creation from a single soul taught that all are kin (4:1); trust laws taught that the strong must guard the weak (4:2–10); inheritance laws taught that every close heir has a named portion after debts and bequests (4:11–12). Now the sūrah lifts those portions and says they are *ḥudūd* — limits — whose keeping is obedience and whose breach is disobedience. The following verse will state the other side — humiliating punishment for crossing them — but this verse is allowed to stand first and to linger. It suggests that a community that respects divine limits in its most sensitive moment — when grief and greed meet over a loved one’s goods — builds a habit that steadies every other limit. Gardens under which rivers flow, forever, is the sūrah’s way of saying that what is surrendered at the division table is not lost; it is transformed. The measurer who gave each his due and sought no more has kept faith with the limits, and with the One who set them.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:14

> But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds their limits will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever. And they will suffer a humiliating punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Side of the Limits**

The previous verse named the shares *ḥudūd Allāh* — limits set by Allah — and promised Gardens for those who obey Allah and His Messenger in those limits (4:13). This verse states the counterpart without softening: *wa man yaʿṣi Allāha wa rasūlahu wa yataʿadda ḥudūdahu yudkhilhu nāran khālidan fīhā* — whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds His limits will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever. The verb *yataʿadda* — to exceed, to overstep — pictures a foot crossing a marked line. The image follows directly from the fractions. A person who takes more than a half where half was assigned, who withholds the mother’s sixth, who redirects a bequest to harm heirs, or who refuses the daughter’s share has not merely made a miscalculation; he has overstepped. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“whoever transgresses Allah’s limits has wronged his own soul”* (65:1), and that self-wrong is made visible here as a lasting abode. The pairing of disobedience to God and His Messenger signals that the limits were both revealed and explained through the Messenger ﷺ, so ignoring the prophetic clarification about debts, bequests, and residues counts as the same crossing.

**Abiding Forever and a Humiliating Punishment**

The threat is doubled in a way that matches the promise before it. The promise spoke of Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay forever, and called that the ultimate triumph (4:13); the warning speaks of Fire, to stay forever, and calls it a humiliating punishment — *ʿadhābun muhīn*. The adjective *muhīn* — humiliating, debasing — was chosen because the sin itself was an attempt at self-exaltation. The heir who seized more did so to appear stronger, to keep the estate consolidated, to show that custom outweighs revelation. The recompense humbles precisely that pride. Commentators noted the symmetry: the one who kept the limits was honoured with rivers and permanence; the one who exceeded them is debased with fire and permanence. The Qur’an elsewhere pairs dishonour with fire when the sin involved arrogance toward God’s bounds, as though the punishment must correct not only the act but the posture that produced it. The sūrah has been training that posture since *“be mindful of your Lord”* (4:1) and *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1); this verse states what becomes of a person who lives as though no watch was kept.

**What Exceeding the Limits Looks Like**

Exceeding the limits is not a single form. It includes refusing to pay the daughter or sister her share, reducing the wife’s quarter or eighth on the pretext of expenses, inflating a debt to shrink the estate before division, writing a bequest beyond one-third to disadvantage fixed heirs, or taking from an orphan’s portion before it is returned (4:10). Prophetic tradition invalidated bequests that favour a fixed heir, precisely to block the most pious-seeming way of exceeding — the deathbed gift that rewrites God’s fractions. The sūrah will later warn generally *“do not devour one another’s wealth illegally”* (4:29) and will say that doing so sinfully and unjustly leads to being burned in the Fire, where *“that is easy for Allah”* (4:30). This verse is the specific application of that general warning to the inheritance code. It tells the family gathered around the estate that the line they are tempted to move is not theirs to move. The fractions after bequests and debts (4:11–12) are not a starting offer; they are the limit. To cross them is to take what was not assigned, and the verse gives that taking its final name.

**Disobedience to the Messenger in a Legal Matter**

The addition *wa rasūlahu* — and His Messenger — deserves attention because the shares were among the most detailed laws recited by the Messenger ﷺ. His role was not only to convey the verses but to show how to apply them: which relatives count as child, which siblings count as kalālah, how debts precede bequests, how the residue is handled, how witnesses secure the handover (4:6). To disobey in these details is therefore to refuse the very explanation that makes the limits practicable. The Qur’an elsewhere links guidance and clarification — *“Allah wishes to make things clear to you and guide you to the noble ways of those before you”* (4:26) — and this verse shows what follows when clarity is rejected. A community that accepts the Messenger’s clarification finds its divisions manageable; a person who sets it aside finds the division becomes a quarrel and then a sin. The sūrah’s repeated closing Names — All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26), All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12) — frame that clarification as knowledge coupled with forbearance, so that the warning here is not abrupt but earned. Clarity was given; limits were drawn; recompense was named.

**Why the Warning Is Severe Yet Just**

Some readers feel the severity — abiding in Fire forever — is disproportionate to a property dispute. The sūrah answers that sense by the stakes it has established. The shares protect the weakest heirs the community had been accustomed to depriving — women, children, and mothers — and the limits protect the trust that widens beyond inheritance into guardianship of orphans (4:2–10). To violate those limits is to reassert the old order that the Qur’an came to correct, and to do so while invoking family loyalty. It is a public reversal of a divine redistribution, not a private miscalculation. The Qur’an elsewhere makes avoidance of major sins the condition for forgiveness of lesser ones (4:31), and it lists eating orphan wealth among destructive sins; violating the obligatory shares belongs in that class because it systematically consumes the rights of those whom God explicitly named as entitled. The humiliation in the punishment matches the humiliation the wrongdoer inflicted when he sent a widow or daughter away empty, telling them their share was not obligatory after all.

**A Boundary That Guards Dignity**

By closing the inheritance suite with both Gardens and Fire, verses 13 and 14 turn a code of fractions into a pledge of faith. The person who keeps the limits is not only being fair; he is obeying. The person who exceeds them is not only being unfair; he is disobeying. That moral framing matters because estates are divided in the heat of grief, where custom, pressure from elders, and personal preference push hard against revelation. The verse gives the hesitant executor a firmer ground to stand on: the limit is God’s, not his, and keeping it is the path to the ultimate triumph named just before. For the heir who receives a smaller portion than he hoped, the same framing offers patience, because the limit that reduced his share also secured the shares of others and secured his own reward for accepting it. The sūrah will move next to other limits that guard the family — chastity, repentance, and marriage — but it earns that movement by first settling wealth. A community that cannot keep limits with property will not keep them with persons; a community that respects them with property learns that boundaries are not humiliations, but protections, and that the only humiliation the sūrah threatens is for those who insist on crossing them.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:15

> ˹As for˺ those of your women who commit illegal intercourse—call four witnesses from among yourselves. If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Procedure for a Grave Breach**

This verse addresses a specific crime within the family and sets a procedure before imposing a penalty. *Wa allātī yaʾtīna al-fāḥishata min nisāʾikum fa astashhidū ʿalayhinna arbaʿatan minkum* — as for those of your women who commit illegal intercourse, call four witnesses from among yourselves. The word *fāḥishah* denotes an act that is openly foul, whose shame is not limited to the actors but extends to the household. The Qur’an treats it as a harm to the family structure the sūrah is building through marriage, dowry, and inheritance. Yet even for that harm, the law demands proof of the highest level: four witnesses, not one or two, and from among your own community — people known, available for scrutiny, and answerable for testimony. The Qur’an elsewhere warns that accusing chaste women without four witnesses brings the accusers themselves to punishment (24:4). By requiring four, the verse shields households from slander and from the ease with which a sexual accusation can destroy reputation. The procedure tells the community that chastity is guarded both by prohibiting the act and by prohibiting careless accusation of it.

**Four Witnesses and Testimony**

The number four was explained as demanding direct sight, not hearsay, inference, or circumstance. Jurists detailed that the witnesses must have seen the act itself in a way that leaves no ambiguity, a standard so high that it is rarely met, which is itself the point. The law makes the crime grave, the proof grave, and the consequence of false testimony grave, so that the social fabric is protected on both sides. The witnesses must be *minkum* — from among you — which the majority understood as upright members of the Muslim community, not outsiders with unknown motives. That requirement also places the matter inside the community’s responsibility, not as a private vengeance. The sūrah will shortly turn to repentance for those who act ignorantly and then repent soon after (4:17), showing that even where proof might exist, the door to return is not closed arbitrarily. Here, the first step is to ensure that no one is confined or punished on the basis of rumour, suspicion, or a single sighting. Four concordant testimonies are needed before the next step is taken.

**Confinement Until Death or Until Another Way**

The sentence *fa in shahidū fa amsikūhunna fī al-buyūt ḥattā yatawaffāhunna al-mawtu aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* — if they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die or Allah ordains a different way — sets a holding measure rather than a fixed corporal penalty. Early authorities understood this confinement as a stage in legislation. At this point in the Medinan period, the community was ordered to keep the women in their homes, both as protection for society and as prevention of further transgression, while awaiting what God would ordain as a way — *sabīl*. Commentators relate that the different way came later through verses on lashing for fornication (24:2) and through Prophetic clarification for adultery where marriage has occurred. The phrase *aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* therefore signals that the law is not yet in its final form; it is awaiting a clarified path. That language of waiting is characteristic of the Qur’an’s gradual legislation, where a ruling is given, held, and then completed. The sūrah will soon emphasize that Allah wishes to make things clear and to guide to the ways of those before, and to turn to you in mercy (4:26), and this temporary confinement is one place where clarity arrived in stages.

**Why Confinement and Why a Way Out**

Confinement to homes — *amsikūhunna fī al-buyūt* — was read in two lights. Practically, it removed the context for repetition by limiting movement and contact, without public shaming beyond the family. Morally, it treated the home as the sphere where the act’s harm first fell, since unlawful intercourse breaches the marital bond and the lineage that inheritance law depends on. The until clause — *ḥattā yatawaffāhunna al-mawtu aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* — holds two possibilities open: life-long seclusion if no new ruling comes, or a new ordained way if God provides it. The community was therefore told to act decisively and to wait expectantly at the same time. That combination keeps law from becoming either lax or hastily severe. The sūrah elsewhere commands *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and describes God as ever Merciful (4:29), and even in this severe matter it leaves the future open to mercy through another way. The verse thus teaches that punishment in this faith is not the urge to harm but the search for a path that protects lineage, deters transgression, and leaves room for divine clarification.

**Temporary Legislation With Permanent Lessons**

Although the specific ruling of confinement was later superseded by detailed penalties for *zinā* in other passages, the principles inside the verse remain. The need for four witnesses remains the Qur’anic standard for proving illicit intercourse, guarding privacy while still naming the act as *fāḥishah*. The requirement that testimony be tested remains, protecting the accused from collusion and protecting the accusers from the grave sin of slander. The idea that some laws are given as an interim holding until a clearer way is ordained remains a model for how revelation unfolds: not all at once in a single form, but step by step as the community can bear and apply. The verse also mirrors the sūrah’s larger concern with entrusted wealth and entrusted persons. Just as the sūrah guarded the orphan’s property from being eaten and the woman’s dowry from being seized, it guards the household’s honour from being destroyed by unverified accusation and from being left without a remedy when the accusation is proven. Four witnesses, confinement, and an awaited way together hold those concerns in balance.

**Between Justice and Mercy**

Placed after the inheritance code and before the verses on repentance, this verse shows how the sūrah holds justice and mercy together without confusing them. The act is named without euphemism, the proof is set at the highest bar, the interim sanction is custodial rather than corporal, and the future is left explicitly to what God will ordain. That structure prevents two equal errors: treating a grave breach as if it were trivial, and treating accusation as if it were proof. The next verses will broaden the picture: both parties who commit the sin are to be disciplined and then relieved if they repent (4:16), and repentance itself has a time and a limit (4:17–18). This verse focuses on one side of the pair and on the evidential threshold that must be crossed before any sanction applies. By insisting on four and by naming the confinement as until death or until another way, the Qur’an keeps the law both firm and open — firm enough to protect the family, open enough to await the completion of its own legislation, and throughout mindful that the One who ordains the way is the One who is All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:16

> And the two among you who commit this sin—discipline them. If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them. Surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Discipline for the Pair**

After addressing women who commit the foul act with a four-witness procedure and confinement (4:15), this verse broadens the scope to the pair: *wa alladhāni yaʾtiyānihā minkum fa ādhūhumā* — and the two among you who commit this sin, discipline them. The dual pronoun *alladhāni* and the dual verb *yaʾtiyānihā* make clear that the act involves two persons, and the command to discipline — *ādhūhumā* — is directed to both. Early exegetes differed on whether this verse concerns two men, a man and a woman, or specifically those not covered by the previous verse’s marital context, but all agreed that the principle of shared accountability is central. The Qur’an does not treat unlawful intercourse as a fault borne by one party alone; it addresses both participants as responsible agents. The type of discipline — *adhā* — was understood as harm through rebuke, exposure, and shaming, rather than a fixed corporal penalty at this stage, because the sūrah immediately adds the exit that later legislation would detail. As with verse 15, this ruling sits in a sequence where final penalties arrive later (24:2 and Prophetic clarification), so the immediate sanction is corrective and social rather than final.

**What Discipline Meant at This Stage**

Commentators described *ādhūhumā* as verbal reproach, harsh words, striking with sandals, or other forms of public disapproval that make the offenders feel the community’s rejection without exceeding what the law authorizes. The purpose was deterrence and moral signalling: the household and neighbours see that the act is not treated as private taste but as *fāḥishah* that damages lineage and trust. At the same time, the discipline was not meant to become a second injustice. The sūrah’s broader ethic of *qawlan maʿrūfā* — speaking kindly where due (4:5, 4:8) — remains the norm for ordinary relations; here, a different register — *adhā* — applies because the act itself breached the trust those kind words normally protect. The distinction matters. The community is not asked to be harsh generally; it is asked to be clearly disapproving where a boundary that guards families has been crossed. The Qur’an elsewhere commands *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and elsewhere describes God as ever Merciful (4:29), so even this disciplinary moment is framed as protection, not cruelty.

**If They Repent and Mend Their Ways, Relieve Them**

The pivot of the verse is *fa in tābā wa aṣlaḥā fa aʿriḍū ʿanhumā* — if they repent and mend their ways, relieve them. Repentance — *tawbah* — is not only regret in the heart; it is accompanied by *iṣlāḥ*, mending, repairing what was broken. That mending was understood to include ceasing the relationship, separating from the partner, showing remorse, and returning to behaviour that guards chastity. When those signs appear, the community is commanded to turn away — *fa aʿriḍū* — to stop the discipline, to cease pursuit, to leave them alone. That turning away is itself an act of worship. The verse does not say continue to remind them or keep them marked; it says relieve them. The sūrah will soon define what counts as accepted repentance — done ignorantly or recklessly and then soon after (4:17) — and what does not count — delay until death is at hand (4:18). This verse supplies the bridge between the two: where repentance is shown with amendment, the community’s role ends and divine acceptance begins. The discipline was never meant to brand a person permanently.

**Ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful**

The closing *inn Allāha kāna tawwāban raḥīmā* — surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful — gives the reason for relieving. *Tawwāb* stresses repetition: the One who accepts repentance again and again, not once. *Raḥīm* stresses the mercy that follows acceptance. The pair appears together where the Qur’an wants to emphasize that God’s mercy is not reluctant. The sūrah elsewhere says *“Allah wishes to turn to you in mercy, but those who follow desires wish you to deviate entirely”* (4:27), and *“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak”* (4:28). Those wishes frame this verse’s command to relieve. To continue harshness after repentance would align the community with the deviaters who want people to fall, not with the turn toward mercy that God desires. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse therefore teaches two kinds of mercy: God’s mercy in accepting the return, and the community’s mercy in expressing that acceptance by ceasing harm. Both are needed; divine pardon without social relief leaves the offender isolated, while social relief without divine pardon would be empty.

**A Ruling Held Until a Way Was Ordained**

As with the previous verse’s *“until Allah ordains a different way for them”* (4:15), this verse’s disciplinary measure was understood as an interim stage. Later revelation specified *“As for the fornicatress and the fornicator, lash each of them with a hundred lashes”* (24:2), and Prophetic practice clarified the penalty for the married adulterer, showing that the community had been held in a preparatory discipline until the final way — *sabīl* — was given. Recognizing that progression prevents two misreadings: that the early verse’s confinement or the second verse’s *adhā* remains the final law, or that the later penalties negate the mercy that these early verses displayed. The progression is additive: the early verses taught procedural caution, shared accountability, measured social discipline, and an open door to return; the later verses kept that caution and added precise penalties where proof and conditions were met. The through line is consistent. The law guards lineage from the act, guards the accused from unproven accusation, and guards the repentant from endless shaming.

**Shared Fault and Shared Mercy**

Read together, verses 15 and 16 form a careful balance. One verse sets a high evidentiary bar and a custodial measure for women, with a future way awaited; the next sets shared discipline for the pair and a clear exit when repentance and mending appear. Both verses refuse to treat illicit intercourse as trivial, and both refuse to treat the offender as beyond return. The sūrah’s surrounding chapters on wealth and marriage show why that balance matters here. Family property is guarded by witnesses and reckoning (4:6); family honour is guarded by witnesses as well (4:15); both guards exist because trust is easy to break in private. Yet trust can also be restored. The command to relieve those who have repented and mended teaches that restoration has a form: stop the harm. That form becomes a habit the sūrah will extend beyond this case, into speaking equitably (4:9), trading by mutual consent (4:29), and appointing mediators when a split is feared (4:35). In each, the law asks not only for justice against wrong but for a path back when wrong is amended, because the One who judges is ever Accepting, Most Merciful.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:17

> Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repent soon after—Allah will pardon them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Repentance That Is Accepted**

This verse answers a question that verses 15 and 16 left open: after an act described as foul and after discipline that ends when repentance and mending appear, whose repentance counts? The answer is precise: *innamā al-tawbatu ʿalā Allāhi lilladhīna yaʿmalūna al-sūʾa bi jahālatin thumma yatūbūna min qarīb* — Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly or recklessly then repent soon after. The particle *innamā* restricts; it tells the reader that not every claim of turning back is weighed equally. The condition *bi jahālah* — ignorantly — was explained by the early authorities not as lack of information that the act was forbidden, but as the state of acting under impulse, desire, and heedlessness even while knowing the ruling. Every person who disobeys God is, in that moment, acting ignorantly in this sense, because knowledge that does not restrain has not governed. The Qur’an elsewhere describes wrongdoing as done out of ignorance and then followed by repentance and reform (6:54), showing that the category is broad enough to include many who will later be forgiven. What the verse therefore accepts is not a narrow excuse but a common condition: the wrong was done in the heat of desire, not as a settled denial of the law.

**What Soon After Means**

The phrase *thumma yatūbūna min qarīb* — then repent soon after — was read as repentance that follows relatively quickly, before habit hardens and before death approaches. Some commentators took *qarīb* to mean before the soul reaches the throat at death, as the next verse will state explicitly: when a person is dying and says now I repent, it is not accepted (4:18). Others took it to mean soon in the sense of closeness to the sin, so that the return interrupts the pattern rather than postponing it indefinitely. Both senses converge: the repentance that counts is the one that does not wait until it is too late. The sūrah’s language of hastening to return matches its broader call to *“compete in returning to Allah”* elsewhere and to seek forgiveness promptly, because delay itself becomes a form of persistence. A person who tells himself he will repent later while continuing the act treats repentance as a final hour amulet rather than a present turning. The verse closes that strategy. The accepted turn is the one that happens while life remains an open field for action, not when the field is closing and the return is forced by sight of the consequence.

**Allah Will Pardon Them**

The promise *fa ulāʾika yatūbu Allāhu ʿalayhim* — Allah will pardon them — places the act of turning on God’s side as well. The same root *t-w-b* is used for the servant’s repentance and for God’s acceptance; the servant turns to God, and God turns to the servant with pardon. The doubling shows that forgiveness is not earned by a formula but received as a turn from the other side. The verse does not require the penitent to offer a ransom or to perform an exact counterweight; it requires ignorance acknowledged, speed in returning, and mending where mending is due, as the previous verse added *wa aṣlaḥā* — and they mend their ways (4:16). When those appear, God’s turn follows as a matter of His own commitment, expressed as *ʿalā Allāhi* — upon Allah — a phrasing that signals a promise He has laid upon Himself in mercy. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Allah loves those who constantly turn to Him”* (2:222), and the same love is implied here where the return is accepted soon. That love is not indiscriminate; it distinguishes the one who returns quickly from the one who persists until the final hour.

**All-Knowing, All-Wise**

The closing *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise — gives the measure by which repentance is judged. *ʿAlīm* knows the state of the heart when the sin was committed — whether it was heedlessness, arrogance, or confusion — and knows the sincerity of the return — whether it was immediate or delayed, full or partial. *Ḥakīm* places that knowledge inside wisdom: not every regret is wisdom, and not every delay is pardonable. The pair appears after the inheritance shares (4:11) and will appear again after the clarification of law (4:26) for the same reason. What seems intricate to people — who has repented enough, who has returned soon enough — is known and wisely judged by God. That closing also deters two equal errors. One person may despair, thinking his ignorant act can never be forgiven; the verse says ignorance with a soon return is precisely what is forgiven. Another may presume, thinking any late cry will suffice; the next verse says it will not. Knowledge and wisdom hold the line between despair and presumption, keeping the door open without removing its frame.

**Ignorance and the Broader Pattern of the Sūrah**

The sūrah has been defining ignorance not as lack of intelligence but as acting without the restraint that knowledge should bring. That is why it pairs this verse with earlier pictures of hasty consumption before the orphan grows up (4:6), mixing wealth to make use easier (4:2), and inheriting women against their will (4:19) — all acts where the actor knows the roster of right yet follows appetite. The remedy is not more information alone but a quick return — *min qarīb* — while the heart is still soft. The Qur’an elsewhere describes the believer’s speed: *“those who, when they commit an indecent act or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins”* (3:135), and that remembering is presented as immediate. The same immediacy is asked here. A community that learns to turn soon — to stop the act, to amend, to seek forgiveness — builds the reflex that keeps smaller wrongs from becoming the major sins whose avoidance secures forgiveness for lesser ones (4:31). The verse therefore trains a habit more than it defines a threshold. The threshold will be defined by death in the next verse; the habit is defined here as soon.

**A Promise That Invites Speed**

Read with what follows, this verse is an invitation to hurry toward mercy. The next verse will close the window for those who persist until they are dying and only then say now I repent, and for those who die as disbelievers (4:18). This verse opens the window wide for everyone else who acted in ignorance and then turned quickly. That pairing shows the sūrah’s method: it does not leave the definition of repentance vague so that people oscillate between anxiety and complacency; it names the conditions — evil done in heedlessness, repentance soon after — and attaches a clear promise — Allah will pardon them. The promise is not conditional on human witnesses or on the discipline being lifted by the community (4:16); it is a direct turn from God to the servant. For the person who has committed the act named earlier as foul, that directness matters. The same One who set limits around property and family (4:13) and who is ever Watchful (4:1) is the One who is ever Accepting when the return is real and soon. The law that seemed only to threaten thus also welcomes, and it does so while life still allows the return to be chosen, not forced.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:18

> However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, “Now I repent!” nor those who die as disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Return That Comes Too Late**

The previous verse defined the repentance that is accepted: evil done ignorantly or recklessly, then a turn soon after (4:17). This verse defines the repentance that is not: *wa laysat al-tawbatu lilladhīna yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāt ḥattā idhā ḥaḍara aḥadahumu al-mawtu qāla innī tubtu al-ān* — repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until death presents itself and then they cry, Now I repent. The image is not of a person who fell and then struggled to return; it is of a person who kept doing wrong while deferring the return, telling himself there would be time later. *Ḥattā idhā ḥaḍara aḥadahumu al-mawtu* — until death is present — places the utterance at the moment when choice is ending. The Qur’an elsewhere describes the same scene with Pharaoh, who believed only when drowning overtook him and was told that his faith then avails nothing, because the trial by which faith is tested has closed. The principle is consistent: repentance is a deed of the living that mattered while life allowed alternatives; once the alternative has been removed by the arrival of death, the words now I repent lose the condition that made them meaningful, which was willingness while unwillingness was still possible.

**Nor Those Who Die as Disbelievers**

The verse adds *wa lā alladhīna yamūtūna wa hum kuffār* — nor those who die as disbelievers. That second group is not deferring repentance; they have rejected the very address to which repentance would return. The pairing shows two ways the window closes: by delay until the last breath, and by death in a state that never turned at all. Both end in the same preparation: *ulāʾika aʿtadnā lahum ʿadhāban alīmā* — for them We have prepared a painful punishment. The verb *aʿtadnā* — We have prepared — stresses that the recompense is not improvised at the moment; it has been readied, as Gardens were readied for those who obey limits (4:13). The symmetry between the two endings is deliberate. Two verses earlier, those who obey limits enter Gardens to stay forever; here, those who persist until death face a penalty already prepared and described as painful — *alīm* — because the wrong persisted was itself a cause of pain to others and to the soul that chose it. The sūrah elsewhere says *“whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire, and that is easy for Allah”* (4:30), and this verse specifies one of the easiest ways to fall into that Fire — by treating time as endless.

**Knowingly Persisting Versus Acting Ignorantly**

The contrast between 4:17 and 4:18 turns on the state during the act. Verse 17 spoke of *bi jahālah* — ignorantly, heedlessly — while 4:18 speaks of persistence — *yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāt* as a continuing practice until death arrives. Persisting was understood by early commentators not as a single grave sin committed once in ignorance and then regretted, but as a settled habit where the person knows what he does and keeps doing it while postponing return. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“they do not persist in what they did while they know”* (3:135), praising those who, when they err, remember and do not persist. That praise implies that the blameworthy pattern is knowing and persisting. The sūrah has already shown what persisting looks like in other domains: consuming an orphan’s wealth hastily before he grows up to demand it (4:6), mixing wealth to make use easier (4:2), inheriting women against their will and then pressuring them to surrender dowries (4:19). Each is a case where the actor knows the roster of right yet continues because the victim cannot yet speak or because death seems distant. This verse collapses that distance and says the time to speak is while speaking remains a choice.

**Why Now I Repent Fails at the Throat**

The phrase *innī tubtu al-ān* — now I repent — fails not because the words are wrong but because the time that gives them weight has passed. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah accepts the servant’s repentance so long as the death rattle has not yet reached the throat, a ḥadīth transmitted in the Sunan and explained as marking the point where the unseen becomes seen and faith ceases to be a trial. The sūrah’s language matches that threshold without needing to detail physiology: *ḥaḍara aḥadahumu al-mawtu* — death is present to him — the moment when the person sees what he had only been told, and when fear replaces willingness. At that moment, to say now I repent is to react to sight, not to turn to the unseen. The Qur’an elsewhere says that faith at the moment of seeing the punishment does not benefit those who had denied before, because the benefit of faith lies in trusting before seeing. The same applies to turning. A return that is accepted is one given while the return remains hard, when the act could still be continued and is instead abandoned. A return forced by the sight of death carries no such cost, and therefore no such pardon, because it does not choose God while another choice was still genuinely open.

**Prepared Punishment and the Sūrah’s Pattern**

The closing *aʿtadnā lahum ʿadhāban alīmā* gathers this verse into the sūrah’s larger pattern of prepared recompense. Those who keep limits receive Gardens prepared and described as flowing water (4:13); those who eat orphan wealth unjustly are told they eat fire in their bellies and will burn in a blazing Hell (4:10); those who cross limits receive a humiliating punishment and abiding in Fire (4:14). This verse adds the temporal border to that pattern: the Garden remains open while repentance remains soon (4:17); the painful punishment becomes prepared when soon is replaced by until death. The lesson for the living is not to measure the exact length of soon but to remove delay as a plan. The Qur’an elsewhere praises *“those who, when they commit an indecent act or wrong themselves, remember Allah immediately and seek forgiveness”* (3:135), and the praise rests on immediacy. The sūrah’s earlier promise that *“if you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of lesser misdeeds”* (4:31) also depends on the habit of turning quickly from smaller faults before they harden into major persistence. Delay is the bridge between small and great; this verse cuts that bridge by naming its end.

**The Mercy That Remains While Breath Remains**

Read with the verses that opened the sūrah, this warning is also a mercy. The call to be mindful of the Lord who created all from a single soul (4:1), to return orphan wealth with witnesses under God as Reckoner (4:6), and to accept discipline and then be relieved when mending appears (4:16) — all of this assumes that breath remains and that a turn is still possible. The sūrah does not treat a person who fell ignorantly as finished; it says Allah will pardon those who turn soon (4:17). It distrusts only the plan to keep persisting until the last hour and then to speak. That distinction keeps the community from two harms: despair that says no return will be accepted at all, and presumption that says the return can be postponed indefinitely. Both are corrected by time. While death has not yet presented itself, the door stands open; when it presents itself, the open door is the one the person chose not to enter. For them, the sūrah says, a painful punishment has been prepared — not as a surprise, but as the stated end of a path that was walked knowingly, step after step, until the time for choosing ran out.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:19

> O believers! It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will or mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry ˹as a ransom for divorce˺—unless they are found guilty of adultery. Treat them fairly. If you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Inheriting Women Was Not Inheritance**

The verse opens with a prohibition that corrects a pre-Islamic practice by naming it for what it was: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā yaḥillu lakum an tarithū al-nisāʾa karhan* — O believers, it is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will. In the custom around the revelation, when a man died, his male kin might claim authority over his widows as part of the estate, either marrying them without their choice, marrying them off to others for a bride-price they would keep, or blocking their remarriage until they ransomed themselves with their dowry or inheritance. The Qur’an calls that *irth* — inheritance — to expose its logic: the woman was treated as property to be passed on. By prohibiting it with *lā yaḥillu* — it is not lawful — the verse removes that logic entirely. The woman is not an asset to be divided after debts and bequests; she is an heir in her own right (4:7, 4:12) and a party to a covenant described as *“a firm commitment”* (4:21). The prohibition therefore stands at the head of the sūrah’s marriage reforms for a reason. After settling that wives have a fixed share and that dowries belong graciously to the woman herself (4:4), the sūrah must ensure that widowhood does not become a loophole where those rights are seized back through control of the person.

**Mistreatment to Reclaim the Dowry**

The second prohibition *wa lā taʿḍulūhunna li tadhhabū bi baʿḍi mā ātaytumūhunna illā an yaʾtīna bi fāḥishatin mubayyinah* — nor mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry as a ransom for divorce, unless they are found guilty of adultery — addresses the companion abuse. A husband who dislikes his wife might make her life straitened — *ʿaḍl* and *ḍirrār* — confining, harassing, or withholding rights, so that she will seek release and offer back her bridal gift to buy her freedom. The Qur’an names that strategy and forbids it, except in the case where the wife has committed a clear indecency — *fāḥishatin mubayyinah* — where scholars differed on whether open adultery lifts the restriction or whether it permits the husband to seek separation without penalty. Apart from that exception, the dowry, once given as a *niḥlah* — a free gift (4:4) — and even where it was a heap of gold — *qinṭār* — as the next verse will say (4:20), is not to be taken back by pressure. The sūrah has already said *“if they waive some of it willingly, with a contented soul, then enjoy it freely”* (4:4), making willingness the only lawful path to any return; this verse shows what unwilling extraction looks like when it is pursued as a tactic, and it blocks it.

**Treat Them Fairly**

The positive command *wa ʿāshirūhunna bi al-maʿrūf* — treat them fairly, live with them in kindness — uses the same root *ʿ-r-f* that elsewhere describes decent speech and customary good — *qawlan maʿrūfā* (4:5, 4:8) and *qawlan sadīdā* (4:9). *Maʿrūf* here is not only avoidance of harm; it is active companionship that is recognized as good — provision without stinginess, conversation without contempt, and intimacy without coercion. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and describes God as ever Merciful (4:29); that mercy is to appear in the home as well. The command to live with women in kindness was read to include what the next verses will detail: giving the dowry, not reclaiming it unjustly, not marrying the former wives of fathers (4:22), and respecting the full list of prohibited degrees (4:23). To live with a wife *bi al-maʿrūf* is therefore to keep the whole marriage ethic the sūrah is building: consent in entry, generosity in maintenance, equity if there is more than one wife (4:3, 4:129), and fairness in separation where it comes. The short phrase carries a long practice, because what is recognized as good is what a faithful community would recognize, not what a private preference would justify.

**If You Happen to Dislike Them**

The verse adds a counsel that reaches the heart at its most private: *fa in karihtumūhunna fa ʿasā an takrahū shayʾan wa yajʿalu Allāhu fīhi khayran kathīrā* — if you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing. Dislike — *kurh* — is not denied; the verse assumes it will occur. A wife’s character, habits, or circumstances may not match what a husband wishes, especially after time, grief, or dispute. Rather than treating dislike as proof that separation must be pressured, the verse asks for patience and for trust in an unseen turn. The same theme recurs elsewhere: *“perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you”* (2:216). Here the good is described as *khayran kathīran* — abundant good — which commentators linked to affection that returns, to righteous children born of the marriage, to the training of patience itself, or to the barakah that comes from keeping a covenant that was called firm. The sūrah’s earlier refrain that *“humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and that God wishes to lighten burdens (4:28) is already anticipated here: dislike is a weakness, and the law lightens it not by forcing immediate release through harm but by asking for fair companionship and by promising that what is kept for God’s sake may yield more than what is seized in haste.

**A Protection for Widows and Wives Alike**

Read together, the two prohibitions cover both ends of a marriage: its ending through death, where kin might claim the widow, and its middle where a husband might force a wife to buy her freedom. Both are blocked by the same principle that property belongs to its owner and that persons are not property. The verse generalises that principle with *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — O believers — addressing the whole community, not only husbands or heirs, because the abuse depended on social acquiescence. A man could only inherit a widow if others accepted that she was inheritable; a husband could only harass his wife into ransoming her dowry if family pressure made divorce shameful. By speaking to believers as such, the verse recruits the community to enforce the change. The next two verses will complete the dowry protection — not to take back even a heap of gold (4:20) and the reminder of *“how could you take it after you have enjoyed each other and she has taken a firm commitment from you?”* (4:21) — so that the entire law of dowry from gift to retention to release is made coherent. This verse is the hinge in that law: it forbids treating the woman as an estate and forbids treating the estate as a tool to coerce the woman.

**From Creation to Kind Companionship**

This verse returns the sūrah to its first note: *“He created you from a single soul, and from it its mate, and spread from both countless men and women”* (4:1), and *“Allah is ever Watchful over you”* (4:1). If humanity shares one origin and the Watcher is present in every transaction, then the widow is not an extra to be claimed and the wife is not a debtor to be squeezed. Both are the mate created from the single soul, the partner in spreading, the one whose womb-tie shares a root with mercy. To live with them *bi al-maʿrūf* is therefore not an additional virtue beyond law; it is the law’s completion. The sūrah has moved from dividing estates to dividing households, and it keeps the same standard: fixed rights honored, voluntary gifts left voluntary, and dislike handled with patience rather than pressure. A husband who finds himself disliking his wife is told to remain fair in company and to trust that God may place abundant good in what he currently dislikes. That trust is the counterpart to *“sufficient is Allah as Reckoner”* (4:6) for orphans and to *“Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing”* (4:12) for heirs. Here, the name behind the trust is the One who can turn dislike into blessing when the marriage is kept with kindness.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:20

> If you desire to replace a wife with another and you have given the former ˹even˺ a stack of gold ˹as a dowry˺, do not take any of it back. Would you ˹still˺ take it unjustly and very sinfully?

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Stack of Gold Does Not Change the Rule**

The condition *wa in aradtum istibdāla zawjin makāna zawj* — if you desire to replace a wife with another — names a common human turn: the wish to end one marriage and begin another. The verse attaches to that wish a stark test: *wa ātaytum iḥdāhunna qinṭāran fa lā taʾkhudhū minhu shayʾan* — even if you have given the former a stack of gold as a dowry, do not take any of it back. *Qinṭār* was explained as a large amount, a heap, a measure that conveys abundance without a fixed figure. By choosing the largest image, the Qur’an makes the rule amount-proof. It is easy to respect a modest gift; the test is whether a person respects a great one when desire shifts. The sūrah has already said to give dowries graciously as a free gift (4:4) and to permit only what is waived with a contented soul, and to forbid pressuring a wife to ransom herself (4:19). This verse removes the last rationalization for reclaiming: that the size of the gift makes it unreasonable to leave. Size does not make what was given freely into something that can be retrieved by pressure. The gift’s owner remains the woman, even when the husband’s preference has moved to another.

**Would You Take It Unjustly and Sinfully**

The rhetorical question *a taʾkhudhūnahu buhtānan wa ithman mubīnan* — would you take it unjustly and very sinfully — does more than forbid; it names the act. *Buhtān* is slander, false imputation, the act of covering one’s own desire with an invented fault in the other. A husband who wishes to replace his wife may be tempted to cast blame to justify retrieval, to suggest she was at fault so that taking back the gift seems like compensation. The Qur’an calls that covering what it is: a lie told to make taking look lawful. *Ithm mubīn* — clear, manifest sin — adds the moral weight. The sin is not hidden or ambiguous; it is open once the gift’s status as *niḥlah* — a free, sincere gift — is remembered. The pairing *buhtān* and *ithm* appears elsewhere for grave violations of trust, showing that to take back the dowry under pretext is not a minor lapse in generosity but a named combination of falsehood and sin. The question form invites the listener to answer no, and by answering no to commit to the rule that follows even when the amount tempts the opposite.

**Why the Qur’an Uses the Wish to Replace**

The phrase *istibdāla zawjin makāna zawj* was read not as a recommendation to replace but as a description of a case that will occur. The Qur’an does not encourage divorce in order to marry another; elsewhere it describes divorce as a hated permitted matter and it sets careful procedure for it. What the verse does is attach a protection to that case when it happens. The man who has decided to replace speaks from a position of power: he is the one initiating change, and he holds the leverage of maintenance, housing, and social expectation. The sūrah, which began with *“be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul”* (4:1) and which has guarded the orphan’s wealth with witnesses (4:6) and the heir’s share with limits (4:13–14), now guards the wife’s wealth at the precise moment when the husband’s power is greatest. That timing matters. Laws that protect only where power is balanced are not protections at all. A protection that speaks at the point of replacement shows that the dowry is not a deposit held by the wife while she remains pleasing and reclaimed when she does not; it is a settled transfer whose permanence does not depend on continuation of the marriage.

**Dowry as Permanent Gift**

The thought that a large gift might be reclaimed rests on treating the dowry as a price for continued marriage rather than as a gift that seals a covenant. The Qur’an rejects that treatment with language that will follow in the next verse: *“how could you take it after you have enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment?”* (4:21). The word *ifḍāʾ* — intimate going through — conveys the privacy and completeness of married life, while *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — firm, weighty covenant — recalls the covenant language used for prophets and for God’s own bond with humanity. Between those two facts — shared intimacy and a weighty pledge — there is no room to treat the bridal gift as a conditional loan. The sūrah has consistently moved wealth toward its owner and then kept it there: the orphan’s property to the orphan (4:2, 4:6), the bystander’s provision from the estate with kind speech (4:8), the heirs’ obligatory shares (4:7, 4:11–12). Here it moves the dowry to the wife and keeps it there, even when the marriage ends and even when the amount is a heap. The consistency is the point. What God has made obligatory is not to be undone by a change of desire.

**Unjust and Very Sinful — Two Names for One Taking**

The verse’s double accusation — *buhtānan wa ithman mubīnan* — was explained as covering both the method and the substance. *Buhtān* covers the false justification: to take the gift, the taker must invent a fault, magnify a dislike, or claim a right that does not exist, especially after being told to live with a wife fairly even when dislike occurs and to trust that God may place abundant good in what is disliked (4:19). *Ithm* covers the taking itself: it violates the law that gave the dowry as *ṣaduqah* with *niḥlah* and that permitted return only with *ṭīb al-nafs* — a contented soul (4:4). Together they show that reclaiming the *qinṭār* is not an isolated act of stinginess but a chain: desire to replace leads to justification by blame, which leads to seizure of what was not his. By naming both links, the verse makes the whole chain visible and therefore harder to walk. A person who sees that his justification would be called slander and his seizure called clear sin is more likely to leave the heap where it is. The sūrah’s earlier warning that consuming orphans’ wealth is eating fire (4:10) and that exceeding limits brings humiliating punishment (4:14) belongs to the same pedagogy: the true name of the act deters where the desire invites.

**The Ethic That Holds Across Replaceability**

Read with the previous verse’s *“live with them fairly”* (4:19) and the next verse’s *“a firm commitment”* (4:21), this verse forms a short sequence that teaches how to act when attachment changes. The first says be fair while you live together, even when you dislike. The second says do not reclaim a heap when you decide to replace. The third asks how could you take it after intimacy and covenant. Together they form an ethic that does not depend on continuity of feeling. The gift was given sincerely — *ṣaduqah* — as a sign of truthfulness at the start; it must be left sincerely at the end, even when the start feels distant. That ethic extends beyond dowry to any entrusted wealth. The sūrah has been training the reader to handle property as a trust watched by God (4:1), reckoned by Him (4:6), and bounded by Him (4:13). A stack of gold tests that training more purely than a small sum, because it offers the strongest reason to make an exception. By forbidding the exception here, the verse teaches that no amount is large enough to turn a gift back into a claim, and that the one who leaves it has preferred truthfulness to advantage and has left the matter to the One who sees both the heap given and the heap left behind.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:21

> And how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment?

**Expanded Commentary**

**How Could You Take It Back**

The question *wa kayfa taʾkhudhūnahu wa qad afḍā baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍ* — and how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately — makes retrieval feel unthinkable. The verb *afḍā* — to go through, to open fully — was explained as the complete privacy of marital intimacy, where two lives have intertwined without barrier. That intimacy is not a metaphor; it is the shared vulnerability of a household where bodies, secrets, and daily matters are known. The Qur’an asks how a person who has known that closeness could then turn and demand back a gift that sealed it, as though the shared history could be undone by reclaiming the *qinṭār* mentioned in the verse before (4:20). The question is rhetorical but also practical. Intimacy creates knowledge — the husband knows his wife as no other does — and that knowledge should generate honour, not a strategy for retrieval. To take back the dowry after *ifḍāʾ* is to treat what was most private as if it were a transaction that can be reversed, which the verse presents as morally incoherent.

**A Firm Commitment She Has Taken From You**

The second fact *wa qad akhadhna minkum mīthāqan ghalīẓā* — and she has taken from you a firm commitment — reframes the dowry as part of a covenant, not a payment for a service. *Mīthāq ghalīẓ* — firm, weighty covenant — is language the Qur’an uses for the bond God took from the prophets and from the Children of Israel, a solemn pledge that is not set aside lightly. To say the woman has taken such a commitment from the man places responsibility on him to stand by his word. The gift that accompanied that word — the *ṣaduqah* with *niḥlah* (4:4) — shares its weight. It was given to mark sincerity at entry; to demand it back at exit undermines the sincerity it marked. Commentators noted that the firmness of the commitment comes from several elements together: the proposal and acceptance, the witnesses, the dowry itself, and the life lived thereafter. Once that covenant has been040 entered and lived, the wealth transferred under it acquires a permanence that even a later wish to replace the wife (4:20) cannot dissolve. The question how could you therefore points to the covenant as witness against retrieval.

**Intimacy and Covenant Together Close the Door**

The verse places two facts side by side to close every justification. *Afḍā* answers the thought that the marriage was brief or formal and therefore the gift can be reclaimed; even a short shared intimacy creates a bond whose gift is not retrievable. *Mīthāq ghalīẓ* answers the thought that vows are light and that a heap of gold deserves reconsideration when circumstances change; the pledge was weighty from the start and remains so. Together they show that the dowry is not a deposit held against performance but a settled transfer that belongs to the woman whether the marriage continues or ends. The sūrah has guarded that transfer from the beginning: given graciously (4:4), not to be reclaimed by pressuring the wife to ransom herself (4:19), and not to be taken even when the husband wishes to replace his wife (4:20). This verse completes the guard by giving it a human and a legal reason. The human reason is shared life; the legal reason is a firm covenant. Both say the same thing: what was given freely under a weighty pledge stays with the one to whom it was given.

**Why the Question Form Teaches More Than a Prohibition**

A direct prohibition — do not take it — would have sufficed legally, as the previous verse gave (4:20). The shift to a question — how could you — moves from law to conscience. It asks the husband to imagine the conversation where he asks for the heap back after months or years of *ifḍāʾ* and after a *mīthāq ghalīẓ* was accepted in front of witnesses. The scene itself exposes the request as shameful without needing to add a new penalty. Elsewhere the sūrah pairs law with an invitation to reflect on what is disliked possibly holding abundant good (4:19); here it pairs law with an invitation to feel the incoherence of demanding back a pledge gift after intimacy. That method is consistent with the sūrah’s earlier pedagogy of asking the guardian to imagine his own weak children left behind (4:9) before handling an orphan’s wealth. Law becomes durable when the person sees why it is right, not only that it is commanded. By leaving the question open, the verse lets the husband answer it himself and, in answering no, strengthen his resolve to leave the dowry where it is.

**The Gift That Marked Truthfulness Remains True**

The root of *ṣaduqah* — truthfulness — helps answer the question. A dowry given as *ṣaduqah* was a sign that the husband’s word was sincere at the time. To reclaim it after intimacy and covenant is to act as though that sincerity can be withdrawn retroactively. The Qur’an treats truthfulness as a quality that, once shown in a covenant, should not be contradicted by later advantage. Other passages describe marital life as *“dwelling in tranquility”* with affection and mercy placed between spouses (30:21), and the same tranquility is injured when wealth given to mark truth is seized back. The verse therefore does more than settle a financial rule; it protects the meaning of the sign. A community that learns to leave the *qinṭār* where it was placed learns to mean what it pledged. That habit extends beyond marriage to every firm commitment the sūrah governs — witnesses at handover (4:6), limits in inheritance (4:13–14), and trade by mutual consent (4:29). In each, the pledge and the lived history make return or seizure incoherent. Here the pledge is the firmest named — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — and the history is the closest known — *afḍā* — so the incoherence of taking back is made most visible.

**Leaving What Was Given Where It Was Given**

The practical outcome is simple: the dowry stays with the woman, whether she was given little or a heap, whether the marriage continues or a new one is desired. The reasoning that stays with that outcome is humane: you have already been close beyond what can be undone, and you have already bound yourself with a weighty word she holds. To ask for the gift back is to ask to keep the closeness while erasing its sign, and to keep the covenant while retrieving its pledge, which cannot be done without *buhtān* — slander — and *ithm mubīn* — clear sin (4:20). The verse leaves the husband with that picture and with no further step to take. It does not add witnesses or a new procedure, because the question itself is sufficient to hold the line. A person who hears *kayfa* — how — and remembers both *ifḍāʾ* and *mīthāq ghalīẓ* will find the answer in the memory of his own home: he cannot, with honour, ask for it back, and so he leaves it where mercy first placed it.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:22

> Do not marry former wives of your fathers—except what was done previously. It was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Marriage the New Community Must Leave Behind**

The command *wa lā tankiḥū mā nakaḥa ābāʾukum min al-nisāʾ* — do not marry former wives of your fathers — addresses a practice that pre-Islamic Arabia allowed and that the new Medinan community had to abandon. In that custom, a son might claim his father’s widow as part of the inheritance, sometimes marrying her himself, sometimes marrying her off for a price, sometimes blocking her marriage until she paid to free herself. The verse severs that chain with a plain prohibition. The exception *illā mā qad salaf* — except what was done previously — lifts blame for marriages already contracted before the ruling, without validating them going forward. The Qur’an uses the same form elsewhere to close a prior allowance while opening a new standard, as with the prohibition of marrying two sisters together except what is past (4:23). By naming the act and then excepting the past, the sūrah shows a community in transition: what was done without knowledge while the old norm stood is left to God’s forbearance, but what is done after clarity is a chosen breach.

**Three Names for One Act**

The condemnation *innahu kāna fāḥishatan wa maqtan wa sāʾa sabīlā* — it was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice — gathers three distinct terms. *Fāḥishah* marks it as openly foul, an act whose indecency is visible. *Maqt* — despicable, hated — marks how God and sound nature regard it; it is not merely improper but loathed. *Sāʾa sabīlā* — evil way, evil path — marks its social effect as a road that spreads harm if taken. The layering is deliberate. A marriage that confuses generations blurs lineage, injures the honour of the father, wounds the son by placing him in his father’s intimate place, and reduces the widow at her most vulnerable moment to an asset passed on. Early commentators noted the specific occasion where a man sought to marry his father’s widow after the father’s death and the verse came to forbid it, but the ruling is general. The severity of the three names matches the gravity of those harms.
