Their *tabyīt* may feel like secret counsel, but the One who knows what is in hearts (4:63) and has perfect knowledge of them (4:39) writes it.

**So Turn Away From Them**

The instruction *fa aʿriḍ ʿanhum* — so turn away from them — repeats the counsel given for those whose hearts are known and whose oaths are hollow — *turn away, caution, and give penetrating advice* (4:63). *Iʿrāḍ* — turning away — was explained as not taking their nightly counsel as guidance, not seeking their approval, and not exposing their schemes with harsh retaliation that would deepen hypocrisy. The same turning was told where hypocrites turned away stubbornly (4:61) — answer with a measured withdrawal rather than with mimicry. The sūrah’s ethic is to return trusts and judge with fairness as noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58); to turn away from the night-plotters is to keep that fairness without being drawn into night-plotting oneself. Early authorities noted that the Prophet ﷺ was not told to punish the group at this stage but to disregard their nightly contradiction, because the record is kept and the trust put in God suffices.

**Put Your Trust in Allah**

The positive *wa tawakkal ʿalā Allāhi* — and put your trust in Allah — follows the turning as its support. *Tawakkul* — to entrust affairs, to rely — was explained as placing the matter of the night-plotters, of the coming fight, and of news that is publicised (4:83) in the hands of the One who is sufficient. The sūrah has built that sufficiency as Guardian and Helper (4:45), as Witness that the Messenger is sent to all people (4:79), and as sufficient to curb the disbelievers’ might (4:84). To trust is to fight in God’s cause after taking precautions (4:71) while knowing that the night-plotters’ weak schemes are ever weak (4:76). The one who says *we obey* and then spends the night contradicting trusts in darkness; the one told to turn away and trust entrusts the darkness to Him who records it. That trust was lived by the Prophet ﷺ when he put trust in God as Trustee after recording their schemes, and it is the same trust the sūrah will commend to believers who refer security or fear to the Messenger and authorities (4:83) rather than publicising it.

**And Allah Is Sufficient as Trustee of Affairs**

The closing *wa kafā bi Allāhi wakīlā* — and Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs — seals both recording and reliance. *Wakīl* — trustee, disposer of affairs, one entrusted with the outcome — was explained as the One to whom trust is returned, as trusts are returned to rightful owners (4:58) and as judgment is referred upward as best outcome (4:59). To say He is sufficient as *Wakīl* is to say that the nightly contradiction, the lagging at disaster, and the wishing at bounty all end in a trust He will dispose. The sūrah has used *kafā bi Allāhi* — sufficient is God — for Guardian, Helper, Witness, Knower — and here for Trustee, showing that each need has one sufficiency. For the community learning to go forth in groups or together, to distinguish blessing from gain (4:72–73), and to fight for the oppressed (4:75), sufficiency as Trustee means the night that others spend contradicting need not be spent fearing, because the recorder and the disposer is one, and His record misses no *tabyīt* and His disposal misses no *faḍl*. That is why the verse pairs recording with trust: what He writes He also handles, and what He handles as Trustee is sufficient.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:82

> Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Do They Not Reflect on the Qur’an**

The question *a fa lā yatadabbarūna al-Qurʾān* — do they not then reflect on the Qur’an — follows the nightly contradiction of those who say *we obey* and then spend the night contradicting (4:81). *Tadabbur* — to reflect, to follow through to the end, to look at the behind — was explained as reading not only the first word but the whole, following each limit to its place and seeing how it connects. The sūrah has shown much to reflect on: creation from one soul and guarding womb-ties (4:1), returning orphan wealth with witnesses (4:6), honouring shares after debts (4:11–12), guarding marriage with dowries and chastity (4:24), making things clear and guiding to noble ways and turning in mercy (4:26–27), taking precautions and going forth (4:71), and fighting for the oppressed (4:75). The night-plotters’ *tabyīt* — spending the night contradicting — is the opposite of *tadabbur*; one spends the night to distort, the other spends the night to understand. The question *a fa lā* — do they not then — implies that reflection would have prevented the contradiction, because the Qur’an’s coherence would have answered the very dispute they took to false judges (4:60) and the excuse they swore after disaster (4:62). The Qur’an elsewhere says that reflection leads to certainty that the Book is from God.

**Had It Been From Other Than Allah**

The test *wa law kāna min ʿindi ghayri Allāhi la wajadū fīhi ikhtilāfan kathīrā* — had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found in it many inconsistencies — was read as proof of divine origin by internal coherence. *Ikhtilāf kathīr* — many inconsistencies, much variance — was explained as contradiction between its rulings: inheritance shares that divide little and much (4:7), dowry as free gift not reclaimed (4:4, 4:20–21), trade by mutual consent (4:29), guardianship with witnesses (4:6), and fighting for the oppressed (4:75) — each could clash if man-made, yet they cohere. Had the Book been from a human — the Prophet ﷺ himself, or a committee, or a school — variance would have appeared as forgetfulness, favour, or change of mind under pressure. The sūrah’s detailed legislation, where a mother’s share shifts from third to sixth when siblings exist (4:11), where a wife’s share is quarter or eighth (4:12), where a bondwoman’s penalty is half (4:25), and where earth purifies where water fails (4:43) — is precisely detailed yet without contradiction, because the distributor is not the community that craves what others have (4:32) but the One who never wrongs by an atom (4:40). To reflect is to see that a Book that governs both *matāʿ qalīl* — little enjoyment (4:77) — and *ajr ʿaẓīm* — great reward (4:40, 4:67) — without tilting — *mayl* — is not a patchwork.

**The Inconsistency They Would Have Found Elsewhere**

Early authorities noted that human works show inconsistencies of three kinds: factual, where a claim made early is forgotten later; moral, where a limit praised in one place is excused in another; and stylistic, where voice shifts betray many hands. The Qur’an, though revealed over years in Makkah and Madinah, in ease and hardship, shows none of that. Its ethic of *iḥsān* — kind doing to parents, relatives, orphans, poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, those in possession (4:36) — appears with the same force where orphans are guarded and where fighting is commanded; its ethic of *ḥudūd* — limits — appears with the same word where inheritance is divided and wherefaces could be wiped (4:47). The hypocrites who spend the night contradicting contradict precisely because their plan is from other than God; it must vary, it must hide, it is recorded (4:81). The Book they hear by day does not vary, which is why the Prophet ﷺ is told to put trust in the sufficient Trustee (4:81); the Trustee’s word does not change between day and night. The sūrah elsewhere says *“do they not reflect, or are there locks on hearts”* and *“had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies”* is the key that would open those locks, if they reflected.

**Reflection as the Opposite of Night-Plotting**

Placed after nightly contradiction, this verse offers the alternative night. The same night that a party spends plotting what contradicts *we obey* could be spent in *tadabbur* — following the Qur’an to its ends. The sūrah has taught that news of security or fear should be referred to the Messenger and authorities, where those with sound judgment would validate it (4:83); reflection is that referral at the level of the individual. A community that reflects will not publicise fear for the weak schemer’s profit, nor will it fear people as God should be feared when the order to fight comes (4:77). It will see that death overtakes wherever you are, even in towers (4:78), and that both good and evil are from God’s decree while good from Him and evil from the self as means (4:78–79), a coherence that only reflection holds together. The verse generalises the sūrah’s method since *“Allah wills to make things clear”* (4:26): clarity is given, but it requires *tadabbur* to be entered. The night-plotters who do not reflect choose the weak scheme that is ever weak (4:76); the reflectors find the Book whose many detailed limits do not contradict because they were not from a weak plotter but from the All-Knowing, All-Wise.

**A Verse That Holds the Book’s Trust**

Between the record of nightly schemes and the publicising of security or fear (4:81, 4:83), this verse holds the Book’s trust. The trust that the sūrah commanded to return — *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* (4:58) — includes the greatest trust: the Qur’an itself. To reflect on it is to return it to its purpose — to be the judge in tangles — *yuḥakkimūka* (4:65) — and the referent for disputes as best outcome (4:59). To fail to reflect is to leave it as sound while contradicting it by night, which is the precise breach the previous verse named. The sūrah’s question *do they not then reflect* is therefore not a critique of intelligence but of will, as the next verse will say *had it not been for God’s grace and mercy you would have followed Satan, except for a few* (4:83). Reflection is grace-enabled, and its fruit is seeing no inconsistency where inconsistency would have been many, had the source been other than God. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, that seeing is itself lightening: the Book that commands a mother’s sixth and a wife’s eighth can be trusted to command fighting and purification without wavering, because its Source does not waver, and the one who reflects will find that the path from orphan to inheritance to marriage to battle is one straight path walked.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:83

> And when they hear news of security or fear, they publicize it. Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan—except for a few.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When They Hear News of Security or Fear, They Publicise It**

The verse says *wa idhā jāʾahum amrun min al-amni aw al-khawfi adhāʿū bihi* — and when news comes to them of security or fear, they publicise it — broadcasting it, spreading it. *Amn* — security, safety — and *khawf* — fear, threat — were explained as reports from the front, rumours of victory or defeat, or news about expeditions like those the believers were told to go forth in groups or together with precautions (4:71). *Adhāʿū bihi* — to publicise, to spread wide — was read as hurrying the news to others without verification, driven by love of being first, by anxiety, or by the laggers’ wish to justify not being present (4:72). The sūrah has shown that news in Madinah could be a trust: the community’s safety depends on whether reports are true and on who hears them when. To spread security prematurely can breed complacency; to spread fear prematurely can breed the fear of people as God should be feared (4:77) that made a group ask *why have You ordered us to fight, delay us*. The verse therefore diagnoses a habit that harms the same community that was taught to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58) and to obey and refer disputes (4:59). News, too, is a trust to be returned to rightful handlers before it is passed on.

**Had They Referred It to the Messenger or Their Authorities**

The corrective *wa law raddūhu ilā al-rasūli wa ilā ulī al-amri minhum la ʿalimahu alladhīna yastanbiṭūnahu minhum* — had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it — was read as the sūrah’s method for reports. *Radd* — to refer, to return — matches *raddūhu ilā Allāhi wa al-rasūl* — refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59). *Ulī al-amr* — those in authority — here are the leaders and those with insight, the same whose obedience within obedience was commanded and whose referral is best (4:59). *Yastanbiṭūnahu* — to draw out, to validate, to extract by sound inference — was explained as the work of those with *istinbāṭ* — expertise, the ability to test a report, to know its source, and to judge its implication before publicising. The sūrah has shown that purification requires knowing what is said in prayer (4:43), that fighting requires *ḥidhr* — precaution — and that judging requires hearing and seeing (4:58). Referring news for *istinbāṭ* is that precaution for information. The hypocrites who spend the night contradicting what was said (4:81) and who do not reflect on the Qur’an (4:82) are the type who would *adhāʿū bihi* — spread without referring — because the nightly plot and the hasty broadcast share the same root: bypassing the lawful handlers.

**Those With Sound Judgment Would Have Validated It**

The phrase *alladhīna yastanbiṭūnahu minhum* was stressed as showing that not every listener can validate news; it is those among the authorities with sound inference who can. The community was therefore taught to distinguish between hearing and validating, as it distinguishes between craving another’s portion and asking God for bounty (4:32). To validate — *istinbāṭ* — includes checking the transmitter, the context, and whether publicising serves security or fear as *amr* — affair — to be managed. Early reports linked the verse to the Prophet’s handling of the expedition to the Confederates, where news of security and fear about the Banū Qurayẓah and the approaching parties needed to be managed rather than broadcast. The sūrah generalises: whether news is good — *ḥasanah from God* — or evil — from the self where hands put forward (4:79) — its handling belongs to those who can draw out its meaning. The believers who were told *“do they not reflect on the Qur’an, had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies”* (4:82) are here told to reflect on news as they reflect on the Book: refer it, extract, and then speak.

**Had It Not Been for Allah’s Grace and Mercy**

The reminder *wa law lā faḍlu Allāhi ʿalaykum wa raḥmatuhu la ittabaʿtumu al-shayṭāna illā qalīlā* — had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few — was read as both history and warning. *Faḍl* and *raḥmah* — grace and mercy — were explained as the sending of the Messenger to be obeyed by God’s leave (4:64), the witness brought and the Day where no statement can be hidden (4:41–42), the earth that purifies where water fails (4:43), and the lightening because humankind was created weak (4:28). Without that, the community that heard security or fear would have followed Satan’s weak schemes (4:76) that the lagger and the fearful already followed when they feared people as God (4:77) and said *this is from you* at evil (4:78). The phrase *illā qalīlan* — except for a few — matches *few would have obeyed* the hard command to sacrifice or leave homes (4:66) and *few believed* among those given a portion (4:55). The few represent those who, by grace, did refer, did validate, and did not publicise. The verse therefore tells the broader community that the habit of broadcasting without referral is not a small slip; without grace and mercy, it is the path by which Satan is followed.

**A Verse That Guards Information as Trust**

Placed between the call to reflect on the Qur’an’s coherence (4:82) and the command to fight where the Prophet ﷺ is accountable only for himself but must motivate believers (4:84), this verse guards information as trust. The sūrah has commanded to return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness as a noble exhortation (4:58); news of security or fear is a trust to be returned to the Messenger and authorities before it is judged publicly. To publicise without referral is to handle a trust as devouring by falsehood (4:29) handles wealth — quickly and without mutual consent — while to refer for *istinbāṭ* is to handle it as trade by consent. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is lightening: you need not decide every report alone; refer it to those with sound judgment, and the validation will be drawn out. The sūrah’s ethic of *iḥsān* — kind doing — to parents, relatives, neighbours, and travellers (4:36) becomes, at the level of news, not spreading fear that harms the weak and not spreading security that lulls the guard. Had the community not been graced, the broadcast of fear would have made it fear people as God; by grace, it can refer, validate, and then, if fighting is required, go forth with precautions, as commanded, rather than as rumour drives.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:84

> So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺. You are accountable for none but yourself. And motivate the believers ˹to fight˺, so perhaps Allah will curb the disbelievers’ might. And Allah is far superior in might and in punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**So Fight in the Cause of Allah**

The command *fa qātil fī sabīli Allāhi* — so fight in the cause of Allah — is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ alone after the diagnosis that many lag, that news of security or fear is publicised without referral (4:83), and that some were told *do not fight, establish prayer and give alms* then feared people as God when fighting was prescribed (4:77). *Fa* — so — ties the command to that diagnosis: though many hesitate, the cause remains God’s, the same *sabīl* that believers fight for while disbelievers fight for the Devil whose schemes are ever weak (4:76), and the same cause for which the oppressed cry for a guardian and helper (4:75). The sūrah has said to take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to let those who sell this life for the next fight with a great reward whether martyred or victorious (4:74); here the Prophet ﷺ is told to fight even if others do not. The cause does not depend on the laggers’ measure — *blessed we were not there* at disaster (4:72) — nor on the fearful’s plea for delay; it is God’s path made clear (4:26) and the straight path to which doing what was advised would have guided (4:68).

**You Are Accountable for None but Yourself**

The clause *lā tukallafu illā nafsaka* — you are accountable for none but yourself — was read as both limit and liberation. The Prophet ﷺ is responsible for his own fighting, not for compelling the hypocrites who turn away stubbornly (4:61) and spend the night contradicting (4:81). The sūrah has said messengers are sent to be obeyed by God’s leave (4:64), that obedience to him is obedience to God (4:80), and that he is not a keeper over those who turn (4:80) but a warner and witness (4:41). To be accountable only for himself frees him from the burden that the laggers’ absence reflects on his mission; the mission remains to convey, to fight, and to motivate. The same clause was read as mercy for the community: each believer is accountable for his own referral to the Messenger and authorities (4:83) and for his own standing at *ḥidhr*. The sūrah elsewhere says *“no soul is charged beyond what it can bear”* and here that charging is individualized at the point of fighting, where fear of people can make a person feel responsible for all.

**Motivate the Believers**

The addition *wa ḥarriḍ al-muʾminīna* — and motivate, urge, rouse the believers — was explained as the Prophet’s second task beyond his own fighting: to stir the believers to fight with reminders of what the sūrah has shown — the Gardens with vast shade for believing and doing good (4:57), the great reward for selling this life for the next whether martyred or victorious (4:74), and the cry of the oppressed who ask for a guardian and helper from grace (4:75). *Taḥrīḍ* — to urge, to sharpen — was read as encouragement that makes the reluctant firm — *ashadda tathbītā* — the firmness that doing what was advised would have given (4:66). The sūrah has shown why urging is needed: some fear people as God (4:77), some lag and call absence a blessing (4:72), some publicise fear. Urging counters each with the sūrah’s measures — *Satan’s schemes are weak* (4:76), *death overtakes wherever you are even in towers* (4:78), *good from God, evil from self by what hands put forward* (4:79). To motivate is therefore not to push the weak beyond lightening (4:28) but to remind them that fighting after precautions, in God’s cause, is the form obedience takes where oppression exists.

**Perhaps Allah Will Curb the Disbelievers’ Might**

The hope *ʿasā Allāhu an yakuffa baʾsa alladhīna kafarū* — so perhaps Allah will curb, restrain, the might of the disbelievers — was read as the divine outcome of the Prophet’s fighting and urging. *Baʾs* — might, force, violence — was explained as the power by which the land of oppressors holds the weak — men, women, children — who cry for deliverance. To curb that *baʾs* is the sūrah’s answer to that cry; the guardian and helper appointed from grace (4:45, 4:75) curbs the might that made the *qaryah ẓalimi ahluhā* — the town of oppressors. The word *ʿasā* — perhaps — was explained as assurance from God, as elsewhere *“perhaps your Lord will...”* means He will, because the speaker is God. The sūrah has shown that curbing comes not by the believers’ numbers alone but by God’s might, as the next clause says He is superior in might and punishment. Early reports placed the verse when the Prophet ﷺ faced the Confederates with few, and God curbed them by wind and division; the type was read as every time believers fight with precautions after referral, God curbs.

**Allah Is Far Superior in Might and in Punishment**

The closing *wa Allāhu ashaddu baʾsan wa ashaddu tankīlā* — and Allah is far superior in might and in punishment — was read as the ground for *perhaps He will curb*. *Ashaddu baʾsan* — more intense in might — than any *baʾs* believers face; *ashaddu tankīlā* — more intense in punishment, in making an example — than any deterrent the disbelievers deploy. The pair matches the sūrah’s earlier *“Satan’s schemes are ever weak”* (4:76) and *“that is easy for Allah”* where deliberate devouring leads to Fire (4:30). The might that appoints heirs after debts (4:11), that renews skin for tasting (4:56), and that multiplies an atom’s weight (4:40) is the might that curbs. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is the final lightening for fighting: you are accountable only for yourself, urge the believers, and perhaps God will curb the might that frightened you as God should be feared. The superior might and punishment are not threats to the believers who fight for the oppressed; they are guarantees that the cause they fight in — God’s — is supported by a might no *baʾs* can match and a punishment no *kayd* can withstand.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:85

> Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. And Allah is Watchful over all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Intercession for Good and for Evil**

The verse states *man yashfaʿ shafāʿatan ḥasanatan yakun lahu naṣībun minhā wa man yashfaʿ shafāʿatan sayyiʾatan yakun lahu kiflun minhā* — whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. *Shafāʿah* — intercession, mediation, joining — was explained as adding one’s effort to another’s so that a matter is accomplished: recommending, urging, or making a cause possible. *Ḥasanah* — good — was read as the causes the sūrah has commended — motivating believers to fight where fighting is in God’s cause for the oppressed (4:74–75, 4:84), appointing mediators who desire harmony where God brings it (4:35), returning trusts to rightful owners and judging with fairness (4:58), and referring news of security or fear to those with sound judgment (4:83). *Sayyiʾah* — evil — was read as the opposite — interceding with *ṭāghūt* (4:60), promoting stinginess (4:37), encouraging lagging (4:72), or publicising fear (4:83). *Naṣīb* — share in reward — and *kifl* — share in burden, portion to bear — were explained as the intercessor’s recorded portion of the outcome, because intercession makes the outcome possible. The sūrah has said that the atom’s weight is not wronged but multiplied (4:40) and that whoever obeys the Messenger is with the blessed (4:69); intercession for good is the social form of that obedience, where the urger shares the reward of the doer.

**A Share in Reward and a Share in Burden**

The pairing *naṣīb* and *kifl* was stressed as exact. *Naṣīb* — share — echoes *naṣīban mafrūḍan* — obligatory share — for heirs (4:7) and *naṣībun mimmā iktasabū* — share of what they earned for men and women (4:32), showing that intercession earns as deeds earn. *Kifl* — portion, like the load on a camel’s side — was explained as the burden of evil intercession, the weight the intercessor bears of the sin he helped make possible, as the sūrah elsewhere warns that deliberate devouring leads to Fire easy for God (4:30) and that trading a portion of the Book for misguidance bears humiliating punishment (4:37). Early authorities gave examples: interceding to free an oppressed person, to reconcile spouses, or to motivate to fight in God’s cause brings a share of reward; interceding to protect an oppressor, to take a widow as inheritance (4:19), or to seek a false judge (4:60) brings a share of burden. The sūrah’s ethic is therefore collective: no one acts alone, and no one’s speech — *we hear and obey* or *we hear and disobey* (4:46) — is without share.

**Why Intercession Follows Motivating to Fight**

Placed after *motivate the believers to fight, perhaps God will curb the might* (4:84), this verse generalizes that urging. *Taḥrīḍ* — to motivate — is a form of *shafāʿah* — intercession — where the motivator joins the fighter’s cause and shares its reward, the *ajr ʿaẓīm* promised whether martyred or victorious (4:74). The verse was linked to the Prophet ﷺ urging the believers while he himself fights though accountable only for himself (4:84); his urging is intercession for a good cause whose share is great. The opposite — interceding for evil — was linked to those who intercede with *ṭāghūt*, who reassure disbelievers they are better guided (4:51), and who lag and wish for gain (4:73). The sūrah has shown that Satan’s schemes are weak (4:76); to intercede for the Devil’s cause is to join weakness and to bear its burden. The verse therefore tells the community that urging matters; the one who says *“do not fight, delay us”* (4:77) will have a share in the burden of those who stay from fighting for the oppressed, while the one who says *take precautions and go forth* (4:71) will have a share in the reward of those who go.

**And Allah Is Watchful Over All Things**

The closing *wa kāna Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin ḥasībā* — and Allah is Watchful over all things, sufficient as Reckoner — was read as the recorder of shares. *Ḥasīb* — reckoner, guardian, sufficient — was explained as counting intercession as deeds are counted, not missing the atom’s weight (4:40) and not wronging by a thread (4:49, 4:77). To say He is Watchful over all things is to say that intercession for good done quietly — a word that moves a hesitant fighter, a mediation that seeks harmony (4:35), a referral of news to sound judgment (4:83) — is known and weighted, and that intercession for evil done by night — *yubayyitūna* what contradicts *we obey* (4:81) — is also known and weighted. The sūrah has used *ḥasīb* for the orphan’s handover — *sufficient is God as Reckoner* (4:6) — and *shahīd* for witnessing the Messenger’s mission (4:79), and *wakīl* for trusting affairs (4:81); here *ḥasīb* gathers them as the watch over every joining. The one who intercedes for a good cause, even if the cause does not fully succeed — *perhaps God will curb* (4:84) — still has his *naṣīb*; the one who intercedes for evil, even if the evil is not fully realized, still bears *kifl*. Watchfulness ensures both, which is why the verse is both invitation and warning.

**A Community Where Urging Earns**

Between the command to fight and the greeting that answers with better (4:86), this verse holds the community’s social economy together. The economy was stated as: do not crave what God gave some over others; ask Him for bounty (4:32) — because shares are from Him. Here it adds: whoever joins a good cause will have a share in it; whoever joins an evil, a burden. The community that was told *“if you avoid major sins We will cover lesser ones”* (4:31) and *“good from God, evil from yourself”* (4:79) is here told that joining amplifies both: joining good multiplies good, joining evil burdens. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is the lightest encouragement to speak: a word of intercession for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75), for the couple seeking mediators, for the fighter needing urging, earns a *naṣīb* as though the speaker had done the deed. The sūrah therefore invites the tongue that once lagged or publicised fear to become a tongue that intercedes for good, whose share is reward and whose watcher is the One who is Watchful over all things.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:86

> And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Respond With a Better Greeting or At Least Similarly**

The verse commands *wa idhā ḥuyyītum bi taḥiyyatin fa ḥayyū bi aḥsana minhā aw ruddūhā* — and when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. *Taḥiyyah* — greeting, gift of life — was explained as *al-salām* — peace — the word the sūrah will soon name where those who offer peace are not to be called *you are no believer* (4:94). The command to answer with better — *aḥsana minhā* — or to return it equally — *aw ruddūhā* — was read as ethic for all greetings among believers, and by extension for any kindness. The sūrah has commanded *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36), and has warned that interceding for good brings a share in reward (4:85). To answer a greeting with better is the smallest *iḥsān* that keeps the larger ones alive; it is intercession for good at the level of a word. The community that was told to take precautions and go forth (4:71), to reflect on the Qur’an that has no inconsistency (4:82), and to refer news of security or fear to those with sound judgment (4:83) is here told that the first sound of meeting is peace, and its reply should be more peace. Early authorities noted that the better greeting was exemplified as *wa ʿalaykum al-salām wa raḥmatu Allāh* for *al-salām ʿalaykum*, and at least the same for where equality is required.

**Greeting as Peace After Battle and Before**

The placement matters. The sūrah has moved through fighting — believers fight for God, disbelievers for the Devil whose schemes are weak (4:76), those who sell this life for the next fight whether martyred or victorious (4:74), and the oppressed cry for a guardian and helper (4:75). In that field, greetings can be mistaken for stratagem, as the next verses warn not to say to one who offers peace *you are no believer* seeking fleeting gain (4:94). This verse establishes the rule before that warning: when a greeting of peace is offered, answer it with better or same. The rule applies to the battlefield where a combatant may offer *salām* and to the town where neighbours meet. The sūrah elsewhere says *“do not kill yourselves, surely Allah is ever Merciful to you”* (4:29), and greeting with peace is the opposite of killing; it is the invitation to keep the bond that the lagger treated as if it were none (4:73). To answer peace with more peace is therefore the opposite of the night-plotters who spend the night contradicting *we obey* (4:81). One adds peace, the other plots harm; the verse chooses which night the tongue should keep.

**At Least Similarly — The Minimum That Protects**

The option *aw ruddūhā* — or at least similarly — was explained as the minimum that prevents greeting from becoming a hierarchy. To return the same — *wa ʿalaykum al-salām* for *al-salām ʿalaykum* — was read as obligatory where better is recommended, so that no one is left without answer. The sūrah has used similar minima elsewhere: the atom’s weight not wronged (4:40), the thread not wronged (4:49, 4:77), and the intercessor’s share for good (4:85) — each ensures that the small is counted. To answer at least similarly ensures the small greeting is counted. The ethic was extended to those in possession — bondspeople — and to neighbours near and distant (4:36); a greeting is due to each without regard to status, because *you are from one another* (4:25) and the sūrah opened with *from a single soul* (4:1). To withhold a greeting or to answer with less would be the stinginess that conceals bounty (4:37) at the scale of a word, while to answer with better is the donation from what was provided (4:39) at the same scale. The sūrah’s measure of *naṣīb* — share — for intercession (4:85) thus includes the share of peace returned.

**Surely Allah Is a Vigilant Reckoner of All Things**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿalā kulli shayʾin ḥasībā* — surely Allah is a vigilant Reckoner of all things — matches the smallness of the act with the greatness of the watcher. *Ḥasīb* — reckoner, guardian, sufficient — was explained as counting the greeting and the reply as deeds, not missing the better — *aḥsan* — nor the equal — *radd* — as intercession’s share is not missed (4:85). The sūrah has used *ḥasīb* for the orphan’s handover — *sufficient is God as Reckoner* (4:6) — and for the watch over all things where intercession’s share is weighed (4:85); here it is the watch over greetings. That continuity shows greetings are not courtesies outside law; they are entries in the ledger that also records trusts and judgments, and that ledger is kept with the same sufficiency that multiplies an atom’s weight. The One who is All-Hearing, All-Seeing over trusts and judgments (4:58) is the Reckoner overpeace offered and peace returned. To answer with better is therefore not only kindness to the greeter; it is reckoning before the Reckoner, where even a better peace is multiplied.

**A Verse That Holds the Community’s Tongue**

Placed between the share for intercession (4:85) and the gathering on the Day about which there is no doubt (4:87), this verse holds the community’s tongue at its first word. The sūrah has diagnosed distorted words — *we hear and disobey* veiled as obedience (4:46), *rāʿinā* played with tongues (4:46), *we obey* spent the night contradicting (4:81) — and has prescribed straight speech — *qawlan sadīdā* (4:9), *qawlan balīghā* that reaches souls (4:63). Greeting with peace and answering with better is the daily practice of that straightness where speech is most frequent. A community that learns to answer *al-salām* with *aḥsan* will be the community that does not say to the one who offers peace *you are no believer* for fleeting gain (4:94), that does not call absence at disaster a blessing (4:72), and that does not wish after gain as if no bond existed (4:73). For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the command is also light: when greeted, add a word. That added word, counted as *ḥasīb* and weighted as an atom, is the least burden that still joins the great reward, and it is the sound of the straight path walked.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:87

> Allah, there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt. And whose word is more truthful than Allah’s?

**Expanded Commentary**

**There Is No God Except Him**

The verse opens with *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa* — Allah, there is no god worthy of worship except Him — the same declaration that the sūrah placed at the root of worship: *worship God and associate none with Him* (4:36) and *association is not forgiven* (4:48). The sūrah has shown what association looks like in practice — belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51), seeking judgment of false judges though commanded to reject them (4:60), and saying to one who offers peace *you are no believer* for gain (4:94). To say *lā ilāha illā huwa* is to deny those rivals at the level of worship, judgment, and truth. The phrase follows the command to answer greeting with better or same and the reckoning of all things by the Vigilant Reckoner (4:86) to remind that the Reckoner is the only God to be worshipped. The sūrah elsewhere pairs *lā ilāha illā huwa* with *there is no helper* (4:48) to show that the One who alone is to be worshipped is the One who alone suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). Here the declaration stands as the premise for what follows: He who alone is God is the One who will gather.

**He Will Certainly Gather You on the Day of Judgment**

The promise *la yajmaʿannakum ilā yawmi al-qiyāmati lā rayba fīhi* — He will certainly gather all of you together on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt — was read as the gathering that the previous witness scene required. *Yajmaʿannakum* — will gather you — with emphatic *lām* and *nūn* was explained as the muster where a witness is brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his (4:41), where those who denied and disobeyed will wish to be dust and will not hide any statement (4:42), and where every soul that tasted death — even in towers (4:78) — is brought. The Day was called *yawm al-qiyāmah* — Day of Standing — because all stand before the Reckoner who counts even a better greeting (4:86) and an intercessor’s share (4:85). *Lā rayba fīhi* — no doubt about it — was stressed as removing the doubt that made a group fear people as God and ask *why have You ordered us to fight, delay us* (4:77) and that made laggers call absence a blessing (4:72). That doubt treats the *dunyā*’s little enjoyment as more certain than the Hereafter; the verse says the gathering is more certain. The One who is Vigilant Reckoner over all things (4:86) is the One who will certainly gather all things.

**About Which There Is No Doubt**

The clause *lā rayba fīhi* was linked to the Qur’an’s opening — *“this is the Book, no doubt in it”* — and to the sūrah’s question *do they not reflect on the Qur’an? Had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* (4:82). To have no doubt about the Day is the fruit of reflecting on the Book that has no inconsistency; the Book that governs inheritance whether little or much (4:7), dowry not reclaimed (4:20–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29) without contradiction is the same Book that promises the gathering without doubt. The sūrah has shown doubt’s practical fruit: publicising news of security or fear without referral (4:83), seeking *ṭāghūt* though commanded to reject it (4:60), and distorting *rāʿinā* (4:46). Each is a doubt about whether the Book and Messenger can handle the affair. To say *no doubt about it* is to answer that doubt at its root: the gathering where every atom is weighed and multiplied (4:40) is as sure as the Book’s coherence, because both are from the same One.

**Whose Word Is More Truthful Than Allah’s**

The question *wa man aṣdaqu min Allāhi ḥadīthā* — and whose word is more truthful than Allah’s — seals the declaration and the promise. *Aṣdaqu* — more truthful, most truthful — was explained as comparison that denies any competitor; no *ḥadīth* — statement, discourse — is truer. The sūrah has shown competing statements: *we hear and disobey* veiled as obedience (4:46), *rāʿinā* twisted, *we obey* contradicted by night-plotting (4:81), *we intended only goodwill* after disaster (4:62), *this is from you* at evil (4:78). Each is a *ḥadīth* that the sūrah said its speakers can hardly comprehend any *ḥadīth* (4:78). Against those, God’s *ḥadīth* — that there is no god except Him, that He will certainly gather, that an atom is not wronged but multiplied — was presented as the only truthful measure. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Allah’s promise is truth”* and that the hypocrites’ oaths are shields; this question asks the listener to choose which *ḥadīth* to trust. The same *ḥadīth* that the sūrah said would be understood if they reflected will, on the Day gathered without doubt, be the one by which every other *ḥadīth* is judged, as no statement can be hidden from God (4:42) and the intercessor’s share is known (4:85).

**A Verse That Holds Worship and Gathering Together**

Placed between greeting with peace and the division over hypocrites who regressed because of misdeeds (4:88), this verse holds worship and gathering together. To say *there is no god except Him* is to worship without association — the first command (4:36); to believe He will certainly gather on the Day about which there is no doubt is to live as one who will be gathered, and therefore to return trusts, judge fairly, and fight for the oppressed where commanded. The two are one, because the One to be worshipped is the Gatherer. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the gathering is not a threat that crushes; it is the assurance that the better greeting answered, the share interceded for good, and the atom donated are all gathered and counted by the Vigilant Reckoner. Whose word is more truthful? The sūrah answers with the Book that, had it been from other than God, would have shown many inconsistencies but shows none, and with the Day that, about which there is no doubt, will show that the truthful *ḥadīth* was God’s, and that to have worshipped Him alone was to have trusted the only word that never varies.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:88

> Why are you ˹believers˺ divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites while Allah allowed them to regress ˹to disbelief˺ because of their misdeeds? Do you wish to guide those left by Allah to stray? And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Why Are You Divided Into Two Groups Regarding the Hypocrites**

The question *fa mā lakum fī al-munāfiqīna fiʾatayni* — why are you believers divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites — addresses the community after the diagnosis that some among you lag (4:72) and some turn away stubbornly from the Book and Messenger (4:61) while claiming *we hear and obey* by day and plotting by night (4:81). *Fiʾatayni* — two groups, two factions — was explained as a split among Companions after the expedition to Uḥud, where hypocrites lagged and believers differed over whether they were still counted as believers to be helped or as a group to be treated as having regressed. The sūrah has shown the hypocrites’ many signs — seeking false judges though commanded to reject them (4:60), publicising security or fear without referral (4:83), and saying to one who offers peace *you are no believer* for gain (4:94) — and the believers’ instruction to refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59). To be *fiʾatayni* about them is to disagree about the very case the sūrah has been clarifying, as though the limits about trust, greeting, and fighting were not yet clear enough to judge.

**While Allah Allowed Them to Regress Because of Misdeeds**

The clause *wa Allāhu arkasa hum bi mā kasabū* — while Allah allowed them to regress to disbelief because of what they earned — was read as divine recompense that inverts progress. *Arkasa* — to turn over, to make regress, to return to the start — was explained as turning them back into disbelief after they had outwardly moved forward, because of *bi mā kasabū* — because of what they earned — the same phrase that ties disaster to hands (4:62) and evil from the self (4:79). The sūrah has tied their earning to many acts: seeking *ṭāghūt* (4:60), distorting *rāʿinā* (4:46), fabricating lies as blatant sin (4:50), believing in *jibt* (4:51), and envying for bounty (4:54). To earn those is to earn regression, because the path God made clear (4:26) and to which He would have guided had they done what was advised (4:68) was left, and the far straying Satan desires (4:60) was followed. The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Guide and that He guides to the straight path whom He wills; *arkasa* shows the opposite dispensation: those who earn deviation are allowed to regress, as the sūrah earlier said *“Allah has condemned them for disbelief, so they do not believe except a few”* (4:46).

**Do You Wish to Guide Those Left to Stray**

The question *a turīdūna an tahdū man aḍalla Allāhu* — do you wish to guide those God has left to stray — was read as correction of the faction that wanted to treat the regressed as still guided. *Man aḍalla Allāhu* — those God has left to stray — was explained as those whom He allowed to regress after they chose what earns regression; the sūrah has warned that whoever He leaves to stray, you will never find a way for them (4:88, 4:143). To wish to guide them as though the choice had not been made is to dispute the divine recompense itself. The sūrah has shown that guidance is favour from God known to Him (4:70) and that whoever obeys is with the blessed (4:69); favour and guidance follow obedience, not claim. To seek to guide as believers those whose earning was to seek false judges and to lag at disaster as if no bond existed (4:73) is to confuse the community’s *mawaddah* — bond — with approval. The sūrah elsewhere says that God guides not those who do wrong after clear signs, and *arkasa* is the term for that wrong’s end where guidance is withdrawn.

**Whoever He Leaves to Stray, You Will Never Find a Way**

The closing *wa man yuḍlili Allāhu fa lan tajida lahu sabīlā* — and whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way — was read as sealing the case. *Sabīl* — way — was explained as the path God wills to make clear (4:26), the noble ways of those before, and the straight path (4:68). To be left without *sabīl* is to be without the straight path that would have been granted had they done what was advised, and without the referral that is best outcome (4:59). The sūrah will repeat this principle where hypocrites are concerned, showing that where God allows regression, human *tawfīq* cannot force guidance. The phrase *lan tajida* — you will never find — was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to any believer, as though to say look for a way for them and you will not find one, because the sūrah has already shown that the distributor of bounty and guidance is not the envious who would not give a speck (4:53) but the One who never wrongs by an atom. To seek a way for those He has left to stray is therefore to seek *sabīl* where He has closed it, while the sūrah’s open *sabīl* — trade by mutual consent (4:29), greeting with better (4:86), and fighting for the oppressed (4:75) — remains for those who have not regressed.

**A Verse That Steadies the Community’s Judgment**

Placed after the gathering on the Day about which there is no doubt and whose word is more truthful than God’s (4:87), this verse steadies judgment before the next verses describe who may be taken as allies and who must be left where they are allies of a treaty people or opposed to fighting (4:89–90). The community divided into two groups about hypocrites is told that division itself is mistaken where God has already allowed regression because of what was earned; the hypocrites are not a middle group to be guided as though they were steadfast, because the sūrah has shown their many signs — night-plotting, publicising without referral, seeking *ṭāghūt* — and their recompense is regression. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is also lightening: you need not guide those God has left to stray; you need only be clear about regressed because of misdeeds, so that the bond *you are from one another* (4:25) is not used to excuse the one who treats it as if it were none. The sūrah therefore teaches the community to judge as God judges — by what was earned — and to keep its two groups as one in that judgment, so that the straight path remains clear.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:89

> They wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. So do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take any of them as allies or helpers,

**Expanded Commentary**

**They Wish You Would Disbelieve as They Have**

The verse states *waddū law takfurūna kamā kafarū fa takūnūna sawāʾ* — they wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. *Waddū* — they wish, they love — was explained as the desire of the regressed hypocrites and those who turned away (4:88) that the believers join their regression. The sūrah has shown that wish before: those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), those given a portion trade it for misguidance and wish you to deviate from the path (4:44), and the lagger wishes after gain to be alike in share (4:73). Here the wish is more radical: that you disbelieve as they have, so that sameness — *sawāʾ* — replaces distinction. To disbelieve as they have was read as leaving the limits about wealth and marriage, the referral to the Messenger (4:59), and the obedience that places with the blessed (4:69), and returning to covering signs (4:56) and belief in *jibt* (4:51). Their wish is not for your opinion but for your sameness; if all are alike in disbelief, their regression is no longer visible. The Qur’an elsewhere says that disbelievers would love you to be as they are, because likeness removes the witness that they were left to stray.

**So Do Not Take Them as Allies Unless They Emigrate**

The command *fa lā tattakhidhū minhum awliyāʾa ḥattā yuhājirū fī sabīli Allāhi* — so do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah — was read as the sūrah’s test of that wish. *Awliyāʾ* — allies, close protectors — was explained as the bond that the sūrah opened as *mawaddah* — affection (4:73) — and as *you are from one another* (4:25). To take them as *awliyāʾ* while they remain regressed would be to accept sameness on their terms. Emigration — *hijrah* — *in the cause of Allah* was the sūrah’s concrete sign of reversal, as the migrants endured the hard command to leave homes that few would have obeyed (4:66) and as fighting for the oppressed required going forth (4:71). Early reports placed the verse after Uḥud where hypocrites lagged and after groups in the desert sought safety with both sides; to emigrate in God’s cause meant to join the community that returns trusts and refers disputes (4:58–59) and that fights where the oppressed cry (4:75). The condition *ḥattā yuhājirū* — until they emigrate — was read as the threshold where sameness could be on belief, not on disbelief. Until then, the believers’ *mawaddah* is not extended as alliance, because the regressed wish the believers to be alike in the wrong direction.

**But If They Turn Away**

The clause *fa in tawallaw* — but if they turn away — was explained as turning away from that emigration, persisting in regression after the test. *Tawallā* — to turn the back — matches the hypocrites’ turning away stubbornly — *yaṣuddūna ṣudūdā* (4:61) — and seeking *ṭāghūt* though commanded to reject it (4:60). To turn away here is to refuse the route that would have shown that doing what was advised is better and more reassuring (4:66). The verse does not command hostility for mere hesitation; it commands it after the wish to make you alike has been displayed and after the path to join has been offered and refused. The sūrah has said that whoever is left to stray you will never find a way for them (4:88); *tawallaw* is the human side of that leaving — they turn, and He allows regression. The community divided into two groups about them (4:88) is here given a single rule: no alliance until emigration, and if they turn from that, then the next measure.

**Seize and Kill Wherever You Find Them**

The measure *fa khudhūhum wa aqtulūhum ḥaythu wajadtumūhum* — then seize them and kill them wherever you find them — was read as the wartime ruling for the regressed who are combatants or who align with combatants against the believers, not as a rule for every individual who errs. Context shows the sūrah immediately adds exceptions: those allied to a treaty people or those opposed to fighting either side (4:90), and those who keep away, offer peace, and refrain from attacking (4:90), for whom God does not permit harm. Early authorities noted that the *khudh* and *uqtilū* here address the hostile group that wishes you disbelieve and that, if it turns away from emigration, remains a threat to the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75). The sūrah elsewhere forbids killing a believer except by mistake with expiation and blood-money (4:92) and promises Hell for killing intentionally (4:93), showing that the permission here is delimited by treaty, by peace offered, and by opposition to fighting. To seize and kill the hostile turner is therefore not a lapse of the ethic *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) but its protection at community scale, where the Devil’s schemes are weak (4:76) yet must still be curbed (4:84).

**No Allies or Helpers Among the Hostile Turners**

The closing *wa lā tattakhidhū minhum waliyyan wa lā naṣīrā* — and do not take any of them as allies or helpers — repeats the opening prohibition with the two sufficiencies the sūrah said God alone provides — *sufficient as Guardian and sufficient as Helper* (4:45). *Walī* and *naṣīr* — guardian and helper — were explained as the two roles the oppressed ask for from grace (4:75). To take the hostile turner as *walī* or *naṣīr* would be to seek guardianship from those God allowed to regress because of misdeeds, and who wish you alike in disbelief. The sūrah has said that whoever is condemned will have no helper (4:52) and that if those given no share of kingdom had it they would not give a speck (4:53); the hostile turners are therefore not helpers in any case. The verse generalises what earlier verses narrowly said for marriage and inheritance: do not seek the bar — the Devil’s cause — where God’s cause is available. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the rule is light: do not take as allies those who wish you to disbelieve as they have; wait for emigration in God’s cause as sign of reversal, and if they turn away as hostile, meet hostility with the measure the sūrah bounds, and otherwise take no ally among them, because the Guardian and Helper who suffices for the oppressed is sufficient for you.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:90

> except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people. If Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you. So if they refrain from fighting you and offer you peace, then Allah does not permit you to harm them.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Except Those With a Treaty or Those Opposed to Fighting**

The verse adds *illā alladhīna yaṣilūna ilā qawmin baynakum wa baynahum mīthāqun aw jāʾūkum ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum an yuqātilūkum aw yuqātilū qawmahum* — except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people, whose chests are constricted at fighting you or their own. The exception follows the command to seize and kill the hostile turners who wish you to disbelieve as they have (4:89). *Yaṣilūna ilā qawmin* — to reach, to join a people — was read as seeking refuge with a tribe allied to the believers by covenant — *mīthāq* — the same word used for the firm commitment — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — of marriage (4:21) and for trusts returned (4:58). To be joined to treaty people is to be covered by that treaty, as the sūrah respects the firm word given. The second group — those whose chests are constricted — *ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum* — was explained as people whose hearts cannot bear to fight either side, neither the believers nor their own. The sūrah has described *ḥaraj* — constriction — as the inner resistance the believer must remove when accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge (4:65); here constriction is the reason some cannot fight, and the sūrah spares them. Both groups are excepted from the hostile measure, showing that hostility, not identity, is the cause.

**If He Had Willed, He Would Have Empowered Them**

The clause *wa law shāʾa Allāhu la sallaṭahum ʿalaykum fa la qātalūkum* — if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you and they would have fought — was read as reminding that the sparing of the constricted is not due to their power but to divine restraint. *Sallata* — to give power, to make prevail — was explained as God’s leave, the same *idhn* by which messengers are to be obeyed (4:64). To say He would have empowered them and they would have fought is to say that the fact they do not fight is itself by His will, as the sūrah elsewhere says both good and evil are from His decree while evil from the self as means (4:78–79). The reminder humbles the believers who might credit their treaty or their deterrence alone; the restraint of the constricted is also God’s doing. Early reports placed the verse among tribes like Banū Mudlij who had treaties or who disliked fighting either side in the conflict between Madinah and the Quraysh; the exemption of such neutrals shows the sūrah’s distinction between the oppressor’s land whose people are oppressors (4:75) and people whose chests are constricted at fighting.

**So If They Refrain and Offer Peace**

The condition *fa in iʿtazalūkum fa lam yuqātilūkum wa alqaw ilaykumu al-salām fa mā jaʿala Allāhu lakum ʿalayhim sabīlā* — so if they refrain from fighting you, do not fight you, and offer you peace, then God does not permit you to harm them, He has not given you a way over them — was read as the sūrah’s rule of peace. *Iʿtazalūkum* — to withdraw, to keep aside — and *alqaw al-salām* — to offer peace, to cast peace — were explained as the two signs of neutrality: withdrawal from fighting and offering *salām*, the same peace the sūrah commanded to answer with better or same where greeting is given (4:86). *Fa mā jaʿala Allāhu lakum ʿalayhim sabīlā* — no way, no permission, no path — was read as removing the *sabīl* — way — over them that was given over the hostile turners (4:89). The sūrah has used *sabīl* for the path God wills to make clear (4:26), the noble ways, and the far straying Satan desires (4:60); to have no *sabīl* over those who withdraw and offer peace is to be kept on the straight path. The verse was linked to the later rule *“if they refrain, you do not kill”* where even the hostile who offer peace are not to be harmed, showing that the ethic of *“do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you”* (4:29) governs the field as well as the home.

**A Verse That Holds Treaty and Conscience Together**

Placed after the wish to make you alike in disbelief and the permission to seize the hostile turner (4:89), this exception holds treaty and conscience together. Treaty — *mīthāq* — is the sūrah’s firm word; conscience — *ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum* — is the heart’s constriction that God sees. Both are respected. The first group is spared because a word was given; the second because a heart cannot bear to fight either side. The sūrah has said that God knows what is in hearts (4:63), knows best who enemies are (4:45), and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper; here that knowledge sees the constricted chest and spares it. The verse therefore draws a line that the community divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) needed: not all who are among the hostile turners are the same as those who fight; some are allies of treaty people, and some are neutral by distress. The exception keeps the sūrah’s larger ethic — return trusts, judge fairly as noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), and fight for the oppressed whose cry is for a guardian and helper from grace (4:75) — from becoming indiscriminate. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is the lightest of burdens: where the other withdraws and offers peace, there is no way over him, and the peace offered is answered with better or same, as the greeting rule already commanded.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:91

> You will find others who wish to be safe from you and their own people. Yet they cannot resist the temptation ˹of disbelief or hostility˺. If they do not keep away, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. We have given you full permission over such people.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Others Who Wish to Be Safe From Both Sides**

The verse opens *sa tajidūna ākharīna yurīdūna an yaʾmanūkum wa yaʾmanū qawmahum* — you will find others who wish to be safe from you and safe from their own people. The pattern is double desire: safety from the believers and safety from their own tribe, without joining either in commitment. The previous exception had spared two groups — those joined to treaty people and those whose chests are constricted at fighting either side (4:90) — for whom God did not give a way. This verse finds a third face that looks like the second but is not: a people who display peace to both sides while keeping a door open to hostility. *Yurīdūna an yaʾmanūkum* — they wish to be safe from you — was explained as showing Islam before the believers and showing hostility’s religion before their own, so that neither side harms them. The sūrah has shown this oscillation before: the lagger who says “God blessed us for not being there” when you suffer, and “would we had been there” when you gain (4:72–73), the speaker whose *mawaddah* — affection — shifts with gain. The wish for double safety is another *mawaddah* that changes with advantage.

**Whenever Returned to Temptation They Are Plunged Back**

The description *kullamā ruddū ilā l-fitnati urkisū fīhā* — yet they cannot resist the temptation, whenever they are returned to temptation they are plunged, thrown headlong into it — was read with *fitnah* as the trial of hostility and sedition, or of idolatry and disbelief. *Fitnah* in the Book ranges from civil strife — *“fight them until there is no strife”* (2:193) — to trial — *“We made some of you a trial for others”* (25:20) — to the testing of beliefs — *“We tried them as We tried the owners of the garden”* (68:17). Here commentators noted the ease of return: whenever they are called back to *fitnah* they fall in, as if their display of safety was only a surface (Ṭ, Q). The sūrah has already described this slide: the hypocrites who turn away stubbornly when called to God and the Messenger (4:61), the people whose trade was for misguidance and who wish you to deviate (4:44), and the regressed whom God allowed to regress because of misdeeds (4:88). Ibn ʿAjībah compared this group to the wavering aspect of the soul, torn between obedience and disobedience, that must be fought when it urges disobedience. The verb *urkisū* — they were cast, plunged — was explained as being turned upside down into it, as one thrown headlong, showing not a slip but a relapse. The phrase gives the criterion that separates this group from the constricted of 4:90: the constricted are distressed at fighting either side and stay withdrawn; these, when returned to hostility, are plunged back without distress.

**If They Do Not Keep Away or Offer Peace**

The condition *fa in lam yaʿtazilūkum wa yulqū ilaykumu al-salām wa yakuffū aydiyahum* — if they do not keep away, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you, do not restrain their hands — repeats the three signs of genuine peace from 4:90 — withdrawal, casting peace — *alqā al-salām* — and restraining hands — but as a negative test. To keep away — *iʿtazala* — was explained as withdrawing from the conflict; to offer peace — as casting *salām* with sincerity, the same peace the sūrah commanded to answer with better or same (4:86); to restrain hands — as refraining from fighting. The triple condition was read as sparing any of the three: if they do any one sincerely they are spared, as the previous verse gave “no way” over those who withdraw and offer peace. Early reports identified such people among tribes between Madinah and Makkah who tried to be at peace with both, and among persons who outwardly professed belief in Madinah then returned to idolatry in Makkah, showing that the category is not an ethnicity but a behaviour — the wish for double safety plus the ease of being returned to *fitnah*. The sūrah’s standard — fight for the oppressed who cry for a guardian and helper (4:75) — does not extend to fighting those who genuinely withdraw; this verse says the same negatively: if they do not withdraw or offer peace or restrain, then they are not the constricted and the permission returns.

**Seize and Kill Where You Find Them — With Clear Warrant**

The measure *fa khudhūhum wa aqtulūhum ḥaythu thaqiftumūhum* — then seize them and kill them wherever you find them — was explained as the same wartime measure given for the hostile turners who wish you alike in disbelief (4:89) and as given generally for idolaters who initiate hostilities (2:191; 9:5), limited by the three signs of peace. To seize — *khudh* — and to kill — *uqtilū* — where you find them — *thaqiftumūhum* — to come upon, to gain mastery — was read as upon encounter in the field, not pursuit into the protected. The closing *wa ulāʾikum jaʿalnā lakum ʿalayhim sulṭānan mubīnā* — We have given you full permission, a clear warrant, an evident authority over such people — was explained as *sulṭān* — proof, warrant, authority — openly shown. The phrase means the law has made the cause clear: those who do not withdraw, do not offer peace, and do not restrain hands, and who whenever returned to *fitnah* are plunged back, may be seized. The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), that the oppressed cry for a helper from grace (4:75), and that good and evil are from His decree while evil from the self as means (4:78–79); the warrant here is the community’s instrument of that guardianship where double-faced hostility would otherwise expose the weak for whom burdens were lightened.

**A Verse That Separates Hesitation From Duplicity**

Placed after the exception for treaty and for the constricted, this verse completes the sūrah’s threefold map: bound by treaty, constricted and withdrawn, and double-seeking. The first two are not to be harmed; the third is to be, unless it meets the same three signs. The distinction matters for the community that was divided into two groups about the hypocrites (4:88) and that was commanded not to take as allies those who wish you alike in disbelief until they emigrate (4:89). To be safe from both sides while ready to be plunged back into hostility is not neutrality; it is duplicity that leaves the oppressed without a guardian. The sūrah’s ethic — *“do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you”* (4:29), do not consume wealth unjustly, return trusts and judge fairly (4:58), and fight so that God may curb the might of disbelievers (4:84) — is therefore not indiscriminate: where a heart is constricted it is spared, where a treaty holds it is respected, and where double safety hides readiness to be plunged back into *fitnah*, the clear warrant is given unless peace is offered and hands restrained. The next verse will turn from the field to the home, and from permission to prohibition, with the rule that a believer does not kill a believer except by mistake (4:92).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:92

> It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer unintentionally must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim’s family—unless they waive it charitably. But if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then a believing slave must be freed. And if the victim is from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money must be paid to the family along with freeing a believing slave. Those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months—as a means of repentance to Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

**Expanded Commentary**

**It Is Not Lawful for a Believer to Kill a Believer**

The verse opens *wa mā kāna li muʾminin an yaqtula muʾminan illā khaṭaʾan* — it is not lawful, it is not for a believer to kill another believer except by mistake. *Mā kāna* — it is not, it is not fitting — was explained as a negation of permissibility, not only of occurrence, the same construction as *“it is not for a believer”* to disobey after God and Messenger decide. The exception *illā khaṭaʾan* — except by mistake, error — was explained as unintentional killing: a slip of aim, a misreading of identity, a cause where intent to kill a believer was absent, as when the sūrah earlier forbade killing yourselves and devouring wealth unjustly (4:29). The rule follows directly after the permission to seize and kill the double-faced who do not withdraw or offer peace (4:89–91); where that permission might be widened, the sūrah narrows it to its limit: the believer’s blood is not lawful to the believer. The Book records the gravity elsewhere: *“the shedding of blood”* is paired with corruption — *nufsid* (2:30) — and with the sanctity of a soul — *“whoever kills a soul it is as if he killed all mankind”* (5:32). The verse anchors that sanctity in law: no believer kills a believer on purpose; if it happens, it is only by error, and error itself has a heavy remedy.

**Freeing a Believing Slave and Paying Blood-Money**

The remedy *fa taḥrīru raqabatin muʾminatin wa diyatun musallamatun ilā ahlihī illā an yaṣṣaddaqū* — then freeing a believing slave and blood-money delivered to the family, unless they waive it charitably as alms — was explained as two rights restored. *Taḥrīr raqabah* — freeing a neck — was read as liberating a believing bonds-person, a life returned for a life taken, recalling that to free a life is to keep humanity alive. *Diyah musallamah* — blood-money delivered, handed over — was explained as wealth paid to the victim’s people, delivered fully, as the return of trusts commanded earlier (4:58). The clause *illā an yaṣṣaddaqū* — unless they waive, give it as charity — was read as remission by the family, who may forgo it charitably; the sūrah has made gracious waiver a virtue where dowry is waived willingly (4:4) and where charity is given from what God provided (4:39). That a mistake still requires freeing and payment shows that the law does not treat error as nothing; it treats it as a harm whose maker must still repair, though without the curse of intention. Early reports noted this freeing applies where the killer has means; where he does not, the alternative is named at the end.

**If the Victim Was From a Hostile People or From a Treaty People**

The two cases *fa in kāna min qawmin ʿaduwwin lakum wa huwa muʾminun fa taḥrīru raqabatin muʾminah, wa in kāna min qawmin baynakum wa baynahum mīthāqun fa diyatun musallamatun ilā ahlihī wa taḥrīru raqabatin muʾminah* — but if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then only freeing a believing slave; and if from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money to the family along with freeing — were explained as the sūrah’s consistent respect for treaty — *mīthāq* — the firm word seen in marriage (4:21) and in trusts (4:58) and in the exception of 4:90. If the mistakenly killed believer was from hostile people — living among those at war while himself a believer — there is no payment to his people who are hostile, lest it strengthen the hostile; the right to God remains as freeing. If he was from treaty people — *baynakum wa baynahum mīthāq* — then the blood-money is delivered to his family, fulfilling the treaty, together with freeing for God. The former was understood to cover a believer who hid belief among the opponent or who joined without being known; the latter covers the covenanted protected person whose blood the treaty guarantees, as 4:90 had spared those joined to treaty people. The threefold pattern — full atonement where family can receive, freeing alone where payment would aid hostility, and payment plus freeing where treaty binds — shows the law weighing life, treaty, and the community’s security together without contradiction.

**Those Unable — Fast Two Consecutive Months**

The alternative *fa man lam yajid fa ṣiyāmu shahrayni mutatābiʿayni tawbatan mina Allāhi* — those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months as repentance, as turning from God — was explained as expiation for the one who cannot free a slave. *Man lam yajid* — whoever does not find, cannot afford — was read as lacking a bonds-person to free or the means to acquire one; for him the bodily worship of consecutive fasting replaces the freeing, as fasting also replaces what is lacking elsewhere in atonements. *Mutatābiʿayni* — consecutive, successive — was stressed: two months without break, showing that the error’s repair requires continuity, not fragments. *Tawbatan mina Allāhi* — repentance from God, a turning granted by Him — was explained as His acceptance of this replacement; the same root *tāba* appears in the sūrah’s promise that if wrongdoers came seeking forgiveness the Messenger prayed for them they would find Him ever Accepting of Repentance (4:64). The closing *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise — was read as the seal that He knows error from intent and judges with wisdom where means fail. The verse was also linked to the wider law where killing a believer intentionally carries Hell and curse (4:93), while error carries freeing, payment, or fasting — a distinction the Community kept when evaluating reports of accidental killings on campaigns.

**A Verse That Guards Blood After Giving Permission Over Hostility**

Placed after the clear warrant over the double-faced (4:91), this verse guards blood where permission might be misread. The sūrah that began by creating from a single soul and commanding mindfulness of ties (4:1), that forbade consuming orphans’ wealth, that said *“do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you”* (4:29), and that promised Hell for intentional killing (4:93), here converts the sanctity of the believer into procedure: freeing, payment, treaty fidelity, and fasting where there is no means. The order itself teaches that permission over hostility (4:89–91) is not permission over belief: the believer’s life is unlawful to the believer except by mistake, and even mistake requires repair. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the closing *tawbatan* is the lightest of burdens: where the hand slipped without intent, the law opens a path back through freeing or, where there is nothing to free, through consecutive fasting as repentance accepted by the All-Knowing, All-Wise. The next verse will set the opposite face — the intentional killing whose reward is Hell — so that mistake and purpose are never confused.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:93

> And whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward will be Hell— where they will stay indefinitely. Allah will be displeased with them, condemn them, and will prepare for them a tremendous punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Whoever Kills a Believer Intentionally**

The verse states *wa man yaqtul muʾminan mutaʿammidan fa jazāʾuhū Jahannam khālidan fīhā* — and whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward, requital, will be Hell where they will stay indefinitely. *Mutaʿammidan* — intentionally, deliberately, with determination — was explained as purposeful killing with knowledge that the victim is a believer and with a lethal means, the opposite of the mistake — *khaṭaʾ* — whose remedy was freeing, blood-money, or fasting (4:92). The sūrah has moved by deliberate steps: hostility is curbed by fighting for the oppressed (4:75), the believer fights for God and the schemes of the Devil are weak (4:76), permission is given over the hostile turners who do not withdraw or offer peace (4:89–91) with clear warrant, then that permission is bounded by the prohibition that a believer does not kill a believer except by mistake (4:92). This verse sets the far limit of that bound: intentional killing of a believer is not a mistake to be repaired but a crime whose requital is named in the same language as Paradise for the obedient — *jazāʾ* — reward. Where obedience brought Gardens forever (4:13), intentional killing brings Hell abiding. Early authorities stressed that the verse pairs intentional killing with associating others with God in several passages: *“those who do not call upon another god with God, nor kill a soul God made unlawful except with right”* (25:68), showing the gravity placed upon it.

**Four Threats Together — Hell, Anger, Curse, and Mighty Torment**

The verse joins four: *wa ghaḍiba Allāhu ʿalayhi wa laʿanahū wa aʿadda lahū ʿadhāban ʿaẓīmā* — Allah will be displeased with them, be angry with them, condemn them, curse them, remove them from mercy, and will prepare for them a tremendous, mighty punishment. *Ghaḍab* — anger — was explained as divine displeasure at the violation of the sanctity established from a single soul (4:1) and from *“do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you”* (4:29). *Laʿnah* — curse — was read as expulsion from mercy, the same word used for those condemned for disbelief who rejected trust (4:52) and for Satan cursed by God (4:118). *Aʿadda* — He has prepared — matches the preparation language elsewhere for punishment: as Paradise was prepared for those who believe and do good (4:57), so a tremendous torment is prepared here. Classical commentators noted that this is one of the few verses where four terrors are gathered for a single sin: abiding in Hell, anger, curse, and mighty torment. The sternness carries a report: Ibn ʿAbbās was asked whether repentance avails the intentional killer, and he held that this verse was among the last revealed on the subject and nothing abrogated it (Bukhārī, Muslim), while the majority understood that repentance remains possible for the sincere because God forgives what is less than association if He wills (4:48) and accepts repentance soon after error (4:17), yet the threat remains severe to block the hand. The sūrah’s balance is therefore not softened: the warning is left as stated.

**Abiding Indefinitely — Khālidan Fīhā**

The phrase *khālidan fīhā* — abiding therein indefinitely — was explained with attention to *khulūd* — remaining, abiding. Some read it as long abiding without end for the one who deems the killing lawful, making it akin to disbelief in sanctity; others read it as the recompense deserved, with ultimate return to divine forgiveness still under *“He forgives anything else of whoever He wills”* (4:48) if repentance intervenes.
