The sūrah says elsewhere *“those who reject Our signs We will cast into Fire, whenever skins are burnt We replace them”* (4:56), joining abiding with renewal of torment; this verse joins abiding with anger and curse for killing a believer. The point for the community is not to settle the unseen calendar but to see that the threat has no light edge: the intentional stripping of a believer’s life that God tied to a single soul (4:1) is met with abiding, anger, curse, and mighty preparation. Where mistaken killing was met with freeing, blood-money, treaty fidelity, and consecutive fasting as repentance accepted (4:92), intentional killing is met with no such procedural remedy in this verse; the remedy is elsewhere in sincere repentance that must answer four terrors.

**A Verse That Closes the Permission Given Over Hostility**

Placed after the clear warrant over the double-faced (4:91) and the detailed law for mistake (4:92), this verse closes the permission precisely where overreach would be most dangerous: on the battlefield where a believer might be mistaken, or in the city where a believer might be envied. The sūrah has shown that envy moved those given a portion of the Book to wish you deviate (4:54) and to trade guidance for misguidance (4:44); if envy or anger were allowed to move a hand to kill a believer intentionally, the claim would be the highest misguidance. The sūrah’s earlier promise — *“whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed: the prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous”* (4:69) — is inverted here: whoever kills a believer intentionally will be in the company of those under anger and curse, with a mighty torment prepared. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse lightens by removing ambiguity: permission to seize the hostile turner (4:89) and the double-seeking who refuse peace (4:91) is not permission over a believer; and the atonement that suffices for mistake (4:92) does not suffice for purpose. The next verse will turn to the search for gain on that same field, warning against calling to a seeker of peace “you are no believer” for fleeting worldly gain (4:94).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:94

> O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight. And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, “You are no believer!”—seeking a fleeting worldly gain. Instead, Allah has infinite bounties ˹in store˺. You were initially like them then Allah blessed you ˹with Islam˺. So be sure! Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When You Struggle — Be Sure of Who You Fight**

The verse opens *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū idhā ḍarabtum fī sabīli Allāhi fa tabayyanū* — O believers, when you strike out, travel, struggle in the cause of God, be sure, verify, make clear. *Ḍarabtum fī sabīli Allāhi* — striking in the path — was explained as going forth to fight for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75) and where permission had just been given over the hostile who do not withdraw or offer peace (4:89–91). *Tabayyanū* — to clarify, to make patent — was read as verification before the sword, the opposite of the haste of spreading untested news of security or fear (4:83) and the haste that kills a believer except by mistake (4:92–93). The command to be sure is placed here because the field blurs: a man may offer peace while his people remain hostile, and the believer must distinguish. The sūrah has said that God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45); to be sure is to act on what can be seen — the casting of peace — and leave the heart to the All-Aware. Early reports linked the verse to a company that met a lone shepherd who greeted them with *al-salām* and was killed for his flock as spoil; the verse came down to forbid that haste (Ṭ, Wāḥidī).

**Do Not Say to the One Who Offers Peace — You Are No Believer**

The prohibition *wa lā taqūlū li man alqā ilaykumu al-salāma lasta muʾminā* — and do not say to those who offer you greetings of peace, You are no believer — was explained with *al-salām* as the greeting of peace, *al-salām ʿalaykum*, or more widely the casting of peace, submission — *salām*. *Last muʾminā* — you are no believer — was read as denying the faith of one who displays its sign. To say it where peace is offered was explained as claiming to see beyond the offered word into the heart, while God alone knows what is in hearts (4:63) and the Book forbids that unveiling. The sūrah has commanded that when greeted, the answer be better or similar and that God is ever Reckoner (4:86); to reply to a greeting with disbelief is the inverse of that ethic. A widely reported incident illustrates the rule: a man — named in reports as Mirda or as a man of Sulaym — offered *al-salām* to a detachment led by Usāmah ibn Zayd, was killed, and his flock taken; the Prophet ﷺ reproved the killing and recited this verse (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4591; Muslim 3025 in similar wording for the same theme). The verse’s wording covers both readings: do not deny belief to one who offers the Muslim greeting, and do not deny it to one who lays down arms and offers *salām* as peace.

**Seeking a Fleeting Worldly Gain**

The motive clause *tabtaghūna ʿaraḍa al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — seeking a fleeting worldly gain, the عرض — chattel — of the nearer life — was explained as the spoil taken — the flock, the goods — for which the hasty hand declares another’s peace false. *ʿAraḍ* — عرض — was read as transient gain that passes, as the enjoyment of this world is little and the Hereafter better for the mindful (4:77). The sūrah has warned against devouring wealth unjustly (4:29) and against envying what God gave some over others (4:32) and against those who were given a portion and who wish you deviate for such gain (4:44). To kill a bearer of peace for his goods is to exchange the infinite bounties with God — *fa ʿinda Allāhi maghānim kathīrah* — for a flock. The clause *fa ʿinda Allāhi maghānim kathīrah* — instead, God has infinite bounties in store — was explained as the true spoil: provision multiplied, forgiveness and mercy and ranks (4:96), and the great reward promised to those who fight or to those excused (4:95). The contrast is not that gain is forbidden — lawful beyond limits is lawful as long as sought with wealth in marriage and trade by mutual consent (4:24–29) — but that the fleeting gain may not be sought by denying peace.

**You Were Initially Like Them, Then God Blessed You**

The reminder *ka dhālika kuntum min qablu fa manna Allāhu ʿalaykum* — you were initially like them then Allah blessed you with Islam — was read as the sūrah’s moral recall. *Kuntum min qablu* — you were before — was explained as that the believers themselves once concealed belief, or once offered peace that was not credited, or once were without the law that now protects them, until God’s grace guided them. The favour — *manna* — is the same word used where God favoured — *manna* — the oppressed? Here it recalls the grace without which they would have followed Satan except for few (4:83) and the way He lightened burdens because humanity was created weak (4:28). The sūrah has said that had they done what they were advised it would have been better and more reassuring and would have brought great reward and guidance (4:66–68), and that obedience places one with the blessed (4:69). To remember that you were as they were is to remove the pride that allows a hand to call another’s peace a lie. The sūrah elsewhere says *“you were on the brink of fire and He saved you”* (3:103); this is the same memory applied to the sword: you too were once a bearer of a tentative *salām* whose acceptance was your life.

**So Be Sure — God Is All-Aware of What You Do**

The double close *fa tabayyanū, inna Allāha kāna bi mā taʿmalūna khabīrā* — So be sure, God is All-Aware of what you do — repeats the opening *tabayyanū* to frame the prohibition with practice. *Khabīr* — All-Aware — was explained as awareness of outward act and inward motive, of whether the hand sought peace or spoil. The sūrah has closed the mistake law with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:92) and the intentional threat with no exit but Hell unless turned from (4:93); here the close is awareness of deeds where mistake and intent look alike. The verse generalises the sūrah’s method: verify reports before spreading (4:83), verify belief before denying it (4:94), verify the fast as consecutive where atonement requires (4:92). For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the command to be sure is a lightening: it spares the bearer of peace from the haste for gain, and it spares the striver from the burden of a killing that would demand Hell, anger, curse, and mighty torment unless repented. The next verse will set the striver against the one who stays behind, both promised good but not made equal (4:95).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:95

> Those who stay at home—except those with valid excuses—are not equal to those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind ˹with valid excuses˺. Allah has promised each a fine reward, but those who strive will receive a far better reward than others—

**Expanded Commentary**

**Not Equal — Those Who Stay and Those Who Strive**

The verse states *lā yastawī al-qāʿidūna mina al-muʾminīna ghayru ulī al-ḍarari wa al-mujāhidūna fī sabīli Allāhi bi amwālihim wa anfusihim* — those who stay at home among believers, except those with valid excuses, are not equal to those who strive in the cause of God with wealth and lives. *Qāʿidūn* — those who sit, stay — was explained as remaining behind from going forth in groups or together as commanded (4:71). *Ghayru ulī al-ḍarari* — except possessors of harm, of valid excuse — was read as blindness, illness, lameness, or need that prevents going forth; the phrase was reported to have been inserted after the first revelation when Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind companion, asked about his excuse and the Prophet ﷺ received the addition (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2832). *Mujāhidūn* — strivers — with *amwālihim wa anfusihim* — wealth and lives — was explained as the two expenditures the sūrah has praised: spending from what God provided (4:39) and offering this life for the Hereafter in fight for the oppressed (4:74–75). To say they are not equal — *lā yastawī* — is not to say the sitter is condemned; the verse immediately promises good to both. It is to rank the acts, as the sūrah has ranked obedience that places with the prophets and truthful (4:69) above disobedience that will be burned (4:14).

**Elevated in Rank — Darajah Above Those Who Stay**

The rank *faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna bi amwālihim wa anfusihim ʿalā al-qāʿidīna darajatan* — God has elevated in rank, preferred, those who strive with wealth and lives above those who stay, by a degree — was explained as a degree of closeness and reward. *Darajah* — rank, degree — was read as the standing given to the striver who verified before fighting (4:94) and who fought where trusts and justice are guarded (4:58–59). The sūrah has used degree language elsewhere where envy of God’s bounties was condemned (4:54) and where God’s favour upon the Prophet ﷺ is great (4:113); here the degree is not of envy but of effort. Early reports noted that the striver who goes forth light or heavy is not the same as the one whose excuse keeps him, though both believe; the former bears the cost that earlier only few would have borne had God commanded to sacrifice selves or abandon homes (4:66). The degree is therefore proportioned to the cost that the lightened burden (4:28) still leaves: to give wealth where stinginess is a temptation (4:37) and to risk life where death will overtake even in fortified towers (4:78).

**Each Promised a Fine Reward — Husnā for Both**

The assurance *wa kullan waʿada Allāhu al-ḥusnā* — Allah has promised each a fine reward, the beautiful — was explained as the promise to both sitter with excuse and striver: Paradise for faith held, as the sūrah promised Gardens under rivers for those who believe and do good (4:57) and as it said bequest and debt precede inheritance yet the limits are from God (4:11–13). “Each” — *kullan* — was stressed: the excused sitter is not erased, because his sitting is not the lagging that rejoices at disaster and envies gain (4:72–73) nor the regression God allowed because of misdeeds (4:88). His harm — *ḍarar* — is real, and the sūrah that lightens burdens for the weak spares him. The promise of *ḥusnā* was also read as goodness in this world where God gives earth spacious for emigration and many refuges (4:100) and goodness in the next where ranks, forgiveness, and mercy follow (4:96). The assurance prevents two errors: that the excused is despised, and that the striver’s degree means the other has nothing. Both have, but not equally.

**A Far Better Reward — Ajran ʿAẓīman**

The increase *wa faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna ʿalā al-qāʿidīna ajran ʿaẓīmā* — but those who strive will receive a far better, mighty reward than others — was explained as beyond the single *darajah*, a mighty wage. *Ajr ʿaẓīm* — mighty reward — appears where charity, kindness, and reconciliation are done seeking God’s pleasure (4:114) and where holding fast to God after repentance is rewarded (4:146); here it is for striving. The detail is given in the next verse: ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him (4:96). The pattern matches the sūrah’s arithmetic of the good deed multiplied many times over by grace (4:40): the base reward — *ḥusnā* — is promised to each, then multiplied for the striver. The verse was also placed against reports where the Prophet ﷺ said the sitter’s prayer at home is not like the striver’s watch, and where the Qur’anic *darajah* was expounded as many degrees between heavens. That detail — degrees as spaces — was noted but left to interpretation, as the text itself names the increase as mighty without numbered limit, and the next verse names its form.

**A Verse That Ranks Without Breaking Brotherhood**

Placed after verification before killing and the warning against seeking fleeting gain by denying peace (4:94), this ranking prevents the opposite error: that staying is the same as striving where striving is required. The sūrah has already distinguished the lagger who stays and then envies (4:72–73) from the one who offers life for the Hereafter (4:74); here it distinguishes the excused stayer from the striver, promising good to both then preferring the striver by degree and mighty wage. The ethic is the sūrah’s own: *“those who believe and do good We will admit into Gardens”* (4:57), yet within good there are ranks. For the community divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) and commanded to be sure before fighting (4:94), the verse steadies judgment: do not equalise what God made unequal, and do not condemn whom God excused. The sūrah’s leniency for weakness — *“He wills to lighten burdens, humankind was created weak”* (4:28) — remains, even while wealth and lives are asked where the oppressed cry for a helper (4:75). The next verse will describe that mighty wage as ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him, the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:96).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:96

> far superior ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Far Superior Ranks From Him**

The phrase *darajātin minhu* — far superior ranks, degrees from Him — completes *“those who strive will receive a far better reward”* (4:95). *Darajāt* — ranks — was explained as levels of reward, stations of nearness, each above the other as the heavens are layered. The plural was stressed: not one degree but degrees, as the mighty wage — *ajran ʿaẓīman* — was said to be beyond a single step. The addition *minhu* — from Him — was read as source: these ranks are not market wages earned by measure alone but grace given, as every good is multiplied many times over by His grace (4:40) and as the great reward for doing what was advised is by grace (4:67). The sūrah has shown that those who obey God and the Messenger will be with the blessed — prophets, truthful, martyrs, righteous — honourable company (4:69), and that obedience is by His will where messengers are obeyed (4:64). The ranks from Him place the striver with the martyrs among that company where striving costs life, and with the truthful where striving costs wealth against stinginess (4:37). Early reports illustrated the breadth: between two ranks is like between heaven and earth, yet the text leaves the count unnamed, keeping the face toward the Giver rather than the number.

**And Forgiveness and Mercy**

The triad *darajātin… wa maghfiratan wa raḥmah* — ranks, forgiveness, and mercy — was explained as the content of the mighty wage. *Maghfirah* — forgiveness — and *raḥmah* — mercy — were read as the removal of fault and the bestowal of favour, the two that make Paradise admission possible. The sūrah has paired them where burdens are lightened because humanity is weak (4:28), where the angry violation of wealth is threatened yet avoidance of major sins brings absolution (4:31), where wrongdoers who come seeking forgiveness find Him ever Accepting of Repentance (4:64), and where repentance soon after error is pardoned (4:17–18). To place forgiveness among the striver’s wages shows that striving is not sinless; the one who goes forth still needs covering for haste, for the claim of peace denied, for the gain sought. The sūrah has just warned not to say to a bearer of peace “you are no believer” for fleeting gain and to remember you were as they were (4:94); forgiveness is the remainder that makes the rank secure. Mercy is the surplus beyond covering, as the sūrah said He multiplies a good deed and gives a great reward from grace (4:40). Forgiveness wipes, mercy lifts — together they make ranks more than wage.

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — And God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — repeats the same two names that seal the removal of mistake by fasting as repentance (4:92) and the reminder that you were as they were (4:94). *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving — was explained as forgiving the striver’s faults where verification was imperfect yet sincere, and forgiving the sitter with excuse whose harm kept him home. *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful, ever Merciful — was read as the mercy that gave ranks from Him and that made Hijrah wide for the oppressed (4:100). The pairing after ranks shows that the whole elevation is inside mercy, not outside it. The sūrah has said *“God does not wrong even an atom, and if it is good He multiplies”* (4:40), and *“if you avoid major sins We absolve lesser”* (4:31): forgiveness and mercy are the mechanism of that multiplication where the good is striving with wealth and life. Where the intentional killer was sealed with anger, curse, and mighty preparation (4:93), the striver — and by inclusion the excused sitter promised *ḥusnā* (4:95) — is sealed with forgiveness and mercy.

**Degrees Are Gift, Not Contract**

The wording *minhu* was read by grammarians as partitive and honorific: ranks that are *from Him* — originating with Him, bestowed as gift, not bargained as wage. That matches the sūrah’s language where the great reward for doing what was advised is *by Our grace* (4:67), where the good deed multiplied is *from His grace* (4:40), and where guidance to the Straight Path is a gift after reward (4:68). To strive with wealth and life where the oppressed cry (4:75) is costly, yet the verse says the cost does not purchase rank as trade purchases goods by mutual consent (4:29); it receives rank as gift from the One who created from a single soul and spread humanity (4:1) and who wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28). The striver’s wealth, given against stinginess (4:37) and hoarding (4:39), is therefore not a loan repaid with interest but an offering answered with degrees whose distance only the Giver measures. That is why the verse leaves the number unnamed: between two degrees is as between heaven and earth in reports, yet the text keeps the eye on source — *minhu* — rather than count — so that striving is not calculated as profit but trusted as bounty.

**A Short Verse That Holds the Sūrah’s Weight Together**

Though only *“ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him, and God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful,”* the verse carries the sūrah’s weight. It follows the prohibition against consuming wealth unjustly (4:29) with the call to spend wealth for God where the oppressed cry (4:75); it follows the command to verify before fighting (4:94) with the assurance that verification’s owner gives ranks; it follows the distinction between sitting and striving (4:95) with the answer that the distinction is not enmity but mercy’s distribution. The sūrah opened by creation from a single soul and commanded mindfulness of ties (4:1), showed envy of God’s bounties as the disease (4:54), and taught that good and evil are from His decree while evil from the self as means (4:79); here the medicine is named as forgiveness and mercy from Him that make degrees real yet keep brotherhood. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the triad is the lightest yet highest: where life and wealth are given, He gives degree; where fault remains, He forgives; where nothing more can be offered, mercy carries. The next passage will turn from those who strive to those who claim oppression while remaining, whose excuse angels will interrogate (4:97).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:97

> When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves—scolding them, “What do you think you were doing?” they will reply, “We were oppressed in the land.” The angels will respond, “Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?” It is they who will have Hell as their home—what an evil destination!

**Expanded Commentary**

**Those Who Wronged Themselves — At the Taking of Souls**

The verse opens *inna alladhīna tawaffāhumu al-malāʾikatu ẓālimī anfusihim* — when the angels seize, take fully, the souls of those who have wronged themselves. *Tawaffā* — to take in full — was explained as the angels’ taking at death, the same taking that will gather all upon a Day about which there is no doubt (4:87). *Ẓālimī anfusihim* — wrongers of themselves — was read as those who abandoned what preserved them, not those wronged by another; as the sūrah said *“whoever does evil or wrongs themselves then seeks forgiveness will find God All-Forgiving”* (4:110), wronging the self is the description of sin that remains with the doer, not imposed from outside. The image is the sūrah’s moral audit at the border: the angels — the same who record schemes by night (4:81) and who bring witness against communities (4:41) — seize the wronger while his claim is still *“we were oppressed.”* The taking is the moment where claims are tested, as the sūrah has shown that God knows what is in hearts (4:63) and that He is Reckoner of all things (4:86).

**What Were You Doing — Fī ma Kuntum**

The question *qālū fī ma kuntum* — scolding them, “What do you think you were doing? What were you in?” — was explained as *“in what state were you? In what affair?”* — not a request for information but a rebuke. *Fī ma* — in what — was read as asking about the religion they were upon, the land they remained in, the company they kept. The answer *qālū kunnā mustaḍʿafīna fī al-arḍ* — they will reply, We were oppressed, deemed weak in the land — was explained as the claim that remaining among the hostile was not choice but oppression, that they could not go forth or declare. The same word *mustaḍʿaf* — deemed weak, oppressed — was used where the oppressed men, women, and children cry for a deliverer (4:75); there the cry is for a guardian and helper from grace and is answered by the command to fight for them, while here the claim is used to justify staying where the way to emigrate was open. The angels’ question exposes the difference between being truly oppressed — the helpless for whom pardon is hoped (4:98) — and displaying oppression as excuse.

**Was God’s Earth Not Spacious Enough to Emigrate**

The reply *qālū a lam takun arḍu Allāhi wāsiʿatan fa tuhājirū fīhā* — Was God’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate? — was read as the sūrah’s definition of the remedy. *Arḍ Allāh wāsiʿah* — God’s earth spacious — was explained as His earth made wide for movement, as emigrants find many refuges and abundant resources (4:100) and as the single soul’s creation spread countless men and women across lands (4:1). *Fa tuhājirū fīhā* — so that you might emigrate therein — recalls the test *“do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in God’s cause”* (4:89) and the warning that to sacrifice selves or abandon homes few would obey had it been commanded (4:66), yet here the same abandonment is shown as the exit from wronging oneself. The sūrah has said that God wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28); emigration is not presented as an unbearable weight but as the spaciousness that makes remaining in hostility unnecessary. Early reports placed the verse concerning Meccans who stayed among the idolaters, were marched to Badr under compulsion, and were killed among the hostile ranks while claiming compulsion; the angels’ answer declares that the earth’s spaciousness was itself the answer to compulsion where the heart could still choose.

**Their Home Is Hell — What an Evil Destination**

The verdict *fa ulāʾika maʾwāhum Jahannam wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — It is they who will have Hell as their home, refuge, what an evil destination, becoming — was read with *maʾwā* — refuge, shelter — inverted: the refuge they sought among the hostile becomes Hell as refuge. *Sāʾat maṣīrā* — evil as destination, as becoming — was explained as the sūrah’s closing formula for the abode of those who remain where belief cannot be lived, matching *“Hell is sufficient as torment”* (4:55) and the threat for intentional killing and for siding with wrong (4:93, 4:109). The contrast with the previous tier is exact: those who strive with wealth and lives are given ranks, forgiveness, and mercy (4:96); those who stay claiming oppression while the earth is wide are given Hell as home. The distinction is not that every stayer is condemned — the next verse will exempt the truly helpless who cannot find a way (4:98) — but that the claim of weakness is audited at soul-taking. Where the sūrah earlier absolved those with valid excuse who stay behind from striving (4:95), here it condemns those whose excuse was a wide earth left unused.

**A Verse That Turns Geography Into Moral Responsibility**

Placed after ranks and mercy for strivers (4:96), this verse turns geography into responsibility. The sūrah that began with a single soul spread across lands (4:1), that promised earth spacious for emigration (4:100), and that taught that good and evil are both destined while evil from the self as means (4:79), here makes the earth’s width the measure of the excuse. To wrong oneself by remaining where the oppressed cry for a helper (4:75) when the earth is wide is not weakness but choice hidden as weakness. The angels’ question — *fī ma kuntum* — and the reply — was not God’s earth spacious — will be heard again where the community is asked why it does not fight for the oppressed; the answer in both is movement. For the weak for whom the sūrah lightens, the next verses lighten further: the helpless who truly cannot afford a way are excepted, and it is right to hope God will pardon them (4:98–99), while the one who does emigrate finds refuge and abundance and, if death overtakes him on the way, his reward secured with God, the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:100).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:98

> Except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out—

**Expanded Commentary**

**Except the Helpless — Al-Mustaḍʿafīn**

The exception *illā al-mustaḍʿafīna mina al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildāni* — except helpless men, women, and children — qualifies the verdict that those who remained claiming oppression while earth is wide will have Hell as home (4:97). *Mustaḍʿaf* — deemed weak, reckoned oppressed, held down — was explained not as moral weakness but as lack of means: those judged weak by circumstance, not those who chose weakness where a way existed. The sūrah has used the same root where the oppressed men, women, and children cry for a saviour (4:75); there the cry was a reason to fight for them, here the same class is a reason to excuse them. To name *men, women, and children* was read as comprehensive: not only fighting men are assessed, but women and children whose movement depends on others and whose legal capacity the sūrah has guarded throughout — in dowry (4:4), in inheritance (4:7–11), in marriage limits (4:3), and in the command to return trusts and judge fairly (4:58). Where 4:97 counted those who wronged themselves by staying when they could leave, this verse counts those who are truly *mustaḍʿaf* and therefore did not wrong themselves by staying because staying was not chosen.

**Who Cannot Afford a Way Out**

The definition *lā yastaṭīʿūna ḥīlatan wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* — who cannot afford a way out, cannot manage stratagem, and cannot find a way — was explained as inability at both ends: no means to move and no knowledge to move. *Ḥīlah* — stratagem, device, means, resource — was read as affordability: provision for journey, mount, guide, refuge at the other end — the same abundance that the emigrant is promised will be found spacious upon His earth (4:100). *Wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* — nor find a way, nor are guided to a path — was explained as not knowing the road, the pass, the contact among believers, the treaty people to join (4:90). The double negation was stressed: neither resource to scheme a departure nor guidance to a road. The sūrah has said that God wills to lighten burdens because humanity was created weak (4:28) and that burdens were eased for the one who cannot afford to marry a free woman (4:25); here the same lightening appears as exemption from the threat of Hell as refuge. Early reports illustrated it with persons in Makkah — the aged, the nursing, the blind — who could not walk or did not know the desert tracks to Madinah, even while they wished to be with the believers. Their inability was not claimed oppression but real lack of *ḥīlah* and *sabīl*.

**A Verse That Holds Two Judgments Together**

The brevity — *“except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out”* (4:98) — was read as the sūrah’s balance between two judgments that might otherwise collide. The first judgment is mobility as duty where the earth is wide: *“Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?”* (4:97). The second is mercy that does not burden beyond capacity: *“God wishes to lighten”* (4:28), *“do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful”* (4:29), *“if you avoid major sins We absolve lesser”* (4:31). To hold both, the sūrah inserts this exception between threat and hope: the threat remains for those who could find *ḥīlah* and *sabīl* and did not, while the hope remains for those who truly could not. The construction also mirrors the earlier distinction between those who stay with valid excuse — *ulū al-ḍarar* — who are promised *ḥusnā* though not equal to strivers (4:95), and those who stay claiming oppression when excuse is absent. Here the women and children are named explicitly because the sūrah earlier quadrupled the weight of infant and female weakness in inheritance and dowry law; their explicit exemption shows that the law that guards the weak also excuses them.

**The Trap That Holds the Sentence Open**

Grammatically the verse is a dependent clause — *except helpless… who cannot…* — whose main clause is the next: *“it is right to hope God will pardon them”* (4:99). The suspension was explained as deliberate: the exception is not left as praise but as the condition for a hoped pardon, keeping both divine threat and divine mercy in place. The sūrah has sealed pardon where error was by mistake with *tawbatan mina Allāhi* (4:92) and strivers’ wages with forgiveness and mercy (4:96); here the pardon for the helpless is left as hope — *ʿasā* — so that neither presumption nor despair settles. Classical commentators noted the inclusion of children — whose accountability is not that of adults — shows that the exception describes a class of persons left behind whose journey depends on guardians; their inclusion underscores that emigration is a household, not only a warrior’s, obligation where household can move. The verse therefore draws a line the divided community (4:88) needed: not every remaining is a hypocrite who wishes you alike in disbelief, and not every claim of *“we were oppressed”* is accepted at soul-taking; only those who cannot afford device and cannot find a way are excepted from the evil destination.

**A Light Verse That Makes the Next Mercy Intelligible**

Though a fragment — five words in Arabic besides the categories — the verse makes the next mercy intelligible. Without it, *“it is right to hope God will pardon them”* (4:99) would have no subject; with it, the hope has precisely these — men, women, children without *ḥīlah* or *sabīl*. The sūrah’s ethic — return trusts, judge fairly, verify reports (4:58, 4:83), be sure before fighting (4:94), and do not confuse permission over hostility with permission over believers (4:92–93) — is here extended to the judgment of the remaining: verify inability, then except. For the weak the sūrah lightens, this is the lightest of sentences: where you truly could not afford device and could not find a way, the evil destination does not attach, and the next verse will place your case under hoped pardon from the Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving . The verse after that will show the opposite face: the one who could find device and way and did emigrate finds many refuges and, if death meets him on the way, his reward secured with the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:100).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:99

> it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them. For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, AllForgiving.

**Expanded Commentary**

**It Is Right to Hope That God Will Pardon Them**

The verse states *fa ulāʾika ʿasā Allāhu an yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — for those, it is right to hope, perhaps, maybe, that God will pardon them, will efface their sin. *ʿAsā* — to hope, to be expected, perhaps — was explained with attention because it follows an exception for the truly helpless (4:98) after a threat of Hell for those who wronged themselves while earth was wide (4:97). When *ʿasā* is from God about Himself, commentators said it carries certainty — His hope is not doubt but a gracious promise phrased as hope to keep both fear and longing alive. The sūrah has sealed other pardons with certainty: *“if you avoid major sins We absolve”* (4:31), *“whoever does evil then seeks forgiveness will find God All-Forgiving”* (4:110), and the striver’s forgiveness as ranks (4:96). Here the phrasing is softer, as befits the helpless whose case is known to God and who remain under His mercy. *Yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — to pardon them, to wipe away, to efface — was read as *ʿafw* — effacement, removal of trace — distinct from *maghfirah* — covering; *ʿafw* removes the record as if it were not written, while *maghfirah* covers it from consequence. The pronoun *ulāʾika* — those — refers precisely to the men, women, and children who cannot manage stratagem nor find a way (4:98), not to those who could and did not emigrate.

**For God Is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿafuwwan ghafūrā* — For God is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving, ever effacing, ever covering — was explained as the suitability of the names to the case. *ʿAfuww* — Ever-Pardoning, much effacing — recurs where an error might be held: where approaching prayer in impurity is taught (4:43) it is sealed *ʿafuwwun ghafūr*, and here where helplessness might still be judged as shortcoming. *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving — adds covering beyond effacement. The sūrah has paired *Ghafūr Raḥīm* for strivers (4:96) and for error requiring fasting (4:92); here the pair is *ʿAfuww Ghafūr*, emphasising that pardon for the helpless is not merely not punishing but wiping the sin of staying. The addition *kāna* — was, is ever — was read as timeless attribute: He was ever Pardoning before they were helpless, and remains so. The two names together show that the hope — *ʿasā* — rests not on the helplessness itself as merit, but on the Pardoner whose nature is to pardon. Classical notes added that the sequence *mustaḍʿafīn* (4:98) → *ʿasā yaʿfuwa* (4:99) → spacious earth for emigrant (4:100) teaches conduct: the helpless hope, the able move, and the Pardoner covers both according to what was possible.

**A Verse That Keeps Fear and Hope Together**

Placed between the evil destination for those who wronged themselves while able (4:97) and the spacious earth promised to the emigrant (4:100), this verse keeps fear and hope together without confusing them. It does not declare the helpless forgiven as a flat verdict, lest staying become light; it does not leave them under threat, lest mercy be despaired. The phrasing *ʿasā* was understood to move the heart to keep seeking means — *ḥīlah* and *sabīl* — even while hoping, and to keep the community fighting for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75) rather than abandoning the helpless to their excuse. The sūrah elsewhere says *“God wills to lighten burdens, humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and *“God does not wrong even an atom”* (4:40); hope for pardon here is that lightening applied to geography — where earth is wide yet unreachable for these, pardon is hoped wide as well. The sūrah has also shown that doing what was advised would have been better and would have brought great reward (4:66–67): for the able that advice was emigration, for the helpless the advice is to remain under hope and to seek means where means appear.

**The Helpless Whose Pardon Is Hoped — Not Declared Indifferent**

The verse was read to define its subject precisely so that no able person borrows it. The helpless are men, women, and children who cannot afford device nor find a way (4:98) — the aged who cannot ride, the mother who cannot walk with infants, the blind who cannot see the pass, the one who does not know a contact among treaty people (4:90) to secure passage. Their helplessness is double — no *ḥīlah* to devise and no *sabīl* to follow — and it is real, not claimed. For them *ʿasā* is not uncertainty in God but the Book’s pedagogy: the believer is taught to hope and to keep purifying intention, while the verdict is left to the Ever-Pardoning. The sūrah has warned against taking disbelievers as allies for honour (4:139) and against envying God’s bounties (4:54); the helpless who remain are not those allies nor envious; they are those left behind whom the community must still remember. The next verse will set the other face: whoever does find device and way and emigrates finds many refuges and abundance, and if death meets him on the way his reward is secured, for the same God who is Ever-Pardoning here is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful there (4:100).

**A Short Verse That Anchors the Sūrah’s Mercy in Geography**

Though only *“it is right to hope God will pardon them, for God is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving,”* the verse anchors mercy in geography. The sūrah that began from a single soul spread across earth (4:1), that asks *“was not God’s earth spacious enough?”* (4:97), and that promises spaciousness to the emigrant (4:100), here says that where earth’s spaciousness could not be reached, pardon’s spaciousness is hoped. The law that counts the sitting excused as promised *ḥusnā* though not equal to strivers (4:95), that counts the mistaken killer as expiating by freeing or fasting (4:92), here counts the truly helpless as under hoped effacement. For the weak this is the lightest sentence: not a burden added, but a hope placed — that the One whose earth was not yet reachable will, being Ever-Pardoning, efface the sin of not reaching it.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:100

> Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth. Those who leave their homes and die while emigrating to Allah and His Messenger—their reward has already been secured with Allah. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Whoever Emigrates Finds Many Refuges and Abundance**

The verse opens *wa man yuhājir fī sabīli Allāhi yajid fī al-arḍi murāghaman kathīran wa saʿah* — whoever emigrates in the cause of God will find in the earth many safe havens and bountiful resources, spaciousness. *Murāgham* — safe haven, place of turning away from hostility, ploy against the oppressor’s nose in the dust (*raghama anfuh*) — was explained as a refuge where the emigrant can live openly, as Madinah became for those leaving Makkah, and as Abyssinia briefly was, and as any land where belief can be practiced. *Saʿah* — spaciousness, abundance, ample provision — was read as breadth of earth and of rizq, the same spaciousness the angels cited — *was not God’s earth spacious enough?* (4:97) — now answered as found. The promise *yajid* — will find — was explained as certainty for the one who moves: the earth that was asked about as question becomes answer as discovery. The sūrah has shown that the oppressed cry for a deliverer from the land of oppressors (4:75) and that the helpless who cannot find *ḥīlah* or *sabīl* are hoped to be pardoned (4:98–99); here the one who can find device and way and uses them finds not desert but refuge and abundance. The verse generalises emigration beyond the historical Hijrah from Makkah: the Hijrah to Madinah after its conquest was declared ended — *lā hijrata baʿda al-fatḥ* (Bukhārī 3080; Muslim 1353) — yet the broader hijrah — abandoning what God forbade, *al-muhājir man hajara mā nahā Allāhu ʿanhu* (Bukhārī 10) — remains, and for it the promise of many havens still holds wherever a land permits God’s worship.

**Those Who Leave Homes and Die — Reward Secured**

The second clause *wa man yakhruj min baytihī muhājiran ilā Allāhi wa rasūlihī thumma yudrikhu al-mawtu fa qad waqaʿa ajruhū ʿalā Allāhi* — those who leave their homes emigrating to God and Messenger, then death overtakes them, their reward has already fallen upon, been secured with God — was explained as the sūrah’s assurance that intention and movement complete the wage even before arrival. *Yakhruj min baytihī* — leaving home — echoes the earlier hypothetical — *“had We commanded them to sacrifice selves or abandon homes few would have done so”* (4:66) — now shown as praised where done for God. *Muhājiran ilā Allāhi wa rasūlihī* — emigrating to God and Messenger — was read as the intention that distinguishes hijrah from mere travel; the same distinction the Prophet ﷺ drew: *“actions are by intentions, and the emigrant’s reward is according to what he emigrated for”* (Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907). *Thumma yudrikhu al-mawtu* — then death overtakes — was explained as dying on the way before refuge is enjoyed; *fa qad waqaʿa ajruhū ʿalā Allāhi* — his reward has fallen upon God, is secured — was read as a completed right upon divine generosity, not upon a treasury. Early reports attached the verse to a man — named as Damrah ibn Jundab or similar — who left Makkah for Madinah while ill, died at Tanʿīm, and was feared to have lost reward, upon which this assurance came. The legal point drawn was that the reward is secured at departure with right intention, not at arrival, which is why those who die after leaving are not counted among those who wronged themselves by staying (4:97).

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — And God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained as the suitability to both clauses: forgiving the emigrant’s past sins in the land left, faults in the manner of leaving, and the incompleteness of a journey cut by death; merciful in giving many havens where one was expected and in securing reward where death intervened. The same pair sealed the pardon hoped for the helpless (4:99) with *ʿAfuww Ghafūr*, and the striver’s ranks (4:96) with *Ghafūr Raḥīm*; here again *Ghafūr Raḥīm* covers both Movement and mortality. The sūrah has said *“God does not wrong even an atom, and if it is good He multiplies”* (4:40) and *“had they done what they were advised it would have been better and would have brought great reward”* (4:66–67); emigration is that advice made spatial, and the multiplication is many havens and secured wage even when death cuts short. The pairing also shows that emigration is not presented as heroic autonomy but as forgiveness and mercy received: the emigrant does not earn spaciousness by might; He finds it because the Ever-Forgiving opens it.

**A Verse That Answers the Angels’ Question With Geography and Grace**

Placed after the angels’ *“was not God’s earth spacious enough?”* (4:97), the exception for the helpless (4:98), and the hope for pardon (4:99), this verse answers the question with geography and grace. To those able to devise and find a way, the answer is *yajid* — you will find — many havens and abundance; to those whose way was cut by death, the answer is *waqaʿa ajruhū* — reward secured. The sūrah that opened from a single soul spread across earth (4:1) and that said God wills to make clear, to guide to noble ways, and to turn in mercy (4:26–27), now makes clear that the earth’s width is not an abstraction but a set of actual refuges where prayer can be shortened without fear (4:101) and where the burdens lightened for the weak (4:28) are lightened further by place. The ethic extends beyond place to intention: the emigrant to God and Messenger is secured even without arrival, as the martyr is secure even without victory — *whether they achieve martyrdom or victory We honour with great reward* (4:74). For the community commanded to go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to be sure before fighting (4:94), the verse lightens departure: you will find refuge and abundance, and if death finds you first, your wage has already fallen upon the One who never wrongs.

**The Hijrah That Remains**

Though revealed about the Hijrah from the land of oppressors, the verse was read as remaining principle: wherever a land makes faith unlivable and another makes it livable, the instruction to find *murāgham* holds. The Prophet’s declaration after the Conquest (8 AH) that no further Hijrah from Makkah as emigration from unbelief’s abode was required (Bukhārī 3080) did not close the wider meaning: the emigrant is one who abandons what God forbade, and such abandonment still finds many havens. The verse therefore holds geography and morality together: to leave a place where the self is wronged for a place where the self can obey is not flight from God’s decree — both good and evil are destined (4:78) — but the means by which the evil that is from the self is refused. The next passage will apply the same spaciousness to prayer itself, permitting its shortening when travel brings fear of attack from those who are your sworn enemies (4:101).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:101

> When you travel through the land, it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer—˹especially˺ if you fear an attack by the disbelievers. Indeed, the disbelievers are your sworn enemies.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When You Travel — Permission to Shorten the Prayer**

The verse opens *wa idhā ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi fa laysa ʿalaykum junāḥun an taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāti* — when you strike through the land, travel through earth, there is no blame, no sin upon you to shorten the prayer, to curtail it. *Ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi* — striking through land — was explained as journeying, the same phrase used for struggling in God’s cause (4:94) and now widened to any travel, as the sūrah has just promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) and wide earth to those asked at soul-taking (4:97). *Fa laysa ʿalaykum junāḥ* — no blame — was read as permission, not sin, to shorten; the sūrah has used *junāḥ* for law’s ease where dowry is adjusted by mutual consent (4:24), where a wife fears indifference and settlement is sought (4:128), and where no sin attaches. *An taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāti* — to shorten from the prayer — was explained as the four-rakʿah prayers — Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, ʿIshāʾ — shortened to two, while Maghrib and Fajr remain. The practice was shown by the Prophet ﷺ on travel before fear was present, establishing that the permission is general, as ʿUmar asked why shorten when now safe and the Prophet ﷺ replied: *“it is charity that God has given you, accept His charity”* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 686). The sūrah that wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28), that taught purification with earth where water lacks (4:43), now lightens prayer itself within spacious earth.

**Especially If You Fear an Attack by the Disbelievers**

The condition *in khiftum an yaftinakumu alladhīna kafarū* — if you fear that those who disbelieve may attack you, may tempt you, may put you to trial — was explained as fear of *fitnah* during travel, where the hostile who do not offer peace may assault the worshippers. *Yaftinakum* — to put to trial, to attack, to seduce from worship — matches *fitnah* as strife and hostility (2:191–93) and as the temptation to which the double-faced are plunged whenever returned (4:91). The phrase *“especially if you fear”* in translation was read to mark the occasion that occasions the permission most clearly, not to limit it to danger alone; the Prophet’s shortening even without enemy present shows the condition is illustrative, as travel itself brings *fitnah* of hardship, exposure, and the need for vigilance. The sūrah has described the oppressed who cry for a helper from the land of oppressors (4:75) and the permission to seize the hostile who refuse peace (4:89–91); shortened prayer is the worship that fits that terrain where worshippers must remain armed and vigilant, as the next verse will detail with ranks of prayer while armed (4:102). The condition also teaches that fear does not cancel prayer but reshapes it, as remembrance remains standing, sitting, lying down when prayers are finished (4:103).

**Indeed the Disbelievers Are Your Sworn Enemies**

The seal *inna al-kāfirīna kānū lakum ʿaduwwan mubīnā* — indeed the disbelievers are — were — your clear, sworn enemies, manifest foes — was explained as reason for the permission and for the caution that follows. *ʿAduww mubīn* — clear enemy — was read as open hostility, not hidden envy only; the sūrah has said God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and here the clarity of enmity is declared so that the traveller does not treat the hostile as neutral. *Kānū* — they were — was read as timeless trait of that hostility where disbelief hardens into fighting, as the Devil’s schemes are weak yet still must be curbed (4:76) and as Satan is the accursed enemy who said he will mislead (4:118–19). The manifest enmity does not contradict the exception for treaty and for the constricted who offer peace (4:90); it defines the default of the hostile collective where no treaty or peace holds. For the weak for whom burdens are lightened, the declaration is a protection: to shorten prayer when traveling is not laxity but realism about a clear foe, and to keep guard while praying (4:102) is not suspicion but obedience to the notice that enmity is manifest.

**A Verse That Lightens Worship for the Road**

Placed after many havens for the emigrant (4:100), this verse lightens worship for the road that leads to them. The sūrah that opened from a single soul, that commanded prayer at appointed times (4:103), that allowed earth for purification when water lacked (4:43), here allows prayer curtailed when earth is struck through. The Prophet’s regular shortening, and the companions’ agreement that even without fear the shortening stands, were read as the sūrah’s principle that God’s earth is spacious and His law is spacious within it. The permission was also linked to the wider ease where fasting by mistake can be consecutive months (4:92) and where settlement between spouses bears no sin (4:128): *lā junāḥ* is the sūrah’s lightest law-terminology, removing blame where burden would crush. The traveller who shortens is therefore not cutting prayer but receiving charity — *ṣadaqah* — from God, whose charity the weak are told to accept.

**Prayer Shortened Without Prayer Lost**

The verse was read to keep two truths together: prayer is shortened, prayer is not abandoned. The sūrah will say when prayers are over, remember God standing, sitting, lying down, and when secure, establish regular prayers, for prayer is a duty at appointed times (4:103). The shortening is within the duty, not instead of it, as the next verse’s armed prayer will show: one group prays while armed, prostrates, then the other prays while the first guards (4:102). The declaration that disbelievers are your clear enemies explains why that choreography is needed, and why mercy in worship — to shorten, to guard — is itself worship. The verse generalises emigration’s spaciousness into law: the earth is wide, the prayer travels with you shorter where the road makes long standing a burden, and the enemy’s clarity does not cancel the prayer but gives its travel form.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:102

> When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer, let one group of them pray with you—while armed. When they prostrate themselves, let the other group stand guard behind them. Then the group that has not yet prayed will then join you in prayer—and let them be vigilant and armed. The disbelievers would wish to see you neglect your weapons and belongings, so they could launch a sweeping assault on you. But there is no blame if you lay aside your weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness—but take precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When You Are With Them and Lead Them in Prayer**

The verse opens *wa idhā kunta fīhim fa aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāta fa l-taqum ṭāʾifatun minhum maʿaka wa l-yākhudhū asliḥatahum* — when you, O Prophet, are among them and you establish prayer for them, let one group stand with you while armed and let them take weapons. *Kunta fīhim* — you being among them, campaigning with them — was explained as the Prophet ﷺ present on expedition, leading the force that earlier was told to go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to be sure before fighting (4:94). *Fa aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāta* — you establish prayer for them — was read as the prayer whose shortening was just permitted for travel (4:101), now given its battle form: the *ṣalāt al-khawf*, prayer of fear. *Ṭāʾifah* — group, party — was explained as a portion of the force dividing into two: one prays with the Imam while armed, the other faces the enemy. *Wa l-yākhudhū asliḥatahum* — let them take weapons — was stressed: even in prayer the sword is not laid aside, because disbelievers are your clear enemies (4:101) and would wish to see weapons neglected. The sūrah that promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) now shows prayer itself finding haven in ranks while still armed.

**When They Prostrate Let the Other Stand Guard**

The instruction *fa idhā sajadū fa l-yakūnū min warāʾikum wa l-taʾti ṭāʾifatun ukhrā lam yuṣallū fa l-yuṣallū maʿaka wa l-yākhudhū ḥidhrahum wa asliḥatahum* — when they prostrate, let the other group be behind you; then the group that has not prayed comes to pray with you, taking vigilance and weapons — was explained as the two-rakʿah exchange in several authentic forms (Bukhārī 413, Muslim 842 for the fear prayer). The first group prays one rakʿah with the Imam, then moves to guard; the second completes with him. *Sajadū* — they prostrated — marks the portion of prayer most exposed, where the worshipper is lowest and least able to see. *Min warāʾikum* — behind you — was read as facing the enemy, guarding the praying rank’s back. *Ḥidhrahum* — vigilance, precaution, guard — was read as alertness distinct from weapons: weapons without vigilance are still neglect. The choreography teaches that prayer is not abandoned before fear, nor fear ignored before prayer; both duties are kept by dividing the body so that worship and warfare each have eyes. The sūrah has said remembrance continues standing, sitting, lying down when prayers are finished (4:103); this arrangement shows the prayer itself contains remembrance while armed.

**They Wish to See You Neglect Weapons and Belongings**

The motive *wadda alladhīna kafarū law taghfulūna ʿan asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum fa yamīlūna ʿalaykum maylatan wāḥidatan* — the disbelievers would wish you neglect, be heedless of weapons and belongings, so they could sweep, assault upon you in one sweep — was explained as the enemy’s wish for a single heedless moment. *Waddū* — they wish — matches the regressed who wish you disbelieve as they have (4:89) and those who wish you deviate greatly (4:27); here the wish is tactical: that you be *ghāfil* — heedless. *Asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum* — weapons and belongings, goods — was read as the two vulnerabilities of a travelling force: arms and baggage. *Maylatan wāḥidah* — one sweeping assault, one inclination — was explained as a single rush while heads are bowed. The warning makes the prior armed prayer intelligible: the Devil’s schemes are weak (4:76) yet the human enemy remains a clear foe (4:101) who watches for neglect. The sūrah has shown that those given a portion wish to trade guidance and make you deviate (4:44); here the wish is more concrete — to find you without sword and without guard on the brow of prayer.

**No Blame to Lay Aside Weapons in Rain or Illness — But Take Precaution**

The ease *wa lā junāḥa ʿalaykum in kāna bikum adhan min maṭarin aw kuntum marḍā an taḍaʿū asliḥatakum wa khudhū ḥidhrakum* — no blame if you lay aside weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness, but take precaution — was explained as the law’s lightening where rain soaks and weight exhausts or wounds prevent bearing. *Adhan min maṭar* — harm from rain — was read as heavy, cold rain that makes holding arms a hardship, as *ḥaraj* — constriction — in religion was removed where ablution with earth replaces water (4:43). *Marḍā* — ill — matches the travel and illness allowances that eased purification; here it eases carrying. Yet *khudhū ḥidhrakum* — take precaution — remains even when weapons are laid aside: vigilance is not laid aside. The pairing shows the sūrah’s method: God wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28) yet does not lighten to heedlessness. Where the sūrah elsewhere says *lā junāḥ* for settlement where a wife fears indifference (4:128) and for shortening prayer (4:101), here *lā junāḥ* permits laying arms aside without permitting neglect. The close *inna Allāha aʿadda li al-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnā* — God has prepared a humiliating punishment for disbelievers — was read as assurance that the guarded prayer is not mere survival; the outcome is His preparation where humiliation corresponds to the humiliation of the weak they would have inflicted.

**A Verse That Keeps Prayer and Guard as One Worship**

Placed after permission to shorten prayer for travel (4:101), this verse gives that shortened prayer its battlefield body. The sūrah that commands firmness in pursuit of the enemy — if you suffer they suffer, yet you hope from God what they do not (4:104) —, that warns not to be an advocate for the deceitful (4:105), here shows the Prophet ﷺ leading prayer in ranks where one prays and one guards, weapons and vigilance together. The lesson for the weak for whom the sūrah lightens burdens is not laxity but measured precaution: prayer may be shortened, weapons may be laid aside in rain or illness, but precaution is not laid aside, because the clear enemy (4:101) wishes precisely neglect. The next verse will extend prayer beyond its formal time: when the rank disperses, remembrance remains standing, sitting, lying down, and when secure, regular prayers are established at appointed times (4:103).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:103

> When the prayers are over, remember Allah—whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down. But when you are secure, establish regular prayers. Indeed, performing prayers is a duty on the believers at the appointed times.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When the Prayers Are Over — Remember Standing, Sitting, Lying**

The verse states *fa idhā qaḍaytumu al-ṣalāta fa adhkurū Allāha qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — when you have finished, completed the prayer — the fear prayer just described (4:102) — then remember God standing, sitting, lying on sides. *Qaḍaytum* — completed, fulfilled, finished — was explained as ending the formal prayer with its bows and prostrations, the shortened travel form (4:101) and its guarded ranking. *Fa adhkurū* — then remember, mention, invoke — was read as keeping remembrance after the guarded rank disperses, so that prayer does not end as awareness. *Qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — standing, sitting, upon sides — was explained as all postures, the same triad used where those given understanding remember God in all states and reflect (3:191). The sūrah has shown that even in the fear prayer one group stands guard while the other prostrates (4:102) and that vigilance remains even when weapons are laid aside in rain or illness; remembrance in all postures is the inward counterpart to that outward vigilance. The verse was also linked to the emigrant’s many havens (4:100): whether moving standing, resting sitting, or fallen on sides from wound, the remembrance accompanies.

**But When You Are Secure — Establish Regular Prayers**

The clause *fa idhā aṭmaʾnantum fa aqīmū al-ṣalāta* — but when you are secure, tranquil, established, then establish the prayer — was explained as returning to full prayer when fear lifts and place is secure. *Aṭmaʾnantum* — you are secure, at rest, hearts at rest — matches the security opposite the fear that shortened prayer (4:101) and that required the guarded rank (4:102). To *aqīmū al-ṣalāta* — establish prayer — after having shortened it on travel is to return to its complete, timed form: four rakʿahs restored, boundaries kept, congregation reformed. The sūrah has used *iqāmah* throughout for prayer established at its time, after purification with earth where water lacked (4:43), and as witness before God (4:41). The shift from shortened to established was read as the law’s responsiveness: prayer’s form follows security, not the other way. Where the emigrant found many havens and abundance (4:100), security is the haven for prayer itself, allowing it to stand at its full height. The instruction shows that the traveller’s shortened prayer is not lesser worship but worship fitted to insecurity; when insecurity leaves, the form returns without needing new command beyond *aqīmū*.

**Prayer Is a Duty at Appointed Times**

The seal *inna al-ṣalāta kānat ʿalā al-muʾminīna kitāban mawqūtā* — indeed performing prayers is a duty, a decree, a writ upon the believers at fixed, appointed times — was explained as the sūrah’s anchoring of all else in time. *Kitāban* — writ, decree, obligation inscribed — was read as a firm obligation, as inheritance shares are *farīḍah mina Allāh* (4:11) and as testament is a writ. *Mawqūtā* — timed, appointed — was explained as fixed moments — *mawāqīt* — that do not move with convenience, whose establishment the sūrah has required. The phrase was linked to *ḥāfiẓū ʿalā al-ṣalawāt* — guard the prayers (2:238) — and to the Prophet’s teaching that the prayer has appointed openings and closings. The sūrah has said that the good deed is multiplied (4:40) and that striving is given ranks, forgiveness, and mercy (4:96); here the daily multiplication — five writs at their times — is the steady practice that makes striving and guarded prayer possible. The appointed time also explains why shortening is permission and remembrance is extension: the writ’s time does not depart; its form adapts while its time holds.

**A Verse That Binds Guarded Prayer to Constant Remembrance**

Placed after the choreography of prayer under arms (4:102), this verse binds that choreography to constant remembrance and to regular establishment when secure. The sūrah that warned the enemy wishes you neglect weapons and belongings for one sweeping assault (4:102) counters that neglect with remembrance in every posture, so that no posture is without guard. The sūrah that declared God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian (4:45) then said disbelievers are your clear enemies (4:101); remembrance is the inward reliance upon that Guardian while the guard is the outward means. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the sequence is a lightening: prayer shortened on travel, guarded under fear, remembered standing, sitting, lying, and established in security, always at its appointed writ, so that no state — fear, rain, illness, security — leaves the believer without prayer. The next verse will turn from prayer’s guard to pursuit’s steadiness: do not falter in seeking the enemy, if you suffer they suffer, and you hope from God what they never can (4:104).

**The Writ That Holds the Sūrah’s Discipline Together**

The final writ — *kitāban mawqūtā* — was read as the sūrah’s discipline. The chapter has commanded returning trusts and judging fairly (4:58), referring disputes to God and Messenger (4:59), verifying reports (4:83), being sure before fighting (4:94), and not confusing permission over hostility with permission over believers (4:92–93). Prayer at fixed time is the training that makes those commands possible: it punctuates the day with reference, divides travel and fear into measured intervals, and returns the community from the rank to the standing, sitting, lying remembrance. The verse therefore closes the passage on prayer that began with purification where water lacked (4:43) and will later meet the judgment passage where the Book was sent to judge by what He has shown (4:105): both begin with a writ — purity and time — that secures justice.

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:104

> Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy—if you are suffering, they too are suffering. But you can hope to receive from Allah what they can never hope for. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Do Not Falter in Pursuit of the Enemy**

The verse opens *wa lā tahinū fī ibtighāʾi al-qawmi* — do not falter, do not weaken, do not flag in seeking, pursuing, going after the people — the enemy. *Tahinū* — to be weak, to waver, to lose heart — was explained as slackening after the strain of travel, fear prayer, and guarded worship just taught (4:101–103). *Ibtighāʾ* — seeking, pursuing — was read as following after, not merely defending where attacked but seeking the hostile that refuses peace (4:89–91) and that wishes you neglect for a sweep (4:102). The prohibition was understood as addressed to a community that had been told to go forth in groups or together (4:71), to fight for the oppressed who cry (4:75), and whose struggles had included Uḥud’s wound and the questioning *“why was fighting ordered now and not delayed a little?”* (4:77). To *not falter* was read as the sūrah’s steadiness: the same discipline that makes prayer a writ at fixed times (4:103) makes pursuit a writ where justice requires it. The sūrah elsewhere says *“do not be like those who left homes boastfully and hinder from God’s way”* (8:47), but here the command is internal: let not wound become weakness.

**If You Are Suffering, They Too Are Suffering**

The measure *in takūnū taʾlamūna fa innahum yaʾlamūna kamā taʾlamūna* — if you are suffering, feeling pain, they too are suffering as you suffer — was explained as the sūrah’s equalisation of pain. *Taʾlamūna* — you suffer, you feel hurt — was read as wounds, fatigue, hunger, fear — the same suffering the sūrah counted as shared: hunger and thirst are human weakness (4:28), and death overtakes even in fortified towers (4:78). To say they suffer as you do removes the illusion that the enemy’s side is without cost; the hostile who wish you to be as they are (4:89) and who plunge back into *fitnah* (4:91) also bear loss. The comparison was linked to *“if a wound touches you, a like wound touched the other people”* (3:140), revealed after Uḥud where both sides were wounded yet the believers faltered. The sūrah that taught that good and evil are both destined while evil from the self as means (4:78–79) here applies that symmetry to pain: pain is destined for both in conflict, but its meaning differs, as the next clause shows.

**But You Hope From God What They Never Can**

The distinction *wa tarjūna mina Allāhi mā lā yarjūn* — but you can hope to receive from God what they can never hope for — was explained as the sūrah’s asymmetry of hope. *Tarjūn* — you hope, expect, await — was read as hope for ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him (4:96), for many havens and secured reward even if death overtakes on hijrah (4:100), for the humiliating punishment prepared for disbelievers where you guarded prayer (4:102), and for the Gardens where the prayer writ is kept (4:103). That hope was explained as the believers’ exclusive because the disbeliever, by turning away from trust and referral to the Messenger (4:58–61), has no standing to expect it. The clause therefore does not deny the enemy’s pain but denies his hope, as the sūrah elsewhere says *“do not think those who disbelieve prolonging time is good; they increase in sin”* (3:178). The hope is not a claim of victory only; it is forgiveness for the mistaken, mercy for the helpless, and reward for the striver — all sealed *Ghafūr Raḥīm* (4:96, 4:100) or *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* (4:99). The sufferers on one side have a door that sufferers on the other do not: the same suffering, divergent destination.

**And God Is All-Knowing, All-Wise**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise — was read as the knowledge that weighs faltering and wisdom that times pursuit. *ʿAlīm* — All-Knowing — was explained as knowing who falters from wound and who from desire to deviate (4:27), who verifies before fighting (4:94) and who seeks fleeting gain by denying peace (4:94), whose earth is wide yet unreachable (4:98) and whose heart can still seek pardon. *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was read as wisdom that commands pursuit where the oppressed cry (4:75), permits shortening where travel and fear constrict (4:101–102), establishes prayer at fixed time (4:103), and will send the Book to judge by what He shows (4:105). The pair *ʿAlīm Ḥakīm* has sealed the law for mistake by fasting (4:92) and for judging between people; here it seals the ethic of pursuit: He knows pain and knows who bears it for hope and who bears it without hope, and He judges with the wisdom that does not command beyond weakness yet does not excuse faltering where hope is offered.

**A Verse That Turns Shared Pain Into Divergent Hope**

Placed after the law that guards prayer under arms (4:102) and the writ that prayer is at appointed times (4:103), this verse turns the shared fact of suffering into divergent hope. The sūrah that began from a single soul and commanded mindfulness of ties (4:1), that promised lightening because humanity is weak (4:28), here acknowledges weakness — you suffer — then refuses to let suffering become faltering where the enemy still refuses peace (4:89–91). The suffering is equal as wound, unequal as meaning, because one side’s suffering can be met with hope for ranks and mercy, the other’s cannot. For the weak this is steadying: to pursue the hostile who would sweep upon neglect (4:102) is not to deny pain but to place pain inside hope, as the sūrah’s later command to be firm for justice though against yourselves (4:135) will place justice inside pain. The next passage will turn from pursuit to judgment, where the Book was sent to judge between people by what He has shown and not to be an advocate for the deceitful (4:105).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:105

> Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth to judge between people by means of what Allah has shown you. So do not be an advocate for the deceitful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**We Have Sent Down the Book in Truth to Judge Between People**

The verse opens *innā anzalnā ilayka al-kitāba bi al-ḥaqqi li taḥkuma bayna al-nāsi bi mā arāka Allāhu* — Indeed We have sent down the Book to you in truth, with truth, to judge between people by what God has shown you, made you see. *Anzalnā* — We sent down — was read as divine descent, the Book given as the noble command from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58) and as the referral point where disputes are taken (4:59). *Bi al-ḥaqqi* — in truth, with truth, as truth — was explained as that the Book’s content is true and its descent is true and its judgment is true, against the false judges — *ṭāghūt* — sought by those who claim belief (4:60). *Li taḥkuma bayna al-nāsi* — to judge between people — was read as judging among humanity without faction — the same *bayna al-nāsi* as *“when you judge between people judge with fairness”* (4:58). *Bi mā arāka Allāhu* — by what God has shown you — was explained as by what He taught, inspired, made clear, not by outward claim alone; the sūrah has shown that God teaches what you did not know (4:113) and that He is the One who guides to noble ways (4:26). Early reports attached the verse to a theft dispute where a Muslim of the Banū Ẓafar was suspected, his armour hidden with a Jew, and pressure came to shield the Muslim — the verse forbade it, commanding judgment by what God shows, which settled on evidence, not tribal tie.

**So Do Not Be an Advocate for the Deceitful**

The prohibition *wa lā takun li al-khāʾinīna khaṣīmā* — so do not be an advocate, disputant, defender for the deceitful, the treacherous — was explained as *khāʾin* — one who betrays trust — the same *khāʾin* as those who betray trusts the sūrah commands to return (4:58) and as those who betray themselves (4:107). *Khaṣīm* — disputant, advocate, pleader — was read as standing in argument for them, contesting on their side; the sūrah will repeat *“do not advocate for those who wrong themselves”* (4:107) and *“you advocate for them in this life, who will advocate for them before God on Resurrection Day?”* (4:109). The command was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ directly, showing that even his advocacy is not for deceit, and through him to every judge and every believer: to be sure before fighting (4:94) is matched here by being sure before judging. The verse generalises emigration’s *murāgham* and spaciousness (4:100): just as earth is wide for the wronged to find haven, the law is wide for the truth to find voice, and it is narrowed when an advocate lends his tongue to deceit.

**A Verse That Makes Revelation the Criterion of Judgment**

The opening *bi al-ḥaqqi* and the condition *bi mā arāka Allāhu* were read together as the sūrah’s theory of judgment: the Book in truth, applied by what God shows. That showing was explained as knowledge given — scripture, sunna, evidence, insight — not as personal desire; the sūrah has warned against following desires that wish you deviate greatly (4:27) and against seeking judgment of false judges (4:60). To judge by what God shows was linked to the Prophet’s reported clarification: *“I am but a human, and you bring disputes to me, and some may be more eloquent, so if I give one his brother’s right by his eloquence, it is a piece of fire”* (Bukhārī 2680; Muslim 1713). The verse therefore makes procedure — evidence, oaths, witnesses as in orphan property (4:6), and referral to God and Messenger (4:59) — the means by which *arāka* is actualised. The sūrah’s promise that if a dispute is referred to God and Messenger it is best and fairest (4:59) is here instantiated as Book judging between people, not clan judging between its own.

**Deceit Is Not a Minor Fault — It Is the Partnership the Sūrah Has Warned Against**

The term *khāʾinīn* — deceitful, treacherous — was read as weighty: those who hide deception from people but cannot hide from God in whose presence they plot by night what He displeases (4:108). The sūrah has shown deceit’s kin: lagging behind with two faces (4:72–73), double safety while plunging into *fitnah* (4:91), denying peace for fleeting gain (4:94), and spending to show off without belief (4:38). To be an advocate for the deceitful was explained as joining that partnership, taking deceit as associate — and whoever takes Satan as associate, what an evil associate (4:38). The sūrah will say God does not like the deceitful, sinful (4:107) and that there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114); advocacy for deceit falls outside that good. The Prophet ﷺ was therefore told not to be *khaṣīm* for them, just as earlier he was told to turn away from hypocrites who turn away stubbornly (4:63) and to put trust in God as Trustee (4:81).

**A Judging Verse Placed After Prayer and Pursuit**

Placed after pursuit without faltering where both sides suffer yet only the believer hopes (4:104), this verse assigns the judge his hope’s discipline: the same hope that steadies pursuit — hoping from God what the enemy does not — steadies judgment — judging by what God shows rather than by clan. The sūrah that began from a single soul (4:1), that promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100), that shortened and guarded prayer (4:101–102) and fixed it at appointed writ (4:103), now places the Book as the haven for disputes, where a people bound by treaty are paid blood-money even if mistakenly killed (4:92, 4:90) because the *mīthāq* is part of what God shows. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is a shield: where power tempts to be advocate for the deceitful, the Book in truth is the advocate for the deceitful’s victim, showing the judge what to see. The next verses will unfold that prohibition: seek forgiveness (4:106) and do not advocate for those who wrong themselves (4:107), for they hide from people what they cannot hide from God (4:108).

---
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:106

> And seek Allah’s forgiveness—indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**And Seek God’s Forgiveness**

The verse states *wa astaghfiri Allāha* — and seek God’s forgiveness, ask Him to forgive, to cover and efface. *Istaghfara* — to seek *maghfirah* — was explained as requesting covering of fault and wiping of trace, as the sūrah has shown that even religious error before prayer is covered by purification with earth where water lacks (4:43) and that mistaken killing is covered by freeing or consecutive fasting as repentance (4:92). The command was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ directly after *“do not be an advocate for the deceitful”* (4:105), showing that even the thought of inclining to defend the deceitful, or the distress of having nearly done so, calls for seeking forgiveness. Through him the command reaches every judge and every believer: where judgment was to be by what God shows (4:105) and not by clan, the fear of having favoured tie over truth requires seeking cover.
